Rubidium-87 EIT & light storage at 795 nm

Rubidium-87 EIT & light storage at 795 nm A study guide and interactive optical bench for building a room-temperature atomic reference platform for EIT and quantum-memory work. It explains Zeeman Λ-EIT from first principles, lays out the chosen one-laser, two-AOM architecture (“Zeeman EIT”), and lets you assemble and test that bench in 3D. The problem

The problem The wider programme aims to test new room-temperature solid-state quantum-memory materials: P3HT microcavities and α-MoO₃ single-photon emitters. The project’s premise is that you cannot meaningfully test an unproven material on an uncalibrated bench. If storage fails, you would not know whether the material or the optics was at fault. So the project first builds a calibrated atomic reference: a warm ⁸⁷Rb vapour cell in which electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) and light storage are well understood and reproducible.

Objectives covered here

Objectives covered here Objective 1: construct a precise optical platform using a locked 795 nm laser and a Rubidium-87 cell. Objective 2: demonstrate EIT and light storage in the atomic rubidium platform. Next stage (outside this guide): Objective 3 replaces the Rb cell with P3HT microcavities and uses α-MoO₃ emitters as the probe source. Every alignment and calibration habit built here carries over.

Why an atomic reference platform

Why an atomic reference platform Every ⁸⁷Rb atom is identical, and the D1 line and ground-state splittings are known to many digits. That makes the atom a ruler, not a variable. Warm vapour needs no vacuum chamber or cooling, only a cell, a heater and magnetic shielding. EIT gives you three measurable handles (OD, ODEIT, γEIT). These are the same figures of merit you will later use to judge solid-state memories. Decision record The project uses Zeeman EIT: a Λ system on Zeeman sublevels, on the ⁸⁷Rb D1 line, with one DFB laser and two AOMs (one per arm, double-pass as reference configuration). This follows Fig. 10 of Finkelstein et al. (2022). The paper calls Zeeman EIT “the least resource-intensive” scheme, requiring only acousto-optic modulation of a single laser at a few tens of kHz. §04 compares the alternatives. Laser safety The 795 nm beam is near-infrared and invisible to the eye. In the drawings and simulator it is shown red. A 20–40 mW single-frequency diode laser (the power range the paper calls sufficient) is an eye hazard, especially from specular reflections off cube faces, waveplates and cell windows. Use IR-rated eyewear for 795 nm, keep beams at one height below eye level, terminate every stray beam (including PBS leakage and AOM zeroth orders) in a dump, remove watches and rings, and use an IR viewing card or camera to find beams. Never look along a beam. Follow your institution’s laser-safety rules and laser classification. Glossary

Glossary Every term used on this page. Type to filter, or pick a category. Longer explanations: Reading Section. Filter glossary EIT (electromagnetically induced transparency)theoryA strong control field makes an otherwise opaque atomic medium transparent for a weak probe in a narrow window around two-photon resonance. The cause is destructive quantum interference: atoms are steered into a dark state that cannot absorb. CPT (coherent population trapping)theoryThe same dark-state physics, usually with two fields of comparable strength. Atoms are “trapped” in a superposition near maximal coherence. CPT is the common term in clocks and magnetometers. EIT usually means a strong control and a weak probe. Dark state |D⟩theoryThe superposition (Ωp|2⟩ − Ωc|1⟩)/Ω of the two ground states, which has zero coupling to the excited state. Atoms in it do not absorb or fluoresce. Bright state |B⟩theoryThe orthogonal superposition (Ωp*|1⟩ + Ωc*|2⟩)/Ω, which is coupled to the excited state with effective Rabi frequency Ω. Λ (lambda) schemetheoryTwo long-lived lower states |1⟩, |2⟩ coupled to one excited state |3⟩ by probe and control. It is the most common EIT configuration because the coherence sits between ground states. Ladder (cascade) schemetheoryGround → intermediate → highly excited state (e.g. Rydberg). The two-photon coherence involves an excited state, so its decay limits the linewidth. Counter-propagating beams minimise Doppler broadening. V schemetheoryOne ground state coupled to two excited states. EIT is possible but offers little advantage for atoms (paper, ref. 17). Hyperfine structureatomSplitting of an electronic level by the coupling of electron angular momentum J and nuclear spin I into levels of total angular momentum F. For ⁸⁷Rb (I = 3/2) the 5S₁/₂ ground state has F = 1 and F = 2, about 6.835 GHz apart. Zeeman structureatomA magnetic field splits each F level into 2F+1 sublevels labelled mF. In weak fields the shift is gF μB mF B. mF (magnetic quantum number)atomProjection of F on the quantization axis, from −F to +F. Absorbing σ⁺ light changes mF by +1, σ⁻ by −1, π by 0. gF (hyperfine Landé factor)atomSets the Zeeman shift per mF per field. For ⁸⁷Rb 5S₁/₂: gF ≈ +1/2 for F=2 and ≈ −1/2 for F=1, i.e. about ±0.70 MHz/G = 0.70 kHz/mG per unit mF. Landé g-factoratomThe general factor relating a level’s magnetic moment to its angular momentum (gJ for the electron, gF for hyperfine levels). Quantization axisatomThe direction against which mF and σ/π polarizations are defined. In Zeeman EIT it is the solenoid field B along the beam direction z. D1 / D2 linesatomAlkali transitions from nS₁/₂ to nP₁/₂ (D1) and nP₃/₂ (D2). For Rb, D1 ≈ 795 nm and D2 ≈ 780 nm. D1 has fewer excited hyperfine levels, which gives cleaner Λ systems. Rabi frequency ΩtheoryStrength of the light–atom coupling, µE/ħ in the paper’s convention (Ωp = µ₁₃Ẽ₁/ħ). It scales with √intensity. One-photon detuning ΔtheoryLaser frequency minus atomic transition frequency for each field: Δi = νi − ωi3. Two-photon detuning δtheoryδ = Δ₁ − Δ₂ = ν₁ − ν₂ − ω₁₂: the mismatch between the probe–control frequency difference and the ground-state splitting. EIT is centred at δ = 0. Raman resonancetheoryA two-photon transition between the ground states. With large one-photon detuning it appears as a narrow absorption line shifted by |Ωc|²/Δ₁. Far-detuned Raman memories are an alternative to EIT memories. Optical pumpingatomUsing light plus spontaneous emission to move population into a particular state. In Zeeman EIT, the σ⁺ control pumps atoms toward the high-mF end of F=2 (mF=+1, +2 are dark to σ⁺ on F=2→F′=1). Susceptibility χtheoryThe medium’s linear response, P = ε₀χE. Im χ gives absorption and Re χ gives the refractive index (n ≈ 1 + Re χ/2 for a dilute gas; the paper writes n = 1 + Re χp). Kramers–Kronig relationstheoryCausality links absorption and dispersion. A narrow transparency window must be accompanied by a steep refractive-index slope, which is the origin of slow light. Group index ng / group velocity vgtheoryng = n + ν dn/dν and vg = c/ng, the speed of a pulse envelope. Under EIT ng can be enormous. Slow lightmemoryPulse propagation with vg ≪ c inside the EIT window. The delay is τ ≈ ODEIT/γEIT. Stopped / stored lightmemoryTurning the control off while the compressed pulse is inside the medium maps it completely onto atomic coherence. Turning the control back on regenerates the pulse. Dark-state polariton (DSP)memoryA quasi-particle mixing the probe photon and the ground-state spin coherence. Its photonic fraction (and speed) is set by Ωc. With Ωc → 0 it becomes purely atomic. Spin wavememoryThe spatially distributed coherence ρ₁₂ left in the ensemble after storage. Its phase pattern follows the two-photon wavevector kp − kc. Optical depth (OD)vapourOD = 2α₀L, the resonant absorption without control: T = e−OD. ODEIT is how much of it the control removes. Storage inefficiency scales as 1/ODEIT. Doppler broadeningvapourMoving atoms see shifted frequencies (δ → δ − k·v). Averaging over Maxwell–Boltzmann velocities gives a Gaussian width σDop ≈ vthk, a few hundred MHz in warm Rb. Voigt profilevapourConvolution of the homogeneous Lorentzian with the Doppler Gaussian. A pseudo-Voigt is a linear mix of the two, often used for fitting. Transit-time broadeningvapourAtoms crossing a finite beam interact only for ~w₀/vth, broadening the EIT line by ~vth/w₀ (ballistic) or D/w₀² (diffusive). With mm beams this is tens of kHz. Buffer gasvapourAn inert gas (He, Ne, N₂; a few to tens of Torr) that turns ballistic Rb motion into slow diffusion. Atoms stay in the beam far longer, at the cost of pressure broadening of the optical line (~10 MHz/Torr). Dicke narrowingvapourWhen the mean free path is shorter than the relevant wavelength, collisions suppress Doppler broadening. For Λ-EIT the two-photon wavelength is long, so the EIT line narrows strongly and becomes tolerant to small beam angles. Diffusion coefficient DvapourSets the diffusive time l²/D across a length l (≈10 cm²/s for Rb in 10 Torr buffer gas, per the paper). Wall (anti-relaxation) coatingvapourParaffin (e.g. tetracontane) or OTS coatings that let atoms bounce off walls without losing spin coherence. They are temperature limited (paraffin breaks down around 60–80 °C). Power broadeningtheoryThe EIT width grows with control power: γEIT = γ₁₂ + |Ωc|²/γ₁₃ (stationary atoms), or |Ωc|²/σDop + γ₁₂ in Doppler-broadened vapour. Ground-state decoherence γ₁₂theoryDecay rate of the ρ₁₂ coherence from transit, collisions (spin exchange, spin destruction), field gradients and so on. It sets the narrowest possible EIT line and the storage lifetime. Spin-exchange / spin-destruction collisionsvapourRb–Rb collisions that redistribute (exchange) or destroy total spin. Their rate grows with density, which is a key trade-off against OD. Radiation trappingvapourRe-absorption of spontaneously emitted photons in a dense vapour. It shortens spin coherence and becomes significant at densities of about 5×10¹¹ cm⁻³ and above for mm-sized beams. Density matrix ρtheoryDescribes mixed states. Diagonals ρii are populations and off-diagonals ρij are coherences. Coherence ρ₁₂, ρ₁₃theoryρ₁₃ (optical coherence) radiates the probe’s response. ρ₁₂ (ground/spin coherence) is the long-lived memory. In the weak-probe limit ρ₂₁ = −ΩpΩc*/(Γ₁₂Γ₁₃ + |Ωc|²). Lindblad / master equationtheorydρ/dt = −(i/ħ)[H,ρ] + L[ρ]. The superoperator L adds decay and dephasing, and the paper uses it to derive EIT. Optical Bloch equationstheoryThe master equation written out element by element for a few-level atom driven by light (paper Eq. 7). RWA (rotating-wave approximation)theoryDropping terms oscillating at ~2ν, valid when Ω and Δ ≪ ν. It turns the Hamiltonian into time-independent form in the rotating frame. Autler–Townes splittingtheoryA strong control splits the excited state into a doublet ±Ωc. It reduces absorption between the peaks without interference, so it is distinct from (but easily confused with) EIT. SAS (saturated absorption spectroscopy)labA strong pump and a weak counter-propagating probe through a reference cell. Only atoms with v ≈ 0 see both, so narrow sub-Doppler features appear on the Doppler-broadened absorption. Lamb diplabThe narrow transmission increase in SAS at an atomic resonance, caused by the pump saturating the v ≈ 0 atoms. Crossover resonancelabAn SAS feature exactly midway between two transitions that share a lower level, from atoms whose Doppler shift puts pump and probe on different transitions. Often the strongest lock point. Error signallabA signal that is zero at the lock point and changes sign across it (e.g. a derivative of the SAS dip, from modulation plus lock-in detection). It drives the feedback loop. PID locklabProportional-integral-derivative feedback that adjusts laser current (and/or temperature) to keep the error signal at zero. Servo (feedback loop)labA loop that measures a deviation (error signal) and applies a correction to pus

Physics from scratch

Physics from scratch From the rubidium atom to stored light, step by step. Background lectures: two-level atom, dark states & EIT. Equation numbers in grey refer to Finkelstein et al., arXiv:2205.10959v2.

3a · The ⁸⁷Rb atom and the Zeeman Λ system

3a · The ⁸⁷Rb atom and the Zeeman Λ system Rubidium is an alkali: one valence electron outside closed shells. Its ground configuration is 5S₁/₂. The first excited configuration splits by fine structure into 5P₁/₂ (reached by the D1 line near 795 nm) and 5P₃/₂ (D2, near 780 nm). The ⁸⁷Rb nucleus has spin I = 3/2. Coupling it to the electron gives hyperfine levels F = 1, 2 in both 5S₁/₂ and 5P₁/₂. In a magnetic field each F splits into 2F+1 Zeeman sublevels mF. EIT needs three levels: two long-lived lower states and one excited state. Zeeman EIT takes all three from the D1 manifold (paper Fig. 9b): |1⟩ = 5S₁/₂, F=2, mF=+2 |2⟩ = 5S₁/₂, F=2, mF=0 |3⟩ = 5P₁/₂, F′=1, mF′=+1 The probe couples |1⟩→|3⟩ (Δm = −1, σ⁻) and the control couples |2⟩→|3⟩ (Δm = +1, σ⁺), with the quantization axis along the solenoid field, which is parallel to the beams. The σ⁺ control also optically pumps atoms toward the high-mF end of F=2. F′=1 has no mF′ = +2 or +3, so on this transition both mF=+1 and +2 are dark to σ⁺. The three-level theory below idealizes this as “all population in |1⟩”, the state the weak probe interrogates. Real multilevel pumping (including leakage to F=1) spreads population and reduces contrast, which is one reason measured numbers deviate from the three-level model. Zeeman Λ system used in Zeeman EIT (after paper Fig. 9b). With B along the beams, the F=2 sublevels shift by gFμBmFB ≈ 0.70 kHz/mG × mF, so |1⟩ and |2⟩ (ΔmF = 2) are split by ≈1.40 kHz/mG × B. Excited-state spacing not to scale. The F′=1↔F′=2 splitting is deliberately not quoted; take it from the current Steck revision.

If δ ≠ 0, the relative phase inside the dark state creeps forward as eiδt, and the atom slowly becomes absorbing again. AnalogyTwo metronomes set to exactly the same tempo stay in step forever. Set one slightly off-beat and they drift in and out of step; how long you can tolerate the drift depends on how long you listen (the coherence time). That is why the EIT width ≈ (π/2)/τcoh. Where it failsMetronomes do not care about a common tempo error. Here too only the difference matters, which is why one laser split into two arms (common noise) works so well. If δ ≠ 0 the relative phase drifts and the atoms slowly become absorbing. A coherence lifetime τcoh therefore gives a transparency width of order δ ≈ (π/2)/τcoh. This is the first hint that EIT linewidth measures ground-state coherence, which is exactly what a memory needs. It also explains why Zeeman EIT tolerates a 1–2 MHz DFB: probe and control come from the same laser, so laser frequency noise is common to both and largely drops out of δ.

Adding decay: the master equation

Adding decay: the master equation Real atoms decay and dephase, so we use the density matrix ρ and a Lindblad term LΓ: Eqs. 6–7 (selected)\[ \frac{d\hat\rho}{dt}=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\big[\hat H_R,\hat\rho\big]+\mathcal L_\Gamma[\hat\rho],\qquad \begin{aligned}\dot\rho_{21}&=-(\gamma_{12}-i\delta)\rho_{21}-i\Omega_p\rho_{23}+i\Omega_c^{*}\rho_{31}\\ \dot\rho_{31}&=-(\gamma_{13}-i\Delta_1)\rho_{31}+i\Omega_c\rho_{21}+i\Omega_p(\rho_{11}-\rho_{33})\end{aligned} \] A bank account with transfers and fees Read it in wordsThe master equation evolves the density matrix ρ. The commutator term is the reversible, coherent part driven by the lasers; the Lindblad term LΓ adds irreversible decay and dephasing. ρ₂₁ (ground coherence) shrinks at γ₁₂ and rotates at δ; ρ₃₁ (optical coherence) shrinks at γ₁₃. AnalogyThink of linked bank accounts. The commutator moves money between accounts (it can flow back). The Lindblad term is fees and leaks: it only ever takes away. Where it failsMoney has no phase. Coherences are complex numbers whose phase matters, and the “fees” can erase phase information without removing any population. Here γ₁₂ is the ground-state (spin) decoherence rate and γ₁₃ the optical-coherence decay rate. In the weak-probe limit all population is pumped into |1⟩ (ρ₁₁ ≈ 1), and in steady state only two linear equations survive. With Γ₁₂ = γ₁₂ − iδ and Γ₁₃ = γ₁₃ − iΔ₁: Eqs. 9–10\[ \rho_{21}=-\frac{\Omega_p\Omega_c^{*}}{\Gamma_{12}\Gamma_{13}+|\Omega_c|^2},\qquad \rho_{31}=i\Omega_p\,\frac{\Gamma_{12}}{\Gamma_{12}\Gamma_{13}+|\Omega_c|^2}. \] A spring scale under a strong steady hand Read it in wordsWith a strong control and weak probe, the ground coherence ρ₂₁ (the memory) and the optical coherence ρ₃₁ (what radiates the probe’s absorption) both respond linearly to Ωp. When |Ωc|² ≫ Γ₁₂Γ₁₃, ρ₃₁ becomes tiny: no optical polarization, so no absorption. AnalogyA strong hand (control) holds a spring scale steady. A small weight (probe) stretches it proportionally. The stiffer the hand holds (larger Ωc), the less the pointer (ρ₃₁) moves.

3c · Susceptibility, transmission and the EIT linewidth

3c · Susceptibility, transmission and the EIT linewidth The probe sees the macroscopic polarization of N atoms per unit volume, i.e. the susceptibility. Writing α₀ for the unsaturated resonant field-absorption coefficient without EIT: Eqs. 11–13\[ \chi_p=\frac{N\mu_{13}^2\rho_{31}}{\hbar\epsilon_0\Omega_p}=i\,\alpha_0\frac{2\gamma_{13}}{k_p}\,\frac{\Gamma_{12}}{\Gamma_{12}\Gamma_{13}+|\Omega_c|^2},\qquad \alpha_0=\frac{k_pN\mu_{13}^2}{2\hbar\epsilon_0\gamma_{13}},\qquad \mathrm{OD}=2\alpha_0L. \] Sheets of tinted glass Read it in wordsχp is how strongly the atomic gas polarizes in response to the probe. Its imaginary part gives absorption. α₀ is the absorption per unit length without EIT, and OD = 2α₀L is the total: transmission without control is e−OD. Natom number densityε₀, ħvacuum permittivity, reduced Planck constantkpprobe wavevector 2π/λLcell lengthAnalogyOD counts sheets of tinted glass, each passing 1/e ≈ 37 %. OD 1 is one sheet; OD 10 is ten sheets in a stack: e−10 ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁵ gets through. Heating the cell adds sheets. Where it failsGlass absorbs every colour more or less equally. Atomic “sheets” absorb only near resonance, and EIT can make the whole stack go transparent in a narrow window. For a resonant probe (Δ₁ = 0) and small δ this takes the canonical EIT form: Eqs. 14–17\[ \alpha_p(\delta)=\alpha_0\,\frac{\gamma_{12}\gamma_{\rm EIT}+\delta^2}{\gamma_{\rm EIT}^2+\delta^2},\qquad \gamma_{\rm EIT}=\gamma_{12}+\frac{|\Omega_c|^2}{\gamma_{13}},\qquad \frac{\alpha_p(0)}{\alpha_0}=\frac{\gamma_{12}}{\gamma_{12}+|\Omega_c|^2/\gamma_{13}}. \] Noise-cancelling headphones for absorption Read it in wordsAbsorption αp(δ) dips in a window of half-width γEIT around two-photon resonance. γEIT = γ₁₂ + |Ωc|²/γ₁₃: the decoherence floor plus a power-broadening term. At the centre, absorption falls to γ₁₂/γEIT of its normal value. γ₁₂ground-state decoherence rate: the floorγ₁₃optical coherence decay rateδtwo-photon detuningAnalogyNoise-cancelling headphones silence noise only in a band where they can produce an exact anti-copy. Outside that band you hear everything. A stronger control is like a more powerful cancellation circuit: a wider quiet band, but you lose fine frequency selectivity. Where it failsHeadphones add a second sound wave. EIT adds no light to cancel the probe: the cancellation is between two quantum pathways inside each atom. Read this as a design rule. The window’s half-width γEIT starts at γ₁₂ and grows linearly with control intensity (power broadening). The residual absorption at line centre falls once |Ωc|² ≫ γ₁₂γ₁₃. A narrow line wants low control power; deep transparency wants high control power. The paper notes that the optimum is often where the two terms of γEIT are equal. In warm vapour, motion broadens the optical transition by σDop (a few hundred MHz), and buffer-gas collisions add pressure broadening γ₁₃col. The power-broadening term is then divided by the whole optical width: Eqs. 33, 40\[ \gamma_{\rm EIT}\simeq\frac{\Omega_c^2}{\sigma_{\rm Dop}}+\gamma_{12}\quad(\text{Doppler-dominated}),\qquad \gamma_{\rm EIT}\simeq\frac{\Omega_c^2}{\gamma_{13}+\gamma_{13}^{\rm col}+\sigma_{\rm Dop}}+\gamma_{12}+\gamma_{12}^{\rm col}\quad(\text{crude general form}). \] Paint spread over a wider wall Read it in wordsIn a warm vapour the power-broadening term is |Ωc|² divided by the whole optical width (natural + collisional + Doppler), not just γ₁₃. Ground decoherence (intrinsic and collisional) adds on top. AnalogyA fixed tin of paint (control power) spread over a wider wall (a broader optical line) gives a thinner coat (less power broadening). That is why warm-vapour EIT lines can be narrower than the stationary-atom formula predicts at the same control power. Where it failsEq. 40 is only a crude interpolation. Real lineshapes need an average over velocities; it is a planning estimate, not a fit function. 3d · Dispersion, slow light, dark-state polaritons and storage

3d · Dispersion, slow light, dark-state polaritons and storage Kramers–Kronig guarantees that the narrow absorption dip comes with a steep, positive refractive-index slope at δ = 0. Near the EIT peak (Δ₁ = 0): Eqs. 26–27\[ n(\delta)=1+\alpha_0\frac{2\gamma_{13}}{k_p}\,\frac{\delta\big(|\Omega_c|^2-\gamma_{12}^2-\delta^2\big)}{(\gamma_{\rm EIT}^2+\delta^2)\,\gamma_{13}^2},\qquad v_g=\frac{c}{n_g}=\frac{c}{1+\nu_p\,\frac{dn}{d\nu_p}\big|_{\delta=0}}. \] Traffic squeezing on a crowded road Read it in wordsNear δ = 0 the refractive index rises steeply with frequency. The group index ng = n + ν dn/dν becomes huge, so the pulse envelope moves at vg = c/ng ≪ c even though n itself is ≈ 1. n(δ)refractive index vs two-photon detuningnggroup index: how much the envelope slowsνpprobe optical frequencyAnalogyA convoy of cars enters a slow, crowded road. The front slows first while the back is still at motorway speed, so the convoy bunches up: it gets shorter and slower. A long optical pulse is compressed in the same way when it enters the EIT medium. Where it failsBunched cars stay cars. In EIT most of the pulse’s energy is temporarily handed to the atoms and the control field, then returned on exit, where the pulse regains its full length and speed c. Evaluating the slope gives a group index that grows as α₀|Ωc|²/(γ₁₃γEIT²) (paper Eq. 28; see the paper for the exact prefactor). In the useful regime γEIT ≈ |Ωc|²/γ₁₃, so weaker control means slower light, and so does higher density. The practical numbers are the delay and the bandwidth, both read straight from a measured spectrum: §IV A\[ \tau_{\rm delay}=\frac{\mathrm{OD}_{\rm EIT}}{\gamma_{\rm EIT}},\qquad B\sim\frac{\gamma_{\rm EIT}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{OD}_{\rm EIT}}},\qquad B\,\tau_{\rm delay}\approx\sqrt{\mathrm{OD}_{\rm EIT}}\ \ (\mathrm{OD}_{\rm EIT}\gg1),\qquad T_{\rm peak}=e^{-\mathrm{OD}+\mathrm{OD}_{\rm EIT}}. \] A long, narrow tunnel Read it in wordsDelay τ = ODEIT/γEIT: more resonant atoms or a narrower window means more delay. Bandwidth B ~ γEIT/√ODEIT: the usable window shrinks as OD grows. Their product ≈ √ODEIT counts how many pulses fit in the medium. AnalogyA long, narrow tunnel delays vehicles a lot but only admits slow, smooth ones. Make it longer (more OD) and it holds more vehicles at once (√OD), but the speed limit (bandwidth) tightens. Where it failsTunnel capacity scales with length; here it only scales as √OD, because the window narrows as OD grows.
p3
From slow light to stored light

From slow light to stored light A pulse entering the EIT medium is spatially compressed by the ratio vg/c, because its front slows down on entry while its tail is still in free space. Inside, it travels as a dark-state polariton: a coherent mixture of the probe field and the spin coherence ρ₁₂. The control strength sets the mixing angle. Ramping Ωc to zero while the pulse is fully inside stops the polariton and converts it entirely into a spin wave, a stationary pattern of ρ₁₂ across the cell. Nothing is absorbed. The information is now in the relative phase and amplitude of mF=+2 and mF=0. Turning the control back on reverses the mapping and the pulse leaves the cell in the original direction. Handing the relay baton from light to atoms Read it in wordsA dark-state polariton is part light, part spin coherence. The control sets the mix: turn it down and the polariton becomes more atomic and slower; turn it off and it is purely a stationary spin wave; turn it on and the light component is regenerated. AnalogyIn a relay race the baton (the quantum information) passes from the light runner to the atom runner, who stands still holding it. When the control says “go”, the baton is handed back and the light runner sets off again in the same direction. Where it failsReal batons are not damaged by waiting. The stored spin wave decoheres (γ₁₂), and atoms diffuse while holding it, so the baton slowly fades and blurs. Storage time is limited by how long ρ₁₂ survives, i.e. by γ₁₂ from diffusion out of the beam, magnetic-field gradients (which dephase a Zeeman coherence), and collisions. Efficiency is limited by OD: for pulses within the bandwidth, the paper states that inefficiency scales as 1/ODEIT. A pulse that does not fit inside the medium leaks out before storage. The project’s planned storage protocol maps one-to-one: AOM 1 slices the attenuated probe into pulses; AOM 2 switches the control off mid-transit; switching it on retrieves the pulse; a final polarisation filter blocks the control before the detector.

3e · What changes in a hot vapour cell

3e · What changes in a hot vapour cell Each motional effect is a time-of-flight T across a length l, giving spectral broadening σ ≈ 1/T. For ballistic motion T ∝ l; for diffusive motion T ∝ l². Eqs. 29–32\[ \sigma\simeq\frac1T,\qquad \sigma_{\rm Dop}=\frac{v_{\rm th}}{\lambda/2\pi}=v_{\rm th}|\vec k|,\qquad w(v)=\frac{e^{-v^2/2v_{\rm th}^2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,v_{\rm th}},\qquad \chi_{\rm ens}(\delta)=\int\chi_p(\delta-kv_z)\,w(v_z)\,dv_z . \] The ambulance siren Read it in wordsAn atom moving at velocity v sees the laser shifted by k·v. Averaging over the Maxwell–Boltzmann spread of velocities turns each sharp line into a Gaussian of width σDop = vthk, a few hundred MHz for warm Rb. vth1-D rms thermal speed √(kBT/m)w(v)velocity distributionχenssusceptibility averaged over velocitiesAnalogyAn ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it recedes. A gas is a crowd of ambulances moving every which way, so the “pitch” is smeared out. But two sirens mounted on the same ambulance shift together, and their pitch difference stays put. That is co-propagating probe and control in Λ-EIT. Where it failsFor sound the source moves; here the atom moves through a fixed laser field. The mathematics (a first-order shift k·v) is the same.
p3
Doppler and the co-propagating trick

Doppler and the co-propagating trick One-photon Doppler broadening (a few hundred MHz) reduces the absorption cross-section and therefore the usable OD, but it does not by itself widen the EIT line. EIT is a two-photon process with effective wavevector keff = kp − kc for a Λ system. For Zeeman EIT the two frequencies differ by only kHz, so co-propagating beams give keff ≈ 0, and every velocity class shares the same transparency window. This is why Zeeman EIT sends probe and control along the same path. A small angle θ between them gives a residual broadening of about σDopθ, tens of kHz already for θ ~ 0.1 mrad without buffer gas.
p3
Buffer gas and Dicke narrowing

Buffer gas and Dicke narrowing A few Torr of inert gas makes Rb diffuse. Broadening over a length l becomes D/l², and when the mean free path is shorter than the two-photon wavelength 2π/|kp − kc| the residual Doppler width collapses to D|kp − kc|² (Dicke narrowing). In the paper’s data (Fig. 10c) the angular sensitivity becomes quadratic in θ rather than linear. The price is pressure broadening of the optical line (~10 MHz/Torr).
p3
Transit time and beam size

Transit time and beam size A finite beam of waist w₀ is crossed in w₀/vth (ballistic) or w₀²/D (diffusive). Without buffer gas the EIT line takes a cusp shape with FWHM 2(vth/w₀)ln2, tens of kHz for mm beams. With a ~0.75 mm probe radius at 60 °C that is ≈52 kHz design estimate. Larger beams help, which is one reason the paper expands the control well beyond the probe (1/e² radii 2.55 mm vs 0.47 mm in Fig. 10c).
p3
Walls, magnetic fields, collisions

Walls, magnetic fields, collisions Uncoated walls fully decohere atoms that reach them. Field inhomogeneity dephases a Zeeman coherence directly, which is why the cell sits in a solenoid inside a triple-layer µ-metal shield that is degaussed before data. Rb–Rb spin-exchange and spin-destruction collisions grow with density, and above ~5×10¹¹ cm⁻³ radiation trapping also shortens coherence. Eqs. 34–35, 38\[ \sigma_{\rm diff}=\frac{D}{l^2},\qquad \gamma_{\rm Dicke}=D\,|\vec k_p-\vec k_c|^2,\qquad \Gamma_{tt}=\frac{v_{\rm th}}{w_0}\ \text{or}\ \frac{D}{w_0^2},\qquad \mathrm{FWHM}_{\rm cusp}=2\,\frac{v_{\rm th}}{w_0}\ln 2 . \] A runner crossing a spotlight, in a crowded room Read it in wordsBroadening ≈ 1 / (time spent in the beam). A ballistic atom crosses a beam of radius w₀ in w₀/vth; a diffusing atom needs w₀²/D. Dicke narrowing: frequent collisions suppress the residual Doppler width to D|kp−kc|². AnalogyA runner crosses a spotlight on a dark stage: the faster they run, the shorter they are lit, and the less precisely you can time them. Put the runner in a crowded room (buffer gas) and they stagger around, staying in the light far longer. Where it failsCollisions with buffer gas also perturb the atom’s internal state a little (pressure broadening of the optical line). A crowded room does not change the runner.

p3
The OD trade-off

The OD trade-off OD is the resource. Efficiency improves as 1/ODEIT falls, delay grows as ODEIT/γEIT, and the time–bandwidth product as √ODEIT. Raising temperature raises density roughly exponentially, but it also raises spin-exchange decoherence, radiation trapping, four-wave-mixing noise, and the heater power needed. The paper also notes coating limits (if used) of ~50–100 °C. The planned polyimide foil heater is rated to 70 °C and the GCH25-75 assembly to 50 °C. Our vapour-pressure estimate gives OD ≈ 4 at 50 °C and ≈ 20 at 70 °C, scaled from the paper’s OD ~10 at ~60 °C design estimate.
p3
What limits storage in practice

What limits storage in practice ODEIT: too low and the pulse cannot be compressed into the cell, so its front leaks out before the control switches off. Bandwidth: pulses shorter than ~1/B are distorted and absorbed. Pulse length, OD and control power must be co-optimised. Coherence time: retrieved energy decays with storage time at a rate set by γ₁₂. Shielding and buffer gas dominate here. Control leakage and noise: at single-photon level, filtering (Glan–Taylor, and later spectral filtering) sets the signal-to-noise ratio. Switching: AOM rise times (beam size ÷ acoustic velocity) must be short compared with the pulse. 04

Zeeman EIT experimental architecture

Zeeman EIT experimental architecture One DFB, two double-pass AOMs, one shielded cell. Block by block, following paper Fig. 10 and the project plan. Zeeman EIT signal chain, simplified from paper Fig. 10(a) and the project plan. The simulator’s reference layout implements exactly this chain on a 25 mm grid.
p4
1 · Source & isolation

1 · Source & isolation A 795 nm DFB laser in a 14-pin butterfly: the Yanban RB-795-DFB-BFW, free space, 100–120 mW, linewidth 200 kHz typical, target 794.97 nm, with no isolator inside. Its collimated beam (about 1.0 × 0.8 mm) goes straight into two free-space isolators (two Thorlabs I795P3D in series, because a retro-reflected beam can damage the chip), then a half-wave plate and a PM-fibre link (two steering mirrors, a FiberPort coupler, a PM780 FC/APC patch cable and an output FiberPort) that hands a clean Ø1 mm beam to the bench. With about ten times the power the paper needs, turn the beam down right after the isolation with a half-wave plate and a PBS into a rated beam dump, and treat the open 100 mW beam as Class 3B. The paper notes that 20–40 mW is enough and that a DFB linewidth of 1–2 MHz is acceptable.
p4
2 · SAS lock

2 · SAS lock A λ/2 + PBS pick-off sends a few percent to a saturated-absorption module (reference Rb cell, pump and probe, photodiode). The photodiode signal goes to a lock box, which makes an error signal and drives the laser controller’s current modulation input, closing the loop near F=2→F′=1 of D1 (paper; ≈794.98 nm). The double-pass AOMs shift the EIT beams by 2 × 80 MHz and the SAS light is not shifted: we lock on F = 2 → F′ = 1 and run the EIT beams 160 MHz off the one-photon resonance (−1 orders; the cell about 3 °C hotter), which needs no third AOM (see the AOM answer in section 09). See the frequency lock.
p4
3 · Control & probe preparation

3 · Control & probe preparation A λ/2 + PBS splits a weak probe from a strong control (paper). Each arm double-passes an AOM through a PBS + cat’s-eye with a λ/4 in the return path. The returning beam has rotated polarization and exits the other PBS port. The double pass gives 2fRF shift and no beam walk while scanning. The two AOMs are driven by twin phase-locked RF signals from the same dual-output generator (paper), so 2(fC − fP) is stable to Hz. The double-pass AOM as a moving staircase Read it in wordsAn AOM’s sound wave is a moving grating. Diffracting off it shifts the light by fRF, and passing twice shifts it by 2fRF. The cat’s-eye sends the beam back along the same line even when fRF (and so the angle) changes. AnalogyThrow a ball onto a moving escalator and it comes off a little faster: that is the frequency shift. Send it back through a second time and it gains the boost twice. The cat’s-eye is a funnel that always returns the ball to the same lane, whatever angle it came in at. Where it failsLight scatters off quantized sound (phonons). The shift is exactly fRF per pass, set by the RF synthesiser, not by speed in the everyday sense.
p4
4 · Polarization & combining

4 · Polarization & combining A PBS recombines the arms (probe H transmitted, control V reflected) onto one co-propagating path. A λ/4 at 45° then makes them opposite circular: control σ⁺, probe σ⁻ relative to B. The paper also expands the control beam well beyond the probe for a uniform Rabi frequency (2.55 mm vs 0.47 mm radii in Fig. 10c). A telescope in the control arm is a recommended addition. design note
p4
5 · Cell, heater, field, shield

5 · Cell, heater, field, shield Quartz ⁸⁷Rb cell (planned) with a polyimide foil heater (≤70 °C) or GCH25-75 assembly (≤50 °C) under a TC300B controller. Heat uniformly and non-magnetically (bifilar winding). Use a solenoid giving B along z (paper: typically 10–100 mG) inside a triple-layer µ-metal shield, degaussed before data. At 50 mG the Λ splitting is 70 kHz.
p4
6 · Separation & detection

6 · Separation & detection A second λ/4 converts the circular beams back to linear. A Glan–Taylor (~10⁵ extinction vs ~10³ for a PBS) passes the probe to a fast photodiode and sends the control to a dump (paper). The probe frequency is scanned around the fixed control by tuning AOM-P. A scan of less than ±100 kHz covers the EIT feature (paper).
p4-lock
The frequency lock: SAS → lock box → laser controller → DFB

The frequency lock: SAS → lock box → laser controller → DFB The SAS module on its own only measures. A real lock is a feedback loop with four parts: SAS photodiode records the reference-cell transmission, with sub-Doppler dips at the atomic lines. Lock box (error-signal generation + PI/PID servo) turns that transmission into a dispersive error signal that crosses zero at the chosen feature and changes sign on either side. It then computes a correction. Laser controller (low-noise current source + TEC controller) adds the correction to the DFB injection current through its modulation input (usually a front-panel BNC). DFB: its frequency follows the current (fast) and the chip temperature (slow). A DFB has no piezo, so slow drifts are taken up by retuning the TEC setpoint (by hand or with a slow second loop), keeping the current correction inside its range. feedback loop\[ e(\Delta)\approx D\,\Delta\ \ (|\Delta|\ \text{small}),\qquad u(t)=-K_P\,e(t)-K_I\!\int_0^t e(t')\,dt',\qquad \delta\nu_{\rm laser}=\kappa\,u(t)\ \Rightarrow\ \Delta\to0 . \] Cruise control on a car Read it in wordsNear the lock point the error signal is proportional to how far the laser is from the chosen SAS feature, with a sign that says which side it is on. The servo turns that error into a correction: a proportional part reacting now and an integral part removing any persistent offset. The laser controller converts the correction into a current change, which shifts the DFB frequency back. e(Δ)error signal; zero at the lock point, slope DKP, KIproportional and integral gains set on the lock boxu(t)correction voltage into the controller’s modulation inputκcurrent-to-frequency tuning of the DFB (read from your laser’s data; not quoted here) AnalogyCruise control. The SAS is the speedometer, the lock box is the logic that decides how hard to press, the injection current is the accelerator (fast, fine), and the TEC temperature is the gear (slow, coarse). The slope sign is which pedal you think speeds the car up: get it backwards and the car races away (the lock runs off). Too much gain and the car surges back and forth (oscillation). Where it failsA speedometer reads speed anywhere. The SAS error signal is only useful within a few feature widths of the line, and several lines look alike, so the loop can happily lock to the wrong one. A car also has no “mode hops”: a diode laser can jump to another frequency abruptly, faster than any servo can follow.
p4
Ways to make the error signal general background

Ways to make the error signal general background Method How Side effects for this experiment (a) Current dither + lock-in Dither the DFB current at tens of kHz through the controller’s modulation input, then demodulate the SAS photodiode at the dither frequency to get the derivative of the SAS spectrum. The dither frequency-modulates all the light, including the EIT beams. In Zeeman EIT, control and probe come from the same laser, so this jitter is largely common-mode for the two-photon resonance. The one-photon detuning still wobbles by the dither depth, so keep the dither small compared with the optical line, or use (b) or (c). (b) Modulation-free: DAVLL or polarization spectroscopy DAVLL: a small magnetic field on the reference cell splits the σ⁺/σ⁻ absorption; the difference of two photodiodes is dispersive. Polarization spectroscopy: a circularly polarized pump makes the cell birefringent near the sub-Doppler lines, read out with a polarizer and balanced photodiodes. No modulation on the laser. More optics in the SAS arm, and the zero point can drift with field, alignment and photodiode balance. (c) Modulate only the SAS beam Put an AOM or EOM in the SAS arm (e.g. frequency- or amplitude-modulate the pump) and demodulate as in (a). The main beam stays clean. Needs an extra modulator and driver in the SAS arm. What the lock actually has to achieve In Zeeman EIT the lock holds the laser near the F=2→F′=1 one-photon resonance, within roughly the MHz scale. That is small compared with the Doppler- and pressure-broadened optical line of hundreds of MHz design estimate. It does not set the kHz-level two-photon resonance: that comes from the phase-locked AOM RF, because probe and control share the laser’s frequency noise. In the simulator, removing the lock box or controller opens the loop and the laser drifts by MHz to tens of MHz illustrative. The EIT signal then degrades and objective 2 fails.

Timing for pulsed storage

Timing for pulsed storage Pulse sequence (project protocol): AOM-P slices an attenuated probe pulse. AOM-C switches the control off once the compressed pulse is inside the cell (dark-state polariton mapped to a spin wave), holds it off for τ, then switches it on to retrieve. Not to scale. The function generator’s two burst channels set t_off and τ.

Bring-up & audit protocol
Bring-up & audit protocol An ordered commissioning sequence. Each step isolates one variable. Numeric pass criteria are design targets unless tagged otherwise.
p6
Objective 1: locked laser and operating cell

Objective 1: locked laser and operating cell Laser characterisation. Mount the DFB with its current and TEC controller. Record power vs current. The beam leaves the package collimated (about 1.0 × 0.8 mm). Measure the beam size before any optic, and run the arrival test of the Yanban answer in section 09 (power against current, the Rb D1 absorption dips and SAS features, polarization). Pass · single-mode output, stable power; waist close to the planned ~1.5 mm. Isolator first. Put two isolator stages straight in front of the package window, input polarizer along the laser polarization, arrows away from the laser; turn each for the highest forward transmission (the second input polarizer then lies at 45° to the first). The PM-fibre link follows: a half-wave plate and PBS send the power the bench does not need (about 90 mW) into a rated dump. Check that a deliberate back-reflection does not disturb the laser (watch the SAS or a Fabry–Pérot). Pass · forward transmission ≳ 70 % (isolator loss ≈ 1–1.5 dB plus connectors); no frequency jumps when a mirror retro-reflects the beam. Mode-hop map. Sweep current and temperature while watching a Fabry–Pérot or wavemeter (both procurement gaps; borrow if needed) and a Doppler-broadened Rb absorption signal. Pass · a continuous, mode-hop-free current scan covers the D1 F=2 lines with margin. SAS signal. Use λ/2 + PBS to pick off a few percent into the SAS module. Overlap pump and counter-propagating probe in the reference cell. Identify Doppler valleys and sub-Doppler dips and crossovers. Note that natural-abundance reference cells also show ⁸⁵Rb lines. Pass · sub-Doppler features clearly resolved; F=2→F′=1 identified unambiguously. Close the frequency lock. Cable SAS photodiode → lock box → laser controller modulation input. Then work in order: Open-loop scan: ramp the laser current slowly (loop open) and view the SAS transmission and the error-signal monitor on the scope. Find the lines: identify the Doppler valleys and the sub-Doppler features, and pick F=2→F′=1 (or a chosen crossover). Set slope and sign: adjust dither depth or modulation-free balance so the error signal crosses zero cleanly at the feature. Choose the sign so that feedback pushes the laser towards zero. Close the loop: stop the ramp with the laser parked near the zero crossing and engage the servo. Start with low gain, raise it until the lock is stiff, then back off from any oscillation. Check it holds: the error signal stays near zero, SAS transmission stays on the feature, and small taps on the table do not unlock it. Offload slow drift to the TEC setpoint. Pass · lock holds ≥ 1 h; residual error ≪ the SAS feature width. milestone 1 Cell thermal control. Install the ⁸⁷Rb cell with the foil heater and TC300B. Step 30 → 60 °C. Keep the cell stem or windows from being the coldest point, so Rb does not condense on the windows. Pass · setpoint held to ±0.1 °C; absorption increases with temperature as expected; no window deposits. Optical depth. With control blocked and a weak probe, scan the laser and fit the resonant absorption to obtain OD(T). Compare with the vapour-pressure estimate. Pass · OD reproducible to ~10 % at a fixed temperature; OD ≳ 5 reachable within the heater limit.
p6
Objective 2: EIT and light storage

Objective 2: EIT and light storage Split and double-pass each arm. Set λ/2 for ~10 % probe. Build each AOM double pass (PBS, AOM, lens + mirror cat’s-eye, λ/4) and select the +1 order with an iris. Pass · double-pass efficiency ≳ 40–60 %; output position does not move when fRF is scanned ±1 MHz. RF coherence. Drive both AOMs from phase-locked channels with a shared clock. Beat the two arms on a fast photodiode (before the cell). Pass · beat note at 2(fC − fP) is stable and narrow at the Hz level on an RF spectrum or FFT. Overlap and polarization. Recombine on the PBS. Check co-propagation over ≥ 1 m (two irises). Set λ/4 at 45°, then verify circularity with a rotating polariser (power variation ≲ 5 %) for each arm separately. Pass · angle between beams well below 1 mrad; both beams circular, opposite handedness. Field control. Degauss the shield. Zero residual fields with the solenoid (and trim coils if available) by minimising EIT width with B ≈ 0. Then apply B ≈ 50 mG and confirm the resonance moves by 1.40 kHz/mG × B. Pass · resonance position vs solenoid current is linear with slope 1.40 kHz/mG paper: 0.7 kHz/mG per mF. First EIT spectrum. Scan AOM-P by ±50 kHz (optical ±100 kHz) around resonance. Separate the probe with λ/4 + Glan–Taylor. Then record FWHM vs control intensity. Pass · a narrow transmission peak at δ = 0 whose width falls roughly linearly with intensity; tens of kHz or below. paper example: 26 and 7.3 kHz Extract OD, ODEIT, γEIT. Take ln(I/Iin) of the spectrum (paper Fig. 8). Compute B and τdelay = ODEIT/γEIT. Pass · ODEIT/OD ≳ 0.5 (high-contrast EIT). Slow light. Send a probe pulse longer than 1/B (via AOM-P burst) with control on, and compare its arrival with a reference pulse (control and cell detuned). Pass · measured delay agrees with ODEIT/γEIT within ~30 %. Storage and retrieval. Switch the control off while the pulse is inside, wait τ, switch on. Record the retrieved energy vs τ and fit the decay. Pass · retrieved pulse clearly above control leakage and noise; decay curve recorded. milestone 2

Q1 Is our 795 nm DFB laser the right specification, and is 5–15 mW enough?

Q1 Is our 795 nm DFB laser the right specification, and is 5–15 mW enough? Update (20 Oct 2026): the Eagleyard BFY12 is no longer in the plan. The laser is the free-space Yanban RB-795-DFB-BFW with two I795P3D isolators and a PM-fibre link (equipment rows L01, L05, L06). Read this answer as the method and the history; the Yanban numbers are in the entry on the Yanban laser. Yes on both counts. It is the manufacturer's Rb D1 spectroscopy part, and its 5–15 mW is the right size: about 1 mW of control light at the cell and under 1 µW of probe need only 5–15 mW at the laser fibre. The part is the Toptica Eagleyard EYP-DFB-0795-00015-1500-BFY12-0005 (datasheet revision 0.93, 5 Feb 2025). Nothing in the datasheet rules it out, and a 40 mW laser would be wasted. Our need Datasheet Fit Rb-87 D1 line, 794.978 nm target 794.98 nm reachable at 10–45 °C chip temperature at 15 mW; 0.06 nm/K yes About 1 mW at the cell 5–15 mW out of the fibre; 160 mA typical for 15 mW yes, about 5× margin Linewidth well below about 100 MHz 0.6 typical, 1.0 MHz at 15 mW yes Lock range mode-hop-free over more than 10 GHz; current tuning about 1.4 GHz/mA yes Single mode side-mode suppression 30 dB minimum, 45 typical yes Clean polarization 20 dB extinction, PM fibre, FC/APC narrow key yes Protection built-in micro-isolator (no figure given) plus our free-space isolator (Thorlabs I795P3D) yes What keeps it from perfect Thin current margin: 15 mW needs 160 mA and the absolute maximum is 170 mA. Set the controller limit to 165–170 mA and run near 10–12 mW for lifetime. The ITC502 20 kΩ thermistor range reads up to 19.99 kΩ and this thermistor is about 20 kΩ at 10 °C: keep the chip at 15 °C or warmer, or switch to the 200 kΩ range (coarser, 10 Ω steps). Toptica Eagleyard lists the part as about to become obsolete (replacement "on request"): consider a spare. The datasheet is a preliminary revision (below 1.0), all figures at beginning of life; the individual test protocol that ships with each laser is what counts. The label says Class 4 (20 mW, IEC 60825-1). Not stated: isolation of the micro-isolator in dB, the fibre type, how the linewidth was measured. Q2 Is an isolator mandatory, even though most of the bench is free space?

Q2 Is an isolator mandatory, even though most of the bench is free space? Update (20 Oct 2026): the plan now uses the Yanban laser, which has no isolator inside, so two free-space I795P3D isolators stand in series straight behind its window (equipment row L06, quantity 2; about −100 dB at the chip, an estimate). The reasoning below, the feedback budget and the thresholds, still holds. Yes. Free space does not remove the need for an isolator: the returning light comes from the free-space part. Our laser has a micro-isolator inside, and a free-space Faraday isolator right after the collimator (Thorlabs I795P3D, BOM L06) is the second stage. For a laser with no isolator inside, a second stage would be mandatory. Why a DFB laser needs one It reacts to very little returned light. In the classic measurements on a DFB laser (Tkach and Chraplyvy, 1986, summarised in section 2.6 of F. Rogister's thesis) mode hopping began near −70 dB of returned power, and from −45 dB to −10 dB the line broke up (coherence collapse, 100 MHz to 25 GHz wide). Those figures belong to that laser and are only a guide for ours, but the lesson holds: the line stays as narrow as the data sheet says (about 1 MHz) only if almost nothing comes back. Our own bench sends light back. Each double-pass AOM arm ends in a cat's-eye mirror that returns the beam exactly along itself. The wave plate and the PBS cube are meant to steer the returning beam out sideways, but no wave plate is perfect: a retardance error of 2° (a plate designed for 780 nm and used at 795 nm is about 1.7° off) or a plate set 1° off its axis lets about 10⁻³ of the returning light (−29 dB) pass the PBS and travel back towards the laser. With the AOM losses and the share of power in the arm, that is about −33 dB at the laser, far inside the coherence-collapse range if nothing blocks it. The 3D simulator uses perfect wave plates, so it shows almost nothing returning and hides this. Flat surfaces add more, and alignment makes it worse. An uncoated quartz window returns about 3.4 % per surface (−15 dB), a bare silicon detector about a third of the light, an AR-coated optic about 0.25 %. The collimator and single-mode fibre accept only light coming back within about 0.3 mrad (0.02°) of the beam, so a surface has to be square to the beam within about 0.01° to count. That is rare by accident, but it is exactly what happens when a beam is aligned by watching its back-reflection, or when a mirror or card is left square to the beam. What protects the laser chip Returned light at the chip (about −33 dB with nothing in front) Against the −70 dB and −45 dB marks nothing −33 dB inside coherence collapse the micro-isolator inside the Eagleyard alone (one stage, typically about 30 dB; its data sheet gives no figure) about −63 dB in the mode-hopping band the Thorlabs I795P3D alone (at least 34 dB at 795 nm) about −67 dB or better at the edge of the mode-hopping band both, as in our design about −97 dB or better far below These are estimates (about ±10 dB), not measurements. They show the order of magnitude and why either stage alone is marginal. What we do Put the I795P3D right after the FC/APC collimator. Thorlabs lists it as a fixed narrowband isolator centred at 795 nm (operating range 775–815 nm), isolation at least 34 dB and transmission 90 % at the centre wavelength, beams up to Ø2.7 mm (our ~1.5 mm beam fits), 0.7 W maximum. Set its input polarizer along the slow axis of the laser fibre, turn it for the highest forward power, and dump both rejected-beam ports. Keep the short gap between the collimator and the isolator clear: nothing in between. The angled FC/APC fibre end and the AR-coated collimator return very little themselves. Check the replacement of the laser. The vendor lists the Eagleyard part in our list as about to become obsolete. If its replacement has no isolator inside, the I795P3D alone gives only about −67 dB: then add a second stage (a second isolator in series, or a dual-stage isolator). Habits that cost nothing: tilt the cell and the detector by a degree or two, dump every unused port, set each double-pass wave plate for the least light in its leak port (not by the scale on the mount), and never leave a mirror or card square to the beam while the laser is on. Verdict: keep both the micro-isolator inside the laser and the free-space I795P3D. One free-space stage is enough while the laser has its own isolator. A feedback fault shows up as a lock that drifts or a line that is wider than the data sheet says, which is slow to trace afterwards, so the isolator goes in before the first alignment. Sources: Rogister, Nonlinear dynamics of semiconductor lasers subject to optical feedback (thesis, section 2.6) · Eagleyard data sheet EYP-DFB-0795-00015-1500-BFY12-0005 (micro-isolator inside, no isolation figure given) · Thorlabs I795P3D and Thorlabs NIR free-space isolators (specification table) Added 10 Oct 2026

Q4 How do we make the free-space Yanban beam equal to a PM-fibre-pigtailed laser (profile, polarization, pointing)?

Q4 How do we make the free-space Yanban beam equal to a PM-fibre-pigtailed laser (profile, polarization, pointing)? Couple it into a polarization-maintaining single-mode fibre ourselves. A PM-pigtailed laser is the same chip with an isolator, a lens and a PM fibre built into the package. The fibre is what makes its output a clean round Gaussian with a fixed polarization axis and a fixed pointing, so the only way to get exactly that output from a free-space laser is to put the same fibre in the path. This is also what our reference design does: Finkelstein et al. (New J. Phys. 25, 035001 (2023), Sec. V.1 and Fig. 10) send their free-space laser through an isolator and then into a PM fibre, to clean the beam profile and the polarization. Free-space optics alone (lenses, prisms, a pinhole) only come close. Our setup: through the PM fibre (decided 19 Oct 2026). The equipment list (Yanban option) now has the fibre link (row L05) to buy; its two steering mirrors and mounts are counted in the mirror rows O01 and O02 (11 in all: the 3D bench draws the whole link, and with the fibre no separate master-axis mirror pair is needed after the output FiberPort). The 3D bench (3D Bench tab) now shows the link: two isolators, steering mirrors, half-wave plate, FiberPort coupler, the yellow PM fibre and the output FiberPort. Was the fibre strictly needed? No. The free-space beam could go straight from the two isolators into the bench (half-wave plate, PBS, AOM arms). The laser already gives a single-frequency, nearly round 1.0 × 0.8 mm beam (a good size for the AOMs) with 20 dB polarization, and the first PBS cleans the polarization. What the direct beam does not give: Pointing decoupling: drift of the laser mount or the isolators (temperature, screws settling) moves the beam on the AOMs (Bragg acceptance about 0.5 mrad), the SAS and the cell; a laser swap means realigning the bench. With the fibre, such drift changes only the coupled power. A guaranteed clean mode: the data sheet gives no beam-quality figure (M²); the fibre passes only its own Gaussian mode. We chose the fibre for exactly these reasons: a guaranteed clean Ø1 mm beam at the AOMs (the direct beam would need a reducing telescope), and a bench that stays aligned whatever happens on the laser side. Direct or through the fibre: which is better? Direct into the bench Through the PM fibre Parts after the isolators none extra half-wave plate, 2 steering mirrors, coupler, patch cable, output collimator Alignment work the laser-to-bench alignment once the same plus fibre coupling and the polarization launch (a few hours, a practised skill) Power at the bench about 80 mW (two isolators at 90 %) tens of mW (coupling losses), still far more than the 5–15 mW needed Beam profile whatever the chip gives (no M² on the data sheet) a clean round Gaussian, guaranteed by the fibre Beam 1 m after the source (at the AOMs) Ø2.3 mm if the data-sheet 0.1° is the full angle, Ø4.4 mm if it is the half angle: larger than the 2 mm AOM aperture, so a lens or a reducing telescope is needed before the AOMs (the data sheet implies M² ≈ 1.7 or 3.4) Ø1.5 mm from a Ø1 mm FiberPort output (1.087 mrad) Polarization 20 dB from the chip, cleaned by the first PBS set by the fibre axis; can wander a little with temperature if the launch is off Pointing on the AOMs, SAS, cell follows any drift of the laser mount and isolators fixed by the output collimator; laser-side drift only changes the power Laser swap or repair realign the bench realign only the coupling Extra maintenance none an occasional touch-up of the coupler See both in 3D: the laser-source simulation shows the two layouts at the 100 mm beam height with the alignment steps, the data-sheet values, and the power, isolation and beam-size budgets. For EIT itself the two give the same result: the experiment needs a stable single-frequency beam of a few mW in a known polarization, and the PBS and the cell do not care about a slightly non-ideal profile. The fibre buys long-term stability and an ideal beam at the price of one more alignment stage. We chose the fibre (19 Oct 2026); the direct beam remains the fallback if the fibre coupling ever becomes a problem. Alignment, in order 1. Laser on, low power: set the ITC502 current limit and the TEC first; check that the laser reaches the Rb line (absorption and saturated-absorption features in the reference cell while scanning the current). 2. Isolators: turn each isolator about the beam until the transmitted power is maximum (its input polarizer is then along the laser polarization); keep the beam centred in the aperture. 3. Order of mirrors and wave plate: the two isolator-side mirrors see the 45° output of the isolator, so first turn the second isolator (or the beam path) so that the beam is horizontal or vertical at the mirrors if the plate is to come after them; the half-wave plate sits just before the coupler and is set in step 5. 4. Fibre coupling: with both mirrors, walk the beam into the coupler while reading the power at the fibre output with the power meter (first mirror for position, second for angle, alternately), then optimise the focus of the coupler, and repeat. Expect a good part of the power to be coupled when the modes match; measure it rather than assume it. 5. Polarization: put a polarizer and the power meter after the output collimator. Turn the half-wave plate for the deepest minimum (the input is then on a fibre axis). Then warm or gently bend the fibre: if the output power through the polarizer changes, the input is not on the axis yet; turn the plate until warming and bending change nothing. That is the standard way to launch into a PM fibre. 6. Lock it down: tighten the locking screws of the mounts and the coupler, write down the coupled power, and check it again the next day. Power: 100 mW from the laser, about 90 % through each isolator stage, then the fibre coupling: tens of milliwatts at the output, still far more than the 5–15 mW we need. Run the laser at a lower current or turn the power down after the fibre. The fixed mount: metal, not PETG. Heat: the butterfly's TEC pushes the chip's heat into its base; a PETG base insulates (several times worse than aluminium), so the TEC cannot hold the temperature, and PETG softens not far above 60 °C. Stability: coupling into a 5 µm fibre core needs micrometre stability. PETG creeps under screw load and expands several times more than aluminium with temperature, so the coupling would drift. What works: a flat aluminium base plate (a casting is fine if its mounting faces are machined flat), the laser mount and the optics on short, low posts, locking screws on every mount, and a cover against air currents. PETG is fine for that cover. Q5 DFB or ECDL? Why not an ECDL, why do the reference papers use one, and is a narrow linewidth crucial?

Q5 DFB or ECDL? Why not an ECDL, why do the reference papers use one, and is a narrow linewidth crucial? A DFB is good enough for this experiment and much cheaper and simpler. An ECDL would be a luxury, not a requirement. The reason is that the laser's own linewidth is not what sets the EIT line. Two linewidths that get mixed up The EIT linewidth is the narrow one (7.3 kHz at 1.3 mW/cm², 26 kHz at 5.5 mW/cm²). It is set by control intensity, magnetic field, buffer-gas diffusion and coherence time, not by the laser. The laser linewidth only has to be well below the optical width of the atoms (Doppler about 500 MHz, wider with buffer gas). Our 0.6–1 MHz is 100× below. What matters more (my reasoning) Relative phase of control and probe. Both come from the same laser through phase-locked RF, so the laser's phase noise is common to both and cancels. A 1 m path difference (about 3 ns) at 1 MHz linewidth gives a relative phase variance of only about 0.02 rad² (0.14 rad rms), so about 98 % of the two-photon drive stays narrow (calculator 4 of the distance calculator). What reaches the atoms is noise from the RF source and drift in the arm lengths. Lock stability. The laser must stay within a fraction of the optical width; the DeRose paper reports drift of about 10 MHz per hour and negligible drift during data taking. DFB against ECDL DFB (our choice) ECDL Linewidth 0.6–1 MHz a few hundred kHz Tuning mode-hop-free over more than 10 GHz by current and temperature wide, but piezo and grating alignment Build one sealed, fibre-pigtailed butterfly with isolator open cavity, more sensitive to vibration, mode hops Lock actuator laser current (fast and simple) piezo plus current feed-forward Cost the lower one typically several times more Why a DFB is enough The papers only ask for a linewidth far below the Doppler width (about 500 MHz), and 1 MHz passes easily. The 10 Torr Ne buffer gas makes the optical line wider still (order 100 MHz). The narrow 7–26 kHz EIT line depends on the control–probe phase relation, not on the laser's own linewidth; both beams share the laser's noise (my reasoning, not quoted from a paper). We need only about 1 mW at the cell. A narrower laser helps only with a very noisy driver or sub-Doppler spectroscopy at the few-MHz level; the SAS features are 6–12 MHz wide (the D1 natural width is 5.75 MHz), which a 1–2 MHz laser resolves. Why the reference papers use ECDLs. No sentence in either paper says why, so this is partly inference. What they do say: ECDLs have a linewidth of a few hundred kHz, DFBs about 1–2 MHz, and either is fine for EIT. Likely reasons (my judgment): Installed base: atomic-physics labs have used ECDLs for decades and these groups already own several. Reuse: an ECDL covers other wavelengths and atoms and scans over several GHz. Narrower line: more margin for sub-Doppler spectroscopy, not needed for EIT. Wavelength availability: DFB diodes exactly on the Rb D1 line used to be less common. Teaching setup: the DeRose paper is an undergraduate set-up where students scan the laser by hand. None applies strongly to us: one fixed target line, no existing ECDL, and a budget. For a real answer, ask the authors. When an ECDL would be better: driver current noise turning into linewidth (1 µA is about 1.4 MHz), scanning several GHz or other lines, a replacement if the DFB is no longer available, or an ECDL already in the building. Q6 What specification do the AOMs and their RF driver need (for a quote)? Two identical 80 MHz TeO₂ AOMs for 795 nm (one per arm, each in double pass), driven by one two-channel RF source with a common clock, an amplifier, an attenuator and a fast switch per channel. Two are enough: the 160 MHz lock offset is handled without a third AOM (see the end). survives an open or shorted output clean sidebands; an unplugged AOM must not kill the amplifier Our planned build meets this from separate parts: Windfreak SynthHD (two channels, one clock), two Mini-Circuits ZHL-1-2W-S+ amplifiers (+33 dBm), ZX76-31R5-PN-S+ attenuators, ZASWA-2-50DR+ switches and ZFDC-20-4-S+ couplers. An integrated driver from an AOM maker is fine only if both channels share one clock. The 160 MHz lock offset without a third AOM. Both EIT arms are shifted by 160 MHz (double pass at 80 MHz) and the SAS light is not, and no SAS feature of the F = 2 line lies 160 MHz from F = 2 → F′ = 1 (the nearest, the F′ = 1/F′ = 2 crossover, is 407 MHz away). Two free solutions: Lock on F = 2 → F′ = 1 and run the EIT beams 160 MHz off the one-photon resonance (recommended). EIT in Zeeman Λ depends on the two-photon detuning (the kHz difference of the two AOMs), not on the one-photon detuning, and in a warm cell the Doppler profile is wide: about 530 MHz FWHM at 60 °C (σ ≈ 225 MHz). At 160 MHz off the line centre the absorption is about 78 % of the peak, so the cell needs about 3 °C more for the same optical depth (the Rb density rises about 8 % per °C near 60 °C). Use the −1 order in both AOMs (−160 MHz): F′ = 2 is then 974 MHz away instead of 654 MHz, so its contribution becomes negligible. Expect a slightly asymmetric EIT line at this detuning in a buffer-gas cell; contrast and width are still measured the same way. Take the SAS light from the control arm after its AOM (a small pick-off after the double pass), so the lock sees the shifted light and the control sits exactly on the line. The catch: when the control is switched off for storage, the lock light disappears too, so the lock box must hold its output during the off time (microseconds, much shorter than the lock response). A third AOM in the SAS arm would also work, but it is not needed and is not in the budget. Update (20 Oct 2026): AOM yes, driver no. The supplier offers the AOM (795 nm, 80 MHz, 2 mm aperture, SMA input, maximum RF power 2 W, diffraction efficiency above 85 %) but cannot make our two-channel driver (the 1 Hz frequency steps). So we buy the two AOMs only and drive them with route A below, the chain already in the equipment list (R01–R06: SynthHD, switch, attenuator, amplifier, coupler) plus the DIY D8 bias box. The SMA input connects straight to that chain. The 2 W limit sets one rule: keep the synthesizer at +1 dBm (about 1 W at the AOM) and never above +2 dBm. (21 Oct 2026: the AOM now chosen, the FAOM-780-80-2, is rated 2 W, so the rule stands; see the FAOM answer.) Still to get in writing: the RF power at which the 85 % was measured (and with which beam size and polarization), the AR coating at 795 nm, the rise time for a 1 mm beam, and a drawing. Is route A "building the driver ourselves"? Mostly not. Nothing is designed or soldered in the RF path: every block is a finished, boxed module with SMA connectors (the SynthHD synthesizer and the Mini-Circuits switch, attenuator, amplifier and coupler), joined with SMA cables. This is how many atomic-physics labs drive their AOMs. The only home-made part is the small bias box (DIY D8) that gives the switches and attenuators their supply voltages and control lines, and it can shrink further: the SynthHD sets its own output level in software, so the step attenuators can be left out, and the switches need only +5 V and −5 V from a bench supply plus a TTL gate. The work is then cabling, the synthesizer software, and the commissioning order of D8 (load the amplifier before switching it on, heat sink, synthesizer never above +2 dBm). A ready-made multi-channel DDS AOM driver from a specialist maker would avoid even that, at a higher price. Status and decision path (16 Oct 2026). An AOM supplier can make the AOM to this specification; the RF driver is the open item. Before confirming the AOM, get in writing: RF connector (SMB or SMA), maximum RF input power, diffraction efficiency at 795 nm and the RF power for it, AR coating covering 795 nm, input polarization, and a drawing. For the driver, three routes are compared: A, our planned build from parts: two-channel synthesizer (SynthHD), per channel an RF switch, a step attenuator, a 2 W amplifier and a monitor coupler, plus the DIY D8 bias box. B, a two-channel box from the AOM supplier built to our block diagram (two tunable channels from one clock, fast TTL gates, analog amplitude inputs, monitor ports, about 1 W per channel, 2 W maximum, a frequency sweep on the probe channel). C, a budget fallback: a four-channel DDS board based on the Analog Devices AD9959 (all channels from one clock, sub-hertz steps) in place of the synthesizer, with the same RF parts, a low-pass filter per channel, and our own control software. B is taken if it meets the specification and costs less than A; C only if the budget forces it. Whatever the route, a fixed-frequency driver (its own oscillator per channel) is never accepted: the 35 kHz difference must come from one clock and stay tunable. Can route A be simplified: no step attenuators, switches powered from the bench supply? (answer of 20 Oct 2026) Possible, and a smaller build, but not proven on this bench, and the guide has no step-by-step version of it yet (DIY D8 describes the full chain with attenuators). What the data sheets and the parts say: What the attenuators (R03) do. They set each arm's RF level in 0.5 dB steps and, with the DIP switches at 31.5 dB, give a safe state at power-up. The SynthHD can set its own level in software (public listings give roughly −40 to +20 dBm; the exact range at 80 MHz must be read from the data sheet of our unit), so the steps are not needed for tuning. What replaces the safe state. (1) The RF switch (R04) keeps its gate input pulled low, so the AOM gets no RF until the gate goes high. (2) Set the synthesizer level before enabling its output, and keep it at +1 dBm with the attenuator in the chain (never above +2 dBm for the 2 W FAOM; without the attenuators +1 dBm already gives about +31 dBm). (3) The amplifier takes at most +10 dBm at its input, so a fixed SMA attenuator of 6 dB in front of it, an inexpensive part, caps the worst case if the synthesizer ever powers up at a high stored level. This pad is my suggestion, not a Mini-Circuits requirement. Switch supply. The ZASWA-2-50DR+ needs +5 V and −5 V and a TTL gate (D8 records the pin numbers from its data sheet). A bench supply with two floating outputs can give ±5 V by joining the minus of one channel to the plus of the other as the common; check in the supply's manual that its channels float, and tie the common

Q7 Is the FAOM-780-80-1-L-T-A-K (780 nm design, 80 MHz, 1 mm free-space AOM) good for our bench? Would it still work if the EIT part is adjusted? Decision (21 Oct 2026): the 2 mm version, FAOM-780-80-2-L-T-A-K, is the AOM we order (same vendor, same price as the 1 mm one). Reasons: the laser has about ten times the light the cell needs, so the lower efficiency of a 2 mm unit at our 1 W of RF costs nothing we use; the Ø0.9 mm FiberPort beam passes the 2 mm aperture without loss and with alignment tolerance; the 2 mm aperture survives a later change of the beam; and its 2 W rating is not strained by our chain. The DIY parts D8 and D9 and the equipment row O17 follow the 2 mm figures. The sections below were written first for the 1 mm sheet and are kept as the audit trail. Workable for the planned bench, but not good to go as it stands: its data sheet leaves out the figures that decide it (maximum RF power, the conditions of the 85 %, both polarizations), and its 1 mm aperture needs a beam smaller than the Ø1 mm we planned. Data sheet read on 21 Oct 2026 (one page, Free-Space Acousto-Optic Modulator, TeO2, longitudinal wave, SMA, metal shell): wavelength 750–860 nm (typical 795), centre 80 MHz, 3 dB bandwidth ±20 MHz, diffraction efficiency 85 % (typical), clear aperture 3 × 1 mm, RF power 1 W, rise time 150–200 ns (160 typical), VSWR 1.2:1, 50 Ω, deflection 14.85 mrad, average optical power 10 W, housing about 41.8 × 25 × 13.5 mm. If the EIT part is adjusted slightly, does it still work? Mostly yes: Zeeman splitting, field or lock offset changed by up to a few MHz: yes, the ±20 MHz bandwidth is far larger than the kHz to MHz differences we use. The 160 MHz double-pass offset can be moved by roughly ±30 MHz (RF 65–95 MHz) at falling efficiency near the edges. Another line or isotope in the 750–860 nm range (the D2 line at 780 nm, ⁸⁵Rb): yes, the centre wavelength code is 780 nm. Longer or shorter pulses: fine from a few hundred nanoseconds upwards; not for pulses under about 100 ns. More control light: the laser has plenty; the AOM handles 10 W. A larger beam at the AOM (the direct free-space beam, the old Ø2 mm collimator, a second laser): no, not without a reducing telescope. This part ties the bench to the fibre-output beam, or to a beam reduced to about Ø0.6 mm. The hyperfine scheme with an EOM: the AOM only gates; no problem. Higher RF drive for more efficiency: not available, the sheet gives 1 W. Vendor reply of 21 Oct 2026 (to our eleven questions). Answered: the price is per unit and includes express shipping to Malaysia (the same for both models they sent data sheets for, the 1 mm and the 2 mm aperture version: I first misread this as "the same for both units"); delivery 4 weeks after payment; warranty 12 months from shipping; TeO₂ in longitudinal mode; it works in CW; the AR coating covers the data-sheet range; the on/off extinction can reach 50 dB with a suitable RF driver (our RF switch adds its own isolation); a heat sink is advised if it runs long at maximum RF power; a test report comes with the delivery. If the efficiency follows the usual sin² law, it would be about 54 % per pass at 1 W and about 69 % at 1.4 W, against 85 % for the 1 mm version at its 1 W. In the double pass that is about 30 % against about 72 % overall. We can afford it: the laser gives about ten times the power the cell needs, so the 2 mm version only costs light we do not need. Which to buy. The 2 mm version is the more robust choice at the same price: no clipping, a larger alignment tolerance, room for a larger beam if the optics change later, and an RF rating (2 W) that our +30 dBm chain does not strain; its cost is lower efficiency at 1 W and a need for a heat sink if it is driven at 2 W for long. Q8 What mirrors do we use, and what is their specification?

Q8 What mirrors do we use, and what is their specification? Equipment row O01: 11 Thorlabs PF10-03-P01 protected-silver mirrors, Ø1″, in KM100 kinematic mounts (row O02). Two steer the beam into the PM-fibre coupler (they are the former master-axis pair: after the output FiberPort the port itself sets the bench axis, so no separate pair is needed), three are in the SAS, two per EIT arm, and one retro mirror in each double pass. Item PF10-03-P01 (Thorlabs drawing) What we need Size Ø25.4 mm, 6.0 ± 0.2 mm thick, clear aperture > 22.9 mm fits the KM100 mount; beams are 1–5 mm Coating protected silver broadband, insensitive to the angle Reflectance average > 97.5 % from 450 nm to 2 µm, at 0–45° incidence high at 795 nm; each mirror loses about 2–3 % Flatness λ/10 at 633 nm λ/4 would do for steering; λ/10 keeps the cat's-eye return clean Surface quality 40-20 scratch-dig less scatter onto the detectors Substrate, parallelism fused silica, < 3 arcmin not critical (only the front surface is used) Things to watch Polarization: at 45° a metal mirror keeps a linear polarization unchanged only if it is s or p (perpendicular or parallel to the plane of incidence); anything in between becomes slightly elliptical. On our bench the beams are linear and horizontal or vertical before the quarter-wave plate, so this holds; there should be no 45° mirror between the quarter-wave plate that makes σ⁺/σ⁻ and the cell. Losses add up: about seven mirrors in a path at 97.5 % each leave about 84 %. That is fine with milliwatts to spare. A broadband dielectric mirror (for example Thorlabs BB1-E03, 750–1100 nm) reflects more but costs more and is more sensitive to the angle and polarization: check its data sheet if a path is short of power. A cheaper supplier is fine if the data sheet gives the same: Ø25.4 mm, protected silver (or a dielectric coating covering 795 nm), reflectance at 795 nm, λ/10 (or λ/4 for steering only), 0–45° incidence. A cheaper catalogue (silver mirror table, part "OQAg"): which one? The OQAg-25.4 (Ø25.4 mm, 5 mm thick, 450–2000 nm, reflectivity > 95 %, clear aperture > 90 %) is the one that matches: the right diameter for the Ø1″ mounts and thick enough to stay flat. Not the OQAg-25 (Ø25.0 mm sits loose in a Ø1″ mount) and not the 3 mm versions if the thicker one is available. Its > 95 % against > 97.5 % costs about 2.5 % more per mirror: seven mirrors leave about 70 % instead of 84 %, still far more than we need. Before ordering, ask what the table does not give: flatness (λ/10 at 633 nm wanted, λ/4 the least for steering), surface quality (60-40 or better), whether the silver is protected (overcoated, so it does not tarnish), the reflectance at 795 nm at 45° for s and p, and the substrate. Is the OQAg-25.4 suitable for every mirror on our table? Yes, for all 11, if the vendor confirms the four open points. What each role asks of a mirror: Where What matters OQAg-25.4 Steering mirrors (fibre coupling, SAS, control and probe arms) reflectance at 795 nm, no polarization change, no scatter; power is low (milliwatts; the two fibre mirrors see about 80 mW) fine: > 95 % (typical silver at 795 nm is higher); 80 mW heats the coating by about 4 mW, far below any limit Retro mirrors of the double pass the beam is focused to about 0.1 mm on the mirror, so flatness hardly matters; centring and a stable mount matter fine: surface quality and a good mount decide, not λ/10 Mirrors in the arms, in the master path the polarization there is horizontal or vertical (s or p), which a silver mirror at 45° leaves unchanged fine The two mirrors before the fibre coupler same rule, so the half-wave plate comes after them (see the sequence above); a flat mirror is not needed over a Ø1 mm beam fine, with the plate after them Where it would not be fine: a 45° mirror between the half-wave or quarter-wave plate and the cell (it would turn a pure polarization into an elliptical one), and any path that needs the last percent of power (a dielectric mirror gives about 99.5 % at its design wavelength). Four open points to put in writing with the vendor (the table gives none of them): the silver must be protected (overcoated), or it tarnishes in months; reflectance at 795 nm at 45° for s and p; flatness (λ/4 is enough for steering, and nothing here needs better); surface quality 60-40 or better. The 5 mm thickness is thinner than the Thorlabs 6 mm and fits the KM100 the same way (check that the retaining ring still clamps it).
