Q9 What specification do the polarizing beamsplitter cubes (PBS) need?

Q9 What specification do the polarizing beamsplitter cubes (PBS) need? Seven broadband cemented PBS cubes (620–1000 nm coating) with a transmitted extinction of at least 1000:1 are enough; laser-line cubes (3000:1) are not needed, because the Glan–Taylor does the final separation after the cell. Our listed part, the Thorlabs CM1-PBS252, was discontinued in 2016: the replacement is the CCM1-PBS252/M (the /M version has metric taps), now in BOM O03. The non-polarizing SAS cube CM1-BS014 was discontinued too; it is replaced by the CCM1-BS014/M (BOM O04). Item Requirement Why Wavelength 795 nm inside the coating band (620–1000 nm broadband is fine); AR-coated faces Rb D1; every bare face would reflect about 4 % Transmitted extinction Tp:Ts ≥ 1000:1 this is the clean port: use it wherever purity matters Reflected extinction Rs:Rp about 20:1 to 100:1 (what cube PBSs give) acceptable: each beam has already been cleaned by an earlier cube, and the Glan–Taylor (10⁵) cleans the probe at the end Transmission Tp > 90 % (Thorlabs figure) the control makes four cube passes; losses multiply Aperture cube ≥ ½″ (12.7 mm); the Thorlabs part is 1″ beams are 1–1.5 mm, the expanded control about 5 mm Damage any catalogue cube even 100 mW in a 1 mm beam is far below the rating Mount 30 mm cage cube with metric taps, or an unmounted cube on a kinematic platform the cage version holds the cube square, with SM1 ports for wave plates and irises Quantity 7 pick-off to the SAS, control/probe splitter, 2 SAS cubes, 2 double-pass separators, recombiner Where the extinction matters Double-pass separators. The returning beam must leave by the other port; whatever passes back goes towards the laser. The 1000:1 cube plus the wave-plate error give about 10⁻³ returned, which is why the isolator is needed (see the isolator answer). Recombiner. Control and probe meet here in orthogonal polarizations. Control light in the probe polarization would reach the detector, because the Glan–Taylor cannot remove light that already has the probe polarization. With clean beams arriving (each from an earlier cube), the leak is of order 10⁻⁶ of the control, a few nW against a probe of about 0.5 µW: acceptable. Pick-off and splitter. Here the cube only sets a power ratio with the half-wave plate in front, so the extinction does not matter. Cheaper option: unmounted cubes from a general optics supplier. The cage housing is most of the cost; the cube itself is a standard part. The Spain-style bench does the same: its videos show uncaged cubes on the boards. Search terms: "polarizing beam splitter cube 780nm", "PBS cube 12.7mm 700-900nm", "polarization beamsplitter cube extinction ratio 1000:1". What to ask for: cemented cube polarizing beamsplitter, 12.7 × 12.7 × 12.7 mm (10 mm or 25.4 mm also fine), N-BK7 or equivalent; design wavelength 795 nm (a 780–800 nm laser-line or a 700–900 nm broadband coating); transmitted extinction Tp:Ts ≥ 1000:1 measured at 795 nm (listings often quote the best point of a broad band; reject 500:1 parts); Tp ≥ 90 %, Rs ≥ 99 %; AR coating on all four faces at 795 nm (R ≤ 0.5 %); cheap cubes are sometimes uncoated; beam deviation ≤ 5 arcmin, flatness λ/4 at 633 nm, scratch-dig 60-40, clear aperture ≥ 85 %; 7 pieces plus 1 spare, with the measured extinction and transmission at 795 nm. K9 or N-BK7? Either. K9 (CDGM H-K9L) is the Chinese equivalent of Schott N-BK7: the same borosilicate crown glass, refractive index about 1.517 and Abbe number about 64, fully transparent at 795 nm. At our milliwatt powers absorption does not matter. What decides the cube is the coating (made for 795 nm), the extinction measured at 795 nm, and a well-annealed, bubble-free glass (stress in the glass is birefringent and lowers the extinction): ask the supplier for the glass grade or the measured extinction, not for N-BK7 by name. The same holds for the non-polarizing cube. A promise is not a data sheet. "We can follow your spec" counts only when the vendor's data sheet or test report states the figures at 795 nm: coating design wavelength, Tp, Ts (or Tp:Ts), AR reflectance per face, size and tolerance, beam deviation. Ask for the measured curve or the batch test data, and check one cube on arrival with our own laser: transmitted power with and without the cube (Tp), then a polarizer after the transmitted port turned for the minimum (extinction), using the power meter. Watch the design wavelength. A supplier sheet that says "@1064 nm" (or 532, 633 nm) describes a cube whose polarizing and AR coatings are made for that line. Its geometry figures (±0.2 mm, λ/10, beam deviation under 3 arcmin) may be excellent, but at 795 nm the extinction and transmission of a laser-line coating fall off and the faces reflect more: ask for the same cube coated for 795 nm (or 780 nm, or 700–900 nm broadband) with the extinction measured at 795 nm. For the SAS 50:50 cube ask: non-polarizing cube, 12.7 mm, 700–900 nm, R/T = 50/50 ± 5 % for both s and p at 795 nm. Mounting an unmounted cube: a kinematic prism platform on a post, or a 3D-printed PETG cube holder on a ½″ (Ø12.7 mm) post at the 100 mm beam height: now DIY part D12, with STL files, a drawing and the build steps. The holder must hold the cube square to the beam (within a degree) and allow rotation about the vertical axis for alignment; fix the cube with a nylon-tipped screw or a drop of removable adhesive, never by clamping the faces. Is a printed holder precise enough? Yes, for a cube PBS, with three conditions. A PBS needs far less precision than its price suggests: Squareness. An FDM print on the Bambu A1 is typically within about 0.1 mm (to be confirmed with a test print and a calliper). Over a 15 mm seat that is about 0.4°. The cube is pushed by a light spring or nylon screw against two printed reference walls, so the angle comes from those walls, not from the clearance of the pocket. A cube a fraction of a degree off normal still separates the polarizations; the reflected beam turns by twice the error, about 0.8°, and the next mirror takes that out during alignment. Height and rotation. The beam height is set by the post in its post holder, and the rotation about the vertical axis by turning the post, so print tolerance in height does not matter. Drift is what matters, not the starting angle. A lever of 0.3 m from the recombiner to the cell turns 0.1 mrad of creep into 30 µm at the cell, small next to the 0.47 mm probe and 2.55 mm control radii. To keep creep that small: a firm joint at the post (an M4 screw through the print into the post, as in the D11 holder, with a steel washer under the head so the plastic is not crushed), and a light load on the cube. Heat is not an issue here: all PBS positions are well away from the heated cell (PETG softens near 80 °C). Where we would still buy a metal mount: nowhere in the PBS positions. The places that need fine tip and tilt are the mirrors and the double-pass retro mirrors, which stay commercial kinematic mounts. Alternative: the lab's resin (MSLA/SLA) printer. Resin gives sharper corners, smoother walls and finer detail than FDM, so the reference walls and a small flexure spring for the cube come out cleaner; layer lines and anisotropy are not an issue. Its weak points are mechanical, not dimensional: Brittleness at the screw. Standard resins crack when an M4 screw is tightened into or onto them. Use a tough or ABS-like resin, a through-hole with a large steel washer, and hand-tight torque; do not use heat-set inserts in resin. Creep, moisture and ageing. Many resins creep under a constant clamp load, take up moisture and keep curing under UV light, which can change a dimension slowly. Wash and fully post-cure, let the part rest a day, then measure it with a calliper before fitting the cube. Supports and shrinkage. Orient the part so the reference walls and the base are not on supports (support marks spoil a datum), and allow for the resin's cure shrinkage when sizing the pocket (measure a test pocket first). Heat. Standard resins soften at lower temperatures than PETG; this does not matter at the PBS positions, which are away from the heated cell. Decided (14 Oct 2026): PETG on the Bambu A1. Our judgement: PETG on the Bambu A1 is the first choice for the cube holders, because it is tough at the screw and already proven on the bench parts. Resin is a good alternative for the seat when a sharper fit is wanted, best in a tough resin; a hybrid (resin seat glued onto a PETG base that takes the screw) combines both. Either way the acceptance test below decides; for resin, repeat it after a week to catch slow creep. Acceptance test before printing seven: print one holder, mount a cube, send the laser (or a red pointer) through it and mark the reflected spot on a wall about 2 m away; check it again after a day and after gently tapping the post. A drift under about 0.5 mm (0.25 mrad) is good enough for every PBS position on our bench. Printed optomechanics has been compared with commercial part

Q10 Is a double-pass AOM practical on our table, how is it arranged, and who uses it?

Q10 Is a double-pass AOM practical on our table, how is it arranged, and who uses it? Yes. It is the standard way to shift and switch a laser beam with an AOM in atomic physics labs. The classic description is Donley et al. (NIST), "Double-pass acousto-optic modulator system", Rev. Sci. Instrum. 76, 063112 (2005), who report 75 % double-pass diffraction efficiency and a 60 MHz tuning bandwidth. The reference guide we follow (Finkelstein et al., New J. Phys. 25, 035001 (2023), Fig. 10) uses one double-pass AOM per beam for Zeeman EIT and notes that "the double-pass AOM configuration suppresses spatial misalignment of the beam during the scanning". Why double pass Twice the shift: the light is shifted by 2 × f_RF (160 MHz at 80 MHz). The beam does not move when the frequency changes: a single pass deflects the beam by an angle that depends on the RF frequency; on the way back the cat's eye sends the beam through the same point, so the output direction stays fixed while the probe is scanned. This is the main reason for using it. Better on/off: the light is diffracted twice, so leakage when the RF is off is squared, which helps the storage pulses. How it is arranged (one arm, about 25–30 cm of table) 1. Half-wave plate, then the PBS: the incoming beam passes the PBS (p-polarized). 2. The AOM on its yaw platform (DIY D9), turned to the Bragg angle (7.6 mrad at 80 MHz and 795 nm). 3. A lens (f = 100 mm, BOM O08) one focal length after the AOM. 4. A quarter-wave plate, then a flat mirror at the focus, one focal length after the lens: lens and mirror form a "cat's eye" that sends every ray back along itself. 5. At the mirror the diffracted beam and the undiffracted (0th order) beam are about 1.5 mm apart (100 mm × 15 mrad): a razor blade or iris there blocks the 0th order. 6. The returning beam is recollimated by the lens, diffracted by the AOM a second time (another +f_RF), and arrives at the PBS turned to s-polarization (it crossed the quarter-wave plate twice), so the PBS reflects it out sideways: this is the arm's output. Alignment, in order 1. Single pass first: set the Bragg angle with the D9 micrometer for the strongest first order (RF at the working level). 2. Place the lens at f and the mirror at its focus; steer the mirror so the beam returns on itself through the AOM. 3. Block the 0th order at the mirror. 4. Turn the quarter-wave plate for the most power out of the PBS side port. 5. Check: change the RF by ±1 MHz; the output beam must not move. Expect about 50–60 % double-pass efficiency with a good AOM (about 70–80 % per pass). All parts are in the equipment list (AOMs O17, lenses O08, mirrors and mounts O01/O02, quarter-wave plates O06, PBS O03) and the D9 platform in the DIY Section. The 3D bench shows both double-pass arms. Sources: Donley et al., Rev. Sci. Instrum. 76, 063112 (2005), NIST PDF · Finkelstein et al., arXiv:2205.10959 Added 16 Oct 2026

Q11 What linewidths and frequencies do we have to set? Item Value Rb-87 D1 line 794.978851 nm in vacuum (about 377.107 THz) Control AOM 80.000 MHz, double pass, so +160.000 MHz Probe AOM 79.965 MHz, double pass, so +159.930 MHz Control–probe difference 70 kHz, the ground-state splitting at 50 mG (1.4 kHz per mG) Solenoid field about 50 mG (the photographed COILS supply showed about 80 mA) Lock dither about 10–100 kHz on the laser current (the ITC502 modulation covers 0–500 kHz) Excited-state splitting 814.5 MHz (F′=1 to F′=2) Ground-state splitting 6.8347 GHz, never needed by the AOMs EIT linewidth target 30 kHz or narrower, approaching 10 kHz at low power Laser linewidth 0.6–1.0 MHz (needs only to be below about 100 MHz) SAS feature width about 6–12 MHz 80 MHz in the RF, 160 MHz in the light. 80.000 and 79.965 MHz are the RF frequencies of the two AOMs. Each beam passes its AOM twice (double pass), so its light is shifted by twice the RF: 160.000 MHz for the control and 159.930 MHz for the probe. The two beams differ by 70 kHz, which is what EIT needs. The 160 MHz that both share is the offset from the laser, which is locked to the F = 2 → F′ = 1 line through the SAS cell (no AOM there): both EIT beams therefore sit 160 MHz off that line. We use the −1 order in both AOMs, so they sit 160 MHz below it, away from F′ = 2. EIT depends only on the 70 kHz difference; the common 160 MHz only costs some absorption (the cell runs about 3 °C warmer). Is the doubling real or only theory? Real, and exact. Each pass through the AOM scatters the light off the moving sound wave: the photon gains or loses exactly one RF quantum, so its frequency changes by exactly f_RF (+1 or −1 order). In the double pass the cat's eye sends the diffracted beam back into the same order, so it is shifted a second time: exactly 2 × f_RF. The shift is as exact as the synthesizer (both channels come from one clock), not an approximation. This is routine in atomic physics labs (Donley et al., Rev. Sci. Instrum. 76, 063112 (2005), measured it with a beat note). What is not perfect is the power: only the light diffracted twice carries 2 × f_RF (40 to 60 % of the input), the rest (unshifted, or shifted once) leaves at other angles and is stopped by the razor blade and the irises. Check it on our bench: overlap the arm output with a little unshifted laser light on a fast photodiode and look for the 160 MHz beat on the oscilloscope (it needs well over 160 MHz of bandwidth); between the two arms the beat is 70 kHz, visible on any photodiode. What the two RF frequencies do (and do not do). 80.000 MHz drives the control AOM and 79.965 MHz drives the probe AOM (megahertz, not kilohertz). They are our design choice: 80 MHz is the centre frequency of the AOMs, and the 35 kHz between them follows the Zeeman splitting we set. An RF frequency only shifts the light frequency; as long as the RF is on, the light is continuous (CW EIT). Pulses come from switching the RF on and off with the TTL gate of each channel: the probe gate cuts a short probe pulse, and the control gate turns the control off and on for storage. So the frequencies decide where the light sits, the gates decide when it is there. Where the numbers come from. The reference guide (Finkelstein et al., New J. Phys. 25, 035001 (2023), Sec. V) gives the method and the scale, not our RF values: double-pass AOMs "driven by twin phase-locked rf signals from the same dual-output waveform generator", Zeeman shifts of 0.7 kHz per mG between adjacent F = 2 sub-levels, a 50 mG solenoid field as the example (adjacent sub-levels 35 kHz apart), and a probe scan of less than ±100 kHz around a fixed control frequency. It gives no AOM centre frequency. The 80 MHz is the centre frequency of the AOMs we buy, and 79.965 MHz follows from our Λ (m = −1 and m = +1, two steps apart: 70 kHz in the light at 50 mG, halved by the double pass). The Spain-style bench does not show its frequencies. Finkelstein's 0.7 kHz per mG and our 1.4 kHz per mG: the same constant. For Rb-87 F = 2 the Zeeman shift is g_F μ_B B m with g_F = ½ and μ_B/h = 1.40 MHz per gauss, so each step of one in m moves by 0.7 kHz per mG: the guide's number, the gap between neighbouring sub-levels. Our Λ spans two steps (σ⁺ control and σ⁻ probe meet at one excited sub-level, for example m = −1 and m = +1 through F′ = 1, m = 0), so the gap the two beams must match is 2 × 0.7 = 1.4 kHz per mG. The other Λ pairs (m = −2 with 0, and 0 with +2) are also two steps apart, so they all meet at the same value and add up to one EIT peak. The double pass then halves it again on the driver: Per mG At 50 mG neighbouring sub-levels (the guide's number) 0.7 kHz 35 kHz our Λ ground states (Δm = 2): light difference needed 1.4 kHz 70 kHz RF difference between the two AOMs (double pass, ÷ 2) 0.7 kHz 35 kHz From the solenoid current to the two AOM frequencies: 14.75 mA, 50 mG, one step 35 kHz, light difference 70 kHz, RF difference 35 kHz, 80.000 and 79.965 MHz (click to open full size) Try it with sliders: the interactive flow page moves the solenoid current, redraws the sub-levels and the Λ gap, updates both RF channels, and shows the EIT peak appear only when the RF difference matches the field. Why do the two RF channels differ by 35 kHz? EIT needs two-photon resonance. In our Λ system the control (σ⁺) connects F = 2, m = −1 to the excited state F′ = 1, m = 0, and the probe (σ⁻) connects F = 2, m = +1 to the same excited state. The probe passes (EIT) only when the frequency difference of the two beams equals the energy difference of the two lower states. The lower states are split by the solenoid field. For F = 2 of Rb-87 the Zeeman shift is g_F μ_B B / h = 0.70 MHz per gauss for each step in m (g_F = 1/2). The two states differ by Δm = 2, so the splitting is 1.40 MHz per gauss, that is 1.4 kHz per mG. At our working field of about 50 mG: 1.4 × 50 = 70 kHz. Each AOM is passed twice. A double pass shifts the light by 2 × f_RF, so the light frequencies differ by 2 × (f₁ − f₂). To get 70 kHz in the light, the RF channels differ by 70 / 2 = 35 kHz: 80.000 MHz and 79.965 MHz. Why a field at all, instead of 0 G and equal frequencies? The solenoid field along the beam sets the quantization axis, so that "σ⁺" and "σ⁻" are well defined, and it is about 50 mG, far above what the shield leaves (well below a milligauss), so stray fields cannot move the resonance. The AOM difference is then simply matched to the splitting that this field produces. Physics or our design? Both. The 1.4 kHz per mG is a constant of the Rb-87 atom (it cannot change). The field is our choice: the solenoid gives 3.39 mG per mA (DIY D1), so 50 mG needs about 14.7 mA from the ITC502. The RF difference is then 0.7 kHz per mG × the field we set. No risk of "missing" the condition with the AOMs we buy. We can always meet it from either side: change the solenoid current until the splitting matches the RF difference, or change the RF difference (the driver is tunable in 1 Hz steps over 70–90 MHz on each channel) until it matches the splitting. Even 0 G with equal frequencies works. The only purchase that would trap us is a fixed-frequency driver, which is exactly why the specification asks for two tunable channels from one clock. The AOMs themselves (80 MHz, 25 MHz bandwidth) do not care about a difference of a few tens of kHz. It is not a magic number. If the field is set differently, the RF difference follows it (35 kHz for 50 mG, 0.7 kHz per mG of RF difference). For the EIT spectrum, the probe channel is swept a little around 79.965 MHz, and the transparency peak appears where the two-photon condition is met. Which channel is higher depends on the field direction and on which beam is σ⁺; if no peak appears, swap the sign of the difference. Because the offset between the two beams is only kHz, a generator with 1 Hz resolution is far more than precise enough. The control–probe difference must stay steady to well under the EIT width (a few kHz): use one two-channel source, or sources sharing a clock. Added 9 Oct 2026

The rule: the laser tunes at about 1.4 GHz per mA, so every 1 µA rms of driver noise can become about 1.4 MHz of linewidth. Controller Noise Verdict G&H EM595 5 µA rms (10 Hz–10 MHz) usable, up to about 7 MHz worst case, the noisiest Thorlabs ITC502 under 1.5 µA rms about 2 MHz worst case: best match ILX LDX-3220 not found current source only, needs a separate TEC controller Thorlabs ITC4001 not found no proven advantage A 5 µA driver does not harm EIT (the optical line is about 100 MHz wide and both beams share the noise) but it blurs the 6–12 MHz SAS features and makes the lock noisier. Q13 Do we tune the laser to 794.98 nm with temperature or with current, and how do the Yanban and BrandNew data sheets compare?

Q13 Do we tune the laser to 794.98 nm with temperature or with current, and how do the Yanban and BrandNew data sheets compare? Short answer: use both, for different jobs. The temperature does the coarse, slow tuning and is set once. The current does the fine, fast tuning and is the one the lock controls. Neither vendor builds a laser "at 794.98 nm" to order: every DFB chip comes out within about ±1 nm of nominal, and each unit is brought onto the Rb line with its own temperature and current. So what counts is the measured wavelength of the actual unit, not the nominal 795 nm. The two knobs, in plain words Temperature (TEC) Current How much it tunes 0.06 nm per °C, about 28 GHz per kelvin 0.004 nm per mA, about 1.9 GHz per mA Range large: ±1 nm needs about ±17 °C small: the whole current range gives only about 0.4 nm Speed slow (seconds to minutes) fast (the modulation input works to 500 kHz) Side effect almost none on the power the power changes too, about 1 mW per mA (estimate from 100 mW at 150 mA and a threshold near 40 mA) Stability very stable once settled, but a drift of 10 mK is already about 280 MHz follows the driver noise: 1 µA is about 1.9 MHz Role set it once, near the line the lock feeds back to it Our example: 795.000 nm to 794.980 nm is 0.02 nm, about 9.5 GHz. That is about 5 mA, or about 0.33 °C. Both are possible, and 9.5 GHz is inside the 20 GHz mode-hop-free range quoted by both vendors. But current alone cannot repair a unit that is 0.5 or 1 nm off (it would need 100 mA or more, which the laser cannot take); that is what the temperature is for. Which is easier and more stable? Easier: the temperature. Set it with the controller, wait a minute, and the wavelength settles. More stable: neither by itself. The temperature is quiet but drifts slowly, the current follows the driver noise. This is why we lock the laser to the saturated-absorption (SAS) signal of the Rb cell: the lock moves the current to cancel any drift, so the laser stays on the line to within about a MHz. The routine: (1) fix the current for the power you want (about 150 mA); (2) tune the temperature until the SAS cell shows the D1 lines, scanning the current by a few mA to see them (the cell itself is the wavelength reference, no wavelength meter needed); (3) switch on the lock, which then moves only the current; (4) if the current drifts far from the middle of its range, nudge the temperature a little. On the ITC502 front panel the steps are coarse (10 µA is about 19 MHz at 1.9 GHz per mA, and the smallest temperature step is a few mK, tens of MHz): tune by hand roughly and let the lock do the fine work. Yanban RB-795-DFB-BFW against BrandNew FS795SM01 (both from the vendors' data sheets, typical values) Yanban BrandNew Wavelength target 794.97 nm (794–796), "guaranteed to hit the Rb D1 line" 795 nm ±1 nm Temperature and current tuning 0.06 nm/°C, 0.004 nm/mA 0.06 nm/°C, 0.004 nm/mA Power 100 mW minimum, 120 mW typical 100 mW (not said whether minimum) Linewidth 200 kHz typical (500 kHz maximum) 2 MHz Mode-hop-free tuning 20 GHz 20 GHz Side-mode suppression 40 dB minimum, 45 dB typical 45 dB Divergence 0.1° (full or half angle not stated) 1° in both axes (looks like a different number or a typing error; to be asked) Current / TEC / thermistor 150 mA typical, 175 mA maximum / 0.4 A / 10 kΩ 150 mA, threshold 40 mA / 4 A, 12 V maximum rating / 10 kΩ Package and pins 14-pin butterfly, free space 14-pin butterfly, free space, the same pin layout Isolator inside none none stated Test report of the unit asked asked Reading: the two data sheets are almost the same laser on paper (same tuning slopes, same mode-hop range, same package and pins). The differences are the BrandNew's looser numbers: the wavelength is only "795 nm ±1 nm", the linewidth is ten times wider, the divergence is ten times larger, and the power is not stated as a minimum. These may be real or typing differences; we asked the BrandNew vendor. Until then the Yanban stays our plan, because it states a measured wavelength for a real unit and the better numbers. Whichever laser we buy, neither has an isolator, so we use two free-space isolators. What to ask a vendor (and what we asked): the measured wavelength of the actual unit at 25 °C and 100 mW, the test report (L-I-V curve, spectrum, wavelength), whether 100 mW is a minimum, and, if the unit does not reach 794.98 nm within 15–35 °C, the return policy. Q19 Which instruments record the result, and which photodetectors do we need? (PDA36A2, PDB210A balanced detector, AD-300/DC) The result comes from a photodetector read on the oscilloscope. The power meter is a setup tool. The EIT signal is the probe transmission while the two-photon detuning is scanned, and the window is only about 7–30 kHz wide. A USB or benchtop power meter updates far too slowly to follow a scan, shows only a number, and the S140C floor (1 µW) is close to the probe power (about 2 µW). Instrument Job Signal photodetector + oscilloscope EIT transmission: the result SAS photodiode (+ ITC502) laser lock signal Power meter (PM100USB + S140C) fibre, control and AOM-efficiency checks before the run Fabry-Perot or wavemeter single-mode and mode-hop check (missing from the budget) Fluxgate or gaussmeter shield and 50 mG field check (the FLC100 answer below) Beam profiler or camera, IR card beam size (sets the intensity) and alignment Fast detector (AD-300/DC) control and probe beat note, AOM pulse shapes Signal detector: the Thorlabs PDA36A2, two needed, a third optional. It is an amplified silicon detector (350–1100 nm, 8 switchable gain steps, 0–70 dB, 3.6 × 3.6 mm chip). One for the probe signal after the Glan-Taylor (the EIT result). One for the SAS lock signal. Optional third: the control beam monitor or a reference channel. The AD-300/DC we own can serve as a diagnostic channel. Gain: the probe is only about 2 µW, so use about 50–60 dB. At 70 dB the bandwidth falls to a few kHz, which is marginal for a 7–30 kHz window. The SAS detector can use a lower gain. The PDA36A2 normally ships with its ±12 V supply; check before buying a separate LDS12B. The 3D bench, the Spain-style bench and the equipment table show the PDA36A2 drawn from the Thorlabs outline drawing (approximate dimensions). The Thorlabs PDB210A balanced detector: not needed, it is overkill. A balanced detector subtracts the laser intensity noise with a second reference beam. The reference papers do without it: Finkelstein et al. 2022: the probe passes a Glan-Taylor and is focused on "a fast photodiode"; the probe is scanned and the EIT spectrum is recorded. DeRose et al.: one New Focus 1621 photodiode on a digital oscilloscope (low detector impedance to avoid cable reflections); the pump leakage was reduced with a Glan polariser, not a better detector. The EIT window is slow (7–30 kHz), so averaging on the oscilloscope recovers any noise. Use the two PDA36A2 detectors. Try balanced detection only if the probe is still too noisy after the Glan-Taylor, scope averaging and a lock-in. The PDB210A datasheet could not be retrieved, so its price and bandwidth are unverified. The Newport AD-300/DC fast detector: a good diagnostic, not the main probe detector. No datasheet was found for this number; the closest Newport parts are the 818-BB amplified detectors (rise time under 400 ps). Use it to watch AOM switching and pulse shapes on the oscilloscope, the control–probe beat note, or the strong SAS beam. For the weak probe (about 2 µW at the cell) a gain-adjustable low-noise detector such as the Thorlabs PDA36A2 is better: EIT pulses last microseconds, so 300 ps speed only adds noise. Check the responsivity at 795 nm, the supply it needs and its output into 50 Ω before use. Sources: Finkelstein et al. 2022, DeRose et al. Added 10 Oct 2026

Q21 How do I use the second ITC502 as the cell-heater controller (connection and set-up)?

Q21 How do I use the second ITC502 as the cell-heater controller (connection and set-up)? Assignment: the first ITC502 with an LDM-4980 mount is reserved for the DFB laser; the second ITC502 runs the cell heater with its TEC half and, if wished, the solenoid with its laser half. Everything below is from the ITC500 operation manual. The plug, the heater and the dummy-load test are drawn and built step by step in the DIY Section (parts D2 and D3). TEC output (15-pin D-sub, rear). TEC (+) is pins 5, 6 and 7, TEC (−) is pins 13, 14 and 15; all three pins of each must be connected. Pins 2 and 9 sense the heater voltage (optional). The output is ±2 A, 16 W, compliance above 8 V, and the (−) side is at ground. Thermistor: pins 3 and 4 (if one lead of the thermistor is grounded, it goes to pin 3). Use shielded cable and connect the shield to pins 13–15. Pin 12 is a supply for Thorlabs mounts: leave it alone. ITC502 rear panel as seen from behind: A = TEC OUT, B = LD OUT, C = DIP switches (click to open full size) ITC502 unit 2: wiring of the cell heater on the TEC OUT jack, drawn as you look into the jack (click to open full size) Heater wiring. 1. TEC (+) → a series power diode (for example 1N5400, 3 A) → the foil heater → TEC (−). 2. A 10 kΩ NTC glued to the cell wall next to the heater, with Kapton tape or thermal epoxy, on a twisted shielded pair away from the heater leads. 3. Twist the two heater leads together along their whole length (and wind the foil bifilar) so that the DC current makes almost no field in the shield. Why the diode. The controller reverses its current when the temperature is above the set-point. A resistor heats for either polarity, so without a diode an overshoot would make it heat more: a thermal runaway (the manual warns that a TEC with wrong polarity can run away and destroy the parts). The diode blocks the reverse current; the 0.8 V drop is small against 8 V. Front panel and DIP switches. Sensor: DIP switches SW7/SW8 to "TH < 20 kΩ" (100 µA measurement current; the setting range is 10 Ω to 19.99 kΩ), and the SENSOR button to thermistor. The display shows the thermistor resistance in ohms, so convert: R = R0·exp[B(1/T − 1/T0)] (temperatures in kelvin; R0 and B from the thermistor datasheet). A 10 kΩ NTC with B ≈ 3900 K reads about 2.1 kΩ at 65 °C. Select the display T SET and dial the value in with the TEC knob. TEC current limit: select the display I TEC LIM and set it with the small screwdriver pot beside its LED; use 0.3 A for the dummy-load test and 0.50 A for the real heater on the open bench and 0.33 A once it is inside the closed shield (so even a runaway stays below about 85 °C), and keep heater resistance × current under about 7 V (a 12 Ω heater at 0.6 A gives about 4 W). Temperature window protection: select T WIN, set about ±200 Ω (a few degrees), and switch SW5 down (WIN on). If the temperature leaves the window the output switches off. PID: start from the factory values (chapter 2.15.4 of the manual), raise P until the temperature oscillates a little, then back off. Raise the set-point in steps of 10 °C. Warm-up for rated accuracy is up to 10 minutes. First switch-on (diode direction). Start with the cell at room temperature and T SET warmer than the cell. Press TEC ON. If I TEC reads a current and T ACT rises towards T SET, the diode is the right way round. If I TEC stays at about 0 mA and nothing heats, reverse the diode. Never start with T SET below the cell temperature, and never remove the diode. (The dummy-load test of the DIY Section settles the direction before the cell is connected.) Check the field. With the fluxgate inside the shield, switch the heater on and off: the change should be small compared with 1 mG (the DIY test uses 0.1 mG). If not, twist the leads tighter. Added 10 Oct 2026

Q22 Is it safe to wrap the bifilar heater directly round the rubidium cell?

Q22 Is it safe to wrap the bifilar heater directly round the rubidium cell? Yes, if the heater stays on the barrel and the controller's current limit is set so that even a runaway stays cool. Glass: 1 to 2 W spread over the 68 × 24 mm heater is about 0.1 W per cm², so the wire runs only a little warmer than the glass. Quartz takes the slow warm-up easily. The heater never covers a window, and no wire crosses one: the runs are 22 mm long on the 24.8 mm barrel between the windows (corrected on 19 Oct 2026; the earlier 25 mm runs would have reached the window joints). Electrical: 12 Ω at under 0.42 A is a few volts. The two Kapton films insulate it (check heater to NTC above 10 MΩ), and the diode of D3 stops the controller from driving the heater backwards. Magnetic: the bifilar pairing cancels the heater's own field. The on-and-off test in the shield must show less than 0.1 mG. Rubidium: keep the windows a little warmer than the stem, so the metal condenses in the stem and not on the windows. Runaway: if the NTC comes off the glass, the ITC502 drives its full limit. So set I TEC LIM to 0.50 A on the open bench (worst case about 84 °C) and 0.33 A inside the closed shield (also about 84 °C). Both still give the power needed at 65 °C, and both stay below the 100 °C rating of the foam and the epoxy. The earlier figure of 0.6 A was too high for a runaway inside the shield. What is the foam sleeve made of, and will silicone foam survive the heater? The sleeve is not printed: it is 3 mm melamine foam or silicone foam, cut from sheet and wrapped on (ID 25.6, OD 31.6, 34 long, a Ø10 hole for the stem). PETG would sit directly on the heater, close to its softening range, and solid plastic insulates several times worse than foam. The rules: no metal at all (no aluminium-foil facing), a temperature rating of at least 100 °C, and exactly 3 mm (the radial room to the former bore is 1.2 mm). Melamine foam Silicone sponge sheet Insulation better less good: more heat needed Handling crumbly, sheds dust: wrap it in polyimide tape tough, easy to cut, no dust Temperature far above our 84 °C worst case commonly rated to about 200 °C (check the data sheet) Silicone does not burn or melt here: the worst case with the current limits is about 84 °C. Buy a sheet that states "silicone" and a temperature rating (some cheap sponge sheets are polyurethane or neoprene), and hold a scrap on the heater during the open-bench test at 0.50 A for an hour: no smell, no darkening, no shrinking. Because silicone insulates less, check that the cell still reaches 65 °C inside the closed shield at 0.33 A; if not, use melamine (a thicker sleeve does not fit). Added 11 Oct 2026

Q23 Can we heat the cell the Duke way (heaters and insulation wrapped in aluminium foil)?

Q23 Can we heat the cell the Duke way (heaters and insulation wrapped in aluminium foil)? Partly. The foil itself is fine and can be added as an outer layer, but the Duke heater cannot be copied as it is: their experiment does not need a milligauss-quiet field, and ours does. The Duke page shows a cell inside "a collection of heating elements and insulation" with aluminium foil wrapped round the outside, held at about 72 °C, inside Helmholtz coils that only cancel the axial part of the Earth's field. No shield, and nothing about how the heater is wound. Part of their method For our Zeeman EIT Why Aluminium foil as the outer wrap yes, optional aluminium is not magnetic; at DC it makes no field. It reflects heat radiation, but inside our closed stack most heat leaves by conduction, so the gain is small. Unspecified heating elements no, use our bifilar heater (DIY D2) an ordinary heater wire or tape carries about 1 A; one loop of it near the cell makes far more than our 0.1 mG budget. The bifilar winding cancels its own field; we test it with the fluxgate before use. 72 °C close to ours (55–65 °C) the temperature sets the vapour density; the target comes from the paper, not from Duke. Helmholtz coils only, no shield no 1.4 kHz per mG: we need the three-layer shield and the solenoid. If you add foil One layer (about 20 µm) over the foam sleeve: it fits in the former bore (radial room about 1 mm). Keep it off the beam: leave both window ends open. Insulate it from the heater leads and the thermistor (it conducts) and do not let it touch the solenoid winding. Do not close it into a loop round the cell with a soldered or overlapping conductive joint if the heater is ever driven with AC or PWM: a closed ring is a one-turn coil. With DC from the ITC502 it does not matter, but leave a small gap anyway. Keep the windows a few degrees warmer than the stem, or rubidium condenses on the windows. The foil should not cover the windows more than the heater does. Accuracy does not depend on the foil: it depends on where the thermistor sits (on the glass, near the beam) and on the controller. With the ITC502 and a 10 kΩ NTC the setting is stable to well below 0.1 K. Verdict: keep our bifilar heater, foam and tubes (DIY D2); an outer foil layer is allowed and harmless, but it is not a replacement for a non-magnetic heater. Added 11 Oct 2026

Q28 How do we make sure every optical part stands at 90° (vertical and square to the beam)? Is it practically doable?

Q28 How do we make sure every optical part stands at 90° (vertical and square to the beam)? Is it practically doable? Yes, and it is routine. Nobody measures 90° with a protractor or a bubble level. The beam itself is the ruler. The standard practice in optics labs has two stages. First, one beam is made parallel to the table at a fixed height (100 mm on our bench) with two mirrors and two irises ("beam walking"). Then every optic is squared to that beam by looking at where its own reflection goes. Both checks are far more sensitive than any angle you could set by eye. How every optic is made square to the beam: beam walking with two irises, constant height, back-reflection check and PBS roll check (click to open full size) Stage 1: one straight, level beam (panels A and B) 1. Screw two irises (BOM O11, ID12/M) into one row of table holes, both set to the same 100 mm centre height with one height gauge: the same post and holder type, a calliper and slip-on post collars. Put I1 near the steering mirrors and I2 as far away as the table allows. 2. Mirror M1 puts the spot on I1, mirror M2 puts it on I2. Repeat until the beam passes both closed-down irises. The first mirror mostly sets the position, the second mostly the angle, so alternating converges. 3. The beam is now on the hole row and level. The error is simply angle × distance: 1 mrad (0.057°) gives 1 mm per metre, which you see at once on the far iris. 4. The irises stay in place as the permanent reference of that axis. Each 90° turn (a mirror or the PBS) gets its own pair of irises on the next hole row. Stage 2: square each part to the beam Part How it is set How it is checked Posts and holders same post, holder and collar type for every part, height set with the calliper the beam passes the reference irises after the part is put in Steering mirrors beam walking (stage 1) no extra check: the two irises fix their angle Wave plates, Glan-Taylor, cube faces, cell windows turn the mount until the weak reflection from the face goes back through the iris hole (panel C) a tilt θ moves the return spot by 2θL: at L = 0.5 m, 1 mrad gives 1 mm PBS cubes (roll about the beam) turn the cube in its holder until the reflected beam stays at 100 mm (panel D) a roll of 1° lifts the reflected beam 17 mm per metre: easy to see Lenses centred so the far spot does not move when the lens is put in or taken out back reflection from the lens surfaces centred on the iris AOMs aperture at 100 mm with the post, beam through the 2 mm aperture Bragg angle by the most first-order power (D9 micrometer), not by a protractor Detector spot centred on the diode with the IR card or the camera signal maximum How exact does it have to be? Much less exact than the checks can show. Tilting a plate by 1° changes its path length through the glass only by 1 − cos 1° = 0.015 %. The things that matter are that the beam stays centred on the small apertures (2 mm AOM aperture, the irises, the 14 mm beam holes in the shield caps), that the control and probe overlap in the cell, and that no reflection goes straight back to the laser. The back-reflection check reaches about 1 mrad. Wave plate and polarizer axes are set by rotating them for a power minimum or maximum, not mechanically. A deliberate exception. After squaring, the cell windows and some plates are often tilted by a small angle on purpose, so that their reflections miss the beam path and do not form etalons or reach the laser. Our free-space isolator (L06) protects the laser in any case. Practical points 795 nm is only faintly visible. Use the IR viewing card or the camera the lab already owns, wear the laser goggles, and turn the laser current down to a few mW while aligning. Block stray reflections, keep the beam at 100 mm (well below eye level), and take off watches and rings. Start at the laser and work outward, one part at a time. After each part, check that the beam still passes the reference irises. Printed holders (D11, D12) are made square by their datum walls; their acceptance test is the reflected spot drift (less than 0.5 mm at 2 m after a day). Q30 How is the magnetic shield of the Spain-style EIT cell probably made? It looks like a small enclosure.

Q30 How is the magnetic shield of the Spain-style EIT cell probably made? It looks like a small enclosure. Most likely a compact cell module: a short, small-diameter shield (one or two layers, closed ends) inside the white 3D-printed housing, with the coil and the heater wound round the cell inside it. This is a reading of one photograph, not a confirmed design: the shield itself is not visible. What the photo does show: A white 3D-printed housing with red leads for the heater and the coil, and nothing larger round it. A long three-layer tube like ours (Ø70 × 250 mm) would be obvious. A HEATER supply at about 2.40 V and 0.50 A (about 1.2 W, plain DC, no temperature loop visible). A COILS supply at about 1.00 V and 80 mA, so the coil is about 12.5 Ω: many turns of thin wire, a short solenoid. Why a small shield works: The shielding factor of a closed cylinder grows as μ·t / D (wall thickness over diameter), so a narrow tube shields better for the same metal. Closed mu-metal ends act like mirrors for the coil inside, so a short solenoid in a short closed shield still gives a fairly uniform field. That is how compact vapour-cell modules are built. It is cheap: little mu-metal, and a printed housing that also holds the cell and the windows. Plain DC heater current: a constant heater current makes a constant field, which only adds to the bias. It becomes a problem when a temperature loop changes the current; that is why our heater is bifilar (D2) and runs in a loop. What this means for our design: we built for 0.1 mG stability and a cell field error of 0.2 %, which needs the long three-layer shield, the 42-turn solenoid with end turns, and degaussing. A compact module like theirs is simpler and cheaper and gives clear EIT, but with a broader, less reproducible line, and its temperature drifts without a loop. A compact version of ours (for example two layers, inner bore about Ø40 mm, about 120 mm long with caps) is possible, but the field uniformity would have to be recalculated with the end caps included before choosing it. Q31 Can we make the mu-metal shield ourselves: roll a sheet into a cylinder and close it with (3D-printed) end caps?

Q31 Can we make the mu-metal shield ourselves: roll a sheet into a cylinder and close it with (3D-printed) end caps? Rolling works only if the shield is annealed afterwards, and a printed end cap is not a magnetic end cap. Mu-metal gets its permeability from a hydrogen anneal (about 1100 to 1150 °C). Bending, cutting, punching or welding after the anneal lowers the permeability many times over in the worked metal. A plastic cap only holds things in place: magnetically the end stays open, and the axial field (the field our 50 mG bias adds to) is the one an open end lets in most. Rough estimate for one closed cylinder, Ø46 mm, against a field across it: S ≈ 1 + μ·t / D (shielding factor S, wall thickness t, diameter D, permeability μ). One layer μ (assumed) S 1 mm sheet, formed, then hydrogen-annealed about 20 000 about 400 1 mm sheet, rolled by hand, not annealed about 2 000 about 40 0.1 mm annealed foil, wrapped gently, not re-annealed about 5 000 about 10 Three layers multiply these roughly, if the gaps between them are a few millimetres. The values of μ are typical figures, not data for a particular alloy, so measure the result. What works Best: buy the shield annealed and finished (BOM C05), with caps, a Ø14 mm beam hole on the axis and a Ø12 mm cable hole 16 mm off it. Give the maker the inner bore (at least Ø46), the inner length (at least 250) and the hole positions. Workshop route: a sheet-metal shop rolls the layers and caps from mu-metal sheet, overlaps the seam, spot-welds it, and then a heat-treatment service anneals them in hydrogen. After that, do no more cutting or bending, and do not drop the layers. DIY without annealing: wrap annealed foil gently (large radius, no creases), overlap the seam by 20 to 25 mm, and hold it with Kapton tape or brass or nylon screws, never steel. It works, but it is much weaker; measure it with the fluxgate (D7) before you trust it. Seam and caps The seam is an overlap, not an end cap: at least 20 × the thickness, pressed flat, magnetically continuous along the whole length. The caps must be mu-metal too: a disc with a collar that overlaps the tube by 10 to 15 mm, with the Ø14 mm beam hole in the middle and the Ø12 mm cable hole beside it. 3D-printed parts are fine as holders: printed rings that keep the three layers concentric with about 4 mm gaps, and printed cap frames that press a mu-metal disc against the tube end. They hold the metal; they do not shield. Check: after assembly and degaussing (D4), measure the residual field at the cell with the fluxgate plate. Then turn the whole shield in the room and read it again: the reading should change by less than about 0.1 mG. Added 11 Oct 2026

The EIT line is about 7 kHz wide, and the field shifts it by 1.4 kHz per mG, so the line is about 5 mG wide. Keeping the field stable to about 0.1 mG (10 nT) shifts the line by only 140 Hz, which is 0.2 % of the 50 mG bias. The solenoid current is small (B = µ0·n·I: about 2 mA for one layer of 0.5 mm wire, tens of mA for several layers), so the allowed noise and drift are only a few to a few tens of microamps. Q33 Can a home-wound solenoid really give 3.39 mG per mA, and how and where do we measure it?

Q33 Can a home-wound solenoid really give 3.39 mG per mA, and how and where do we measure it? Yes, close to it, and the exact value does not have to be reached: it has to be measured. 3.39 mG/mA is the calculated field per milliampere of our 42-turn coil (DIY D1) in free space. It depends only on the number of turns and the coil geometry, so a careful winding gets within a few percent. Inside the µ-metal shield the value changes (the shield carries part of the return flux), which is why D1 says "calibrate in the shield". The experiment never needs exactly 3.39: it needs to know the field, so that the RF difference can be matched to it (or the current to the RF difference). What can make it differ, and by how much Number of turns: counted while winding, so exact. Coil radius and length: the printed former holds them to a fraction of a millimetre, a change of well under 1 %. The shield: can raise the field inside by a larger amount than the winding errors; only a measurement in the shield gives the real value. Uniformity matters more than the absolute value: 0.2 % over the cell, that is about 0.1 mG at 50 mG, which broadens the EIT line by about 0.14 kHz, small against its 10–30 kHz width. How and where to measure (three steps, from rough to exact) 1. On the bench, before the shield (D1): put the fluxgate (FLC100, DIY D7) on the coil axis where the cell will sit. Step the current (for example 0, ±5, ±10, ±15 mA, both directions) and plot the field against the current. The slope is the coil constant in free space; reversing the current cancels the Earth's field and the sensor offset. 2. Inside the shield, after degaussing (D1 step 10, D4): replace the cell by the fluxgate plate (D7) at the cell position and repeat ±5, ±10, ±15 mA. This slope is the working value. The fluxgate reads differences well (noise about 0.03 mG) but its absolute accuracy is only about ±2 % and ±3 mG offset, so it gives the slope, not the absolute zero. 3. With the atoms, the final and absolute calibration: with the cell back in place and EIT running, sweep the probe RF channel and note where the EIT peak sits for several solenoid currents. The two-photon resonance moves by exactly 1.4 kHz of light frequency (0.7 kHz of RF difference) per mG, an atomic constant, so the peak positions give the field directly, and the current at which the peak sits at zero RF difference shows the residual field left by the shield. In short: wind it carefully, measure the slope with the fluxgate in free space and in the shield, and let the atoms give the final number. Whatever value comes out, the current (about 15 mA for 50 mG) or the RF difference is adjusted to it. Why the fluxgate goes in first and then comes out. The order on the bench (and in the D1 build simulator) is: shield closed, degauss, fluxgate plate at the cell position, calibrate mG per mA, then swap the plate for the cell stack, degauss again, heat the cell, and do the final calibration with the atoms. This is the usual practice for a magnetometer and a vapour cell that need the same spot: They need the same place. The sensor must sit where the atoms will be (centre of the solenoid, on the axis), and our bore holds either the cell stack or the sensor plate, not both. The sensor would disturb the measurement. A fluxgate drives its permalloy core with a kHz excitation current: a small AC field and a piece of magnetic metal next to the cell. It is fine for a calibration, not next to the atoms during EIT. What survives the swap and what does not. The coil constant (mG per mA) depends only on the winding, so it stays valid. The residual field does not: opening the caps to swap lets the Earth's field magnetise the layers again, which is why the stack goes in and the shield is degaussed a second time. The atoms are the final judge. The fluxgate offset is about ±3 mG, so the absolute zero and the final constant come from the EIT peak itself (1.4 kHz per mG, an atomic constant); the fluxgate gives the quick, independent first numbers and checks each later degauss when the cell is out. Could it stay inside during the whole experiment? Not at the cell position: that place belongs to the cell. It could stay as a drift monitor a little away from the cell, with four conditions: Where: in the far-end Delrin tube, about 60 mm from the cell centre, off the axis so it stays clear of the beam (the 14 mm wide board fits beside the beam inside the Ø26.5 mm bore of the tube). It then reads the field there, not at the atoms: good for changes (drift), not for the absolute value. Test with the atoms first: a fluxgate drives its core into saturation at kHz, so it makes a small AC field of its own. Record the EIT line with the sensor powered and unpowered; if the position or the width changes, power it only between measurements. The cable: it adds about 7 mm² to the cable hole of the end caps, which is already close to full (see the DIY audit); with the thinner degaussing wire there is room. Temperature: the tube near the heated cell runs warm, and the sensor zero drifts with temperature (data sheet: below 2 nT per kelvin, 0.02 mG/K), so read it as a relative monitor. During EIT the best field monitor is the atoms themselves: the EIT peak moves 1.4 kHz per mG, far more sensitively than the fluxgate. Added 16 Oct 2026

The FLC100 is a small single-axis fluxgate sensor board (44.5 × 14 × 5.5 mm, 5 V ± 5 %, about 2 mA, differential analog output). Figures below are from the Stefan Mayer data sheet: range ±100 µT, ±1 V per 50 µT, noise below 0.5 nT rms or 3 nT peak-to-peak (0.1 to 10 Hz), DC to 1 kHz at −3 dB, zero drift below 2 nT per kelvin, accuracy ±2 % ± 0.3 µT at 20 °C. The Alibaba page itself could not be read. Ask Stefan Mayer for the calibration sheet. Need FLC100 Verdict Resolution: 1 mG = 100 nT; the working field is about 50 mG = 5 µT noise 3 nT peak-to-peak (0.1–10 Hz) = 0.03 mG: about 30 times finer than 1 mG more than enough Range ±100 µT (±1 G): covers the shield interior and the 50 mG solenoid field, and even the Earth's field outside fine Bandwidth DC to 1 kHz fine Absolute zero accuracy ±0.3 µT (±3 mG) at 20 °C not enough for the absolute residual field: use differences (coil current reversed, heater on and off, one degauss against the next), the end-for-end flip, and the atoms (1.4 kHz per mG) Axes one, along the long axis of the board the 44.5 mm board fits the former only axially; a transverse field changes the total field only at second order (1 mG across 50 mG is 0.01 mG) Wiring (yes, you wire it yourself). The data sheet shows five solder pads on a 0.1 inch grid at the end of the board away from the detection coil; from top to bottom in the drawing: 0V, +5V, SYNC, OUT−, OUT+. The output is differential: OUT+ is read against OUT−, which is a 2.5 V reference, so use a floating multimeter across the two pads, never OUT+ against ground. The scale is 20 mV per µT, 2 mV per mG. Supply it from a quiet linear 5 V regulator. The pads, the supply, the cable and the holder are drawn in the DIY Section (part D7). Cautions. (1) The zero offset and its drift decide how well you can null the field; flip the sensor end for end and average the two readings to cancel the offset. (2) The sensor and its leads must be kept clear of the shield and the solenoid while the shield is open; it fits through a port of about 16 mm or more. (3) It is a bare sensor: you need a 5 V supply, a stable readout (the oscilloscope or a 6½-digit multimeter) and a calibration against a known coil field. (4) A "new stock" listing on Alibaba is a counterfeit and old-stock risk (the manufacturer's page warns about replicas): order from Stefan Mayer Instruments or an authorised distributor and ask for the calibration sheet. Q35 Can the degaussing coil use 0.25 mm² wire instead of 0.5 mm²? Will it still degauss properly?

Q35 Can the degaussing coil use 0.25 mm² wire instead of 0.5 mm²? Will it still degauss properly? Yes. Degaussing needs enough ampere-turns to saturate the shield layers and a slow, smooth ramp-down; it does not need an accurate current, and the wire cross-section changes only the resistance and the heating, not the field. The field in the wall comes from the turns and the current: H = N·√2·I / (2π r), which for our 30 turns is about 190 A/m peak per ampere rms in the outer layer, far above the few tens of A/m that saturate mu-metal. With 0.25 mm² wire nothing in that formula changes. 0.5 mm² (design now) 0.25 mm² Coil resistance (24 m of copper) 0.83 Ω 1.65 Ω Voltage for 2 A rms with the 4.7 Ω series resistor 11.1 V 12.7 V Variac setting for 2 A (24 V secondary of 230 V) about 106 V about 122 V Heat in the coil at 2 A 3.3 W 6.6 W Worst-case temperature rise of the wire (no heat loss, 20 s search at full current + 100 s ramp) about 4 K about 17 K Field in the wall at 1 A rms 190 A/m 190 A/m What to watch. The rise above is an upper bound for a bundle of 30 wires in the bore; with PTFE or silicone insulation it is harmless, but keep the 2 A rms limit and use a 2.5 A slow-blow fuse on the 24 V side instead of 3.15 A, because the thin wire is the weak link in a fault. The 24 V secondary still has margin (12.7 V used). The thinner wire is easier to thread and takes less of the Ø12 mm cable hole in the end caps (about 34 % full instead of about 48 %). Use stranded flexible wire, not enamelled solid wire, and keep the bundle from kinking. Measure it anyway. After the first degauss, check the result with the fluxgate (D7) as for any coil: the resistance of the finished coil, the current reading at a given variac setting, and the remanent field before and after. Q36 Is the Spain-style arrangement correct, in theory and in practice?

Q36 Is the Spain-style arrangement correct, in theory and in practice? It is a correct Zeeman EIT chain, with three drawing faults (fixed) and several practical cautions. Everything rests on one photograph, so the real bench may differ. What checks out (simulator run): control and probe orthogonal and co-propagating (opposite circular after the quarter-wave plates); 160.000 and 159.930 MHz after the double pass, so a 70 kHz difference equal to the ground-state splitting at 50 mG; the SAS lock closes; no light returns to the laser; control 0.75 mW (7.3 mW/cm², the paper used 1.3–5.5), probe about 2 µW; predicted optical depth 10 at 60 °C, linewidth about 34 kHz, contrast 0.96; no parts closer than 30 mm. Three faults, now fixed The control beam expander had two lenses 40 mm apart: not a telescope. It is now f = 30 mm plus f = 100 mm, 130 mm apart (×3.3). The cat's-eye lenses in the AOM arms need f of about 75 mm (80 mm after the AOM, 70 mm to the mirror); the guide's parts list has only 100 and 50 mm lenses. The simulator hides a lock offset: the double-pass AOMs add +160 MHz and the SAS arm has no AOM. A real bench needs the lock moved by about 160 MHz (for example an AOM in the SAS arm); the photo does not show how. Practical cautions Heater: 2.4 V at 0.5 A is about 1.2 W through a 3D-printed housing; reaching 60 °C is doubtful (PLA softens near 60 °C), and a plain DC heater wire makes a magnetic field that shifts the Zeeman line (use bifilar, or switch it off while measuring). No temperature sensor or controller is visible. AOM drive: Rigol generators give about +10 to +20 dBm, typical AOMs need about +27 to +33 dBm: amplifiers must exist off-camera. No lock box is visible; without a real lock the laser drifts and EIT disappears. A white plastic box is not a magnetic shield; Zeeman EIT is first-order field sensitive, so a µ-metal shield is probably inside. The blue PM fibres suggest fibre between the boards (about half the power lost, axis alignment needed); the simulator draws free space. No beam dumps or tubes are visible (laser safety). The AOM tilt is exaggerated to 8° in the drawing, hence the 160 mm from separator cube to AOM; a real build can be tighter but needs an iris or block for the zeroth order. Do not use the drawing as a build recipe. Added 9 Oct 2026

Self-check before you start Q1. What is eiπ + 1?Zero. By Euler’s formula eiπ = cos π + i sin π = −1. Complex exponentials are the language of phases (P3). Q2. A short history: from light quanta to stored light

A short history: from light quanta to stored light Learning goalsPlace the main ideas (quantum, photon, coherence, laser, EIT, memory) in order. See that EIT and light storage are built from much older tools (magnetic resonance, optical pumping, the laser). Know which papers are the original sources. The physics in this project did not arrive in one step. It is the meeting of three older lines: quantization of light and matter (1900–1930), coherent control of two-level systems by oscillating fields (1937 onward, first with spins, then with lasers), and the laser itself (1960). Electromagnetically induced transparency was observed in 1991, and the step to slow, stopped and stored light followed within a decade. The timeline lists the landmark papers; every entry links to its source in the bibliography. 1900Planck proposes that energy is exchanged in discrete amounts to explain the spectrum of thermal radiation (Planck 1901). 1905Einstein proposes that light itself comes in quanta, using the photoelectric effect as the test (Einstein 1905). 1913Bohr’s atom: discrete energy levels, spectral lines from jumps between them (Bohr 1913). 1917Einstein introduces the coefficients A and B for spontaneous emission, absorption and stimulated emission (Einstein 1917). Stimulated emission is the process behind the laser, and the same coefficients set the natural linewidth. 1922Stern and Gerlach show that the direction of an atom’s magnetic moment is quantized (Gerlach & Stern 1922): the origin of the mF sublevels of L5. 1923Compton scattering of X-rays supports the idea that a light quantum carries momentum (Compton 1923). 1925–26Matrix mechanics (Heisenberg 1925), wave mechanics (Schrödinger 1926) and the probability interpretation of the wavefunction (Born 1926) give quantum mechanics its modern form (P4). 1927Dirac quantizes the electromagnetic field and derives spontaneous emission from first principles (Dirac 1927); this is the root of P5. 1937Rabi analyses a spin in a gyrating (rotating) magnetic field (Rabi 1937): the Rabi oscillation of L3. The matching equations for nuclear magnetic resonance follow in 1946 (Bloch 1946). 1954–60The maser (Gordon et al. 1954), the proposal to extend it to light (Schawlow & Townes 1958), and the first laser (MAIMAN 1960). Narrow, intense, tunable light opens atomic coherence to experiments. 1956Hanbury Brown and Twiss measure correlations between photons in two beams (BROWN & TWISS 1956): the technique behind g(2)(0) of L11. 1957Feynman, Vernon and Hellwarth show that any two-level problem can be pictured as a vector precessing on a sphere (Feynman et al. 1957): the Bloch-sphere picture of L2–L4. 1963Glauber’s quantum theory of optical coherence (Glauber 1963; Glauber 1963) defines coherent states and photon correlations (Nobel Prize 2005, Nobel 2005). Jaynes and Cummings compare quantum and semiclassical descriptions of an atom in a field (Jaynes & Cummings 1963). 1972Happer’s review of optical pumping (HAPPER 1972) collects the methods for preparing atoms in chosen sublevels. 1976Alzetta and colleagues observe coherent population trapping, a dark resonance in sodium vapour driven by two laser frequencies (Alzetta et al. 1976). It is the same dark state as in L7. 1977Kimble, Dagenais and Mandel observe photon antibunching in resonance fluorescence (Kimble et al. 1977): the first observation of this signature of non-classical light. 1991Boller, Imamoğlu and Harris report the observation of electromagnetically induced transparency (Boller et al. 1991); Harris’s article in Physics Today (Harris 1997) is a short, readable overview. 1995Bose–Einstein condensation of dilute atomic gases (Anderson et al. 1995; Davis et al. 1995) gives the ultracold, long-lived samples used in the first slow-light experiments. 1999Light speed reduced to 17 metres per second in an ultracold atomic gas (Hau et al. 1999). In the same year slow light was reported in hot or warm atomic vapours (Kash et al. 1999; Budker et al. 1999), the regime of this project. 2000–01The dark-state polariton picture (Fleischhauer & Lukin 2000; the quantum-memory version in Fleischhauer & Lukin 2002); halted light pulses and coherent storage of optical information (Liu et al. 2001); storage of light in atomic vapour (Phillips et al. 2001); and the proposal to use atomic ensembles for long-distance quantum communication (Duan et al. 2001). 2001–10EIT carries over to other systems: ultraslow and stored light in a solid (Turukhin et al. 2001); stopped light with storage times of over a second in a solid (Longdell et al. 2005); EIT on a single artificial atom (Abdumalikov et al. 2010); optomechanical analogues (Weis et al. 2010; Safavi-Naeini et al. 2011). 2005The standard review of EIT (Fleischhauer et al. 2005), and storage and retrieval of single-photon pulses in atomic ensembles (Chanelière et al. 2005; Eisaman et al. 2005). 2008–09The vision of a quantum internet (Kimble 2008) and the review of optical quantum memory (Lvovsky et al. 2009). 2012Nobel Prize in Physics to Haroche and Wineland for methods of measuring and manipulating individual quantum systems (Nobel 2012; Nobel lectures Haroche 2013, Wineland 2013). 2018–23A highly efficient EIT-based optical memory (Hsiao et al. 2018) and the practical guide to EIT in atomic vapour (Finkelstein et al. 2023) that Zeeman EIT follows. 2022Nobel Prize in Physics to Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger for experiments with entangled photons and the pioneering of quantum information science (Nobel 2022). What the history teaches The equations are old; the experiments are new. The Bloch and Rabi equations come from magnetic resonance in the 1930s–40s. The laser let them be applied to optical transitions, where EIT appears. EIT is the optical cousin of a dark resonance seen in 1976. What changed in 1991 and after is the viewpoint: use the dark resonance to control light (slow it, store it) rather than to study the atom. Memory is the application that kept the field alive. From 2000, “store a quantum state of light” (dark-state polaritons, DLCZ) turned an optical curiosity into a building block for quantum networks (P2). Many platforms, one idea. The same transparency window appears in vapours, crystals, superconducting circuits and mechanical resonators; the project’s later stage asks whether it can be made to work in a solid-state material (L12). Further reading: the history is told with technical detail in Scully & Zubairy 1997 and Loudon; Harris’s overview Harris 1997 and the review Fleischhauer et al. 2005 cover the EIT part. P2

Why this project: quantum memories and quantum networks

Why this project: quantum memories and quantum networks Learning goalsExplain why quantum information needs both light and matter. Explain why long-distance links need quantum memories. State what Objectives 1, 2 and 3 of the project are, and why the order matters. Light is the natural carrier of quantum information: photons travel fast, interact weakly with their surroundings and can be sent through fibre or free space. Quantum key distribution (the 1984 proposal of Bennett and Brassard, reprinted in Bennett & Brassard 2014), quantum communication in general (Gisin & Thew 2007) and the proposals for a quantum internet (Kimble 2008) all rely on photons as “flying qubits”. But weak interaction is also the problem: photons are hard to hold, to delay or to make interact. Matter is the natural place to store and process information. Atoms, ions, spins in crystals and superconducting circuits keep a state for a useful time and can be controlled precisely, but are poor at travelling. A quantum memory is the interface: it takes in a photon’s quantum state, holds it, and gives it back on demand (Lvovsky et al. 2009; Hammerer et al. 2010). Why can the photon not simply be amplified and sent on? Because an unknown quantum state cannot be copied (the no-cloning theorem). The only way to cover a long distance is to split it into segments, create entanglement across each segment, and join the segments. The segments succeed at random times, so each must be held until its neighbours also succeed. That holding device is a quantum memory, and the scheme is the quantum repeater (Briegel et al. 1998; Sangouard et al. 2011). The DLCZ proposal showed how atomic ensembles and linear optics could do this (Duan et al. 2001). P2.1\[ T_{\rm fibre}=10^{-\alpha_{\rm dB}L/10},\qquad \alpha_{\rm dB}\sim0.2\ \mathrm{dB/km}\ \ (\text{typical telecom fibre near 1550 nm})\ \Rightarrow\ T(1000\ \mathrm{km})\sim10^{-20}. \] A message across a desert with rest stops Read it in wordsTransmission falls exponentially with distance: every extra 15 km in a 0.2 dB/km fibre costs half the light (3 dB). Over a thousand kilometres essentially nothing arrives, however bright the source. A repeater breaks the path into short hops, each of which has a decent chance of working. AnalogyYou cannot carry water across a desert in one trip, but you can with rest stops: carry it to the first stop, rest, then carry it on. The memory is the rest stop: it holds the “water” (the quantum state) safely until the next leg is ready. Where it failsWith water you could simply pour a copy into a second bucket. A quantum state cannot be copied, so each rest stop must hand the same state on, and the stop itself must not disturb it.

What a good memory needs

P2
Why atoms in a warm vapour

Why atoms in a warm vapour EIT-based memories store light as a collective ground-state coherence of many atoms (Fleischhauer & Lukin 2000; Phillips et al. 2001). A warm vapour needs no laser cooling or vacuum chamber, only a cell, a heater and magnetic shielding, which makes it the simplest platform on which to learn the physics (Novikova et al. 2011; Finkelstein et al. 2023). Its price is motion: atoms fly through the beam at hundreds of metres per second, which L9 deals with. The same idea has been demonstrated in cold atoms, in rare-earth-doped crystals and in other media; L10 gives a short survey with sources. EIT-type effects are also used outside memories, for example in coherent-population-trapping clocks (Vanier 2005) and in optical magnetometry (Budker & Romalis 2007).

Maths toolkit: complex numbers, matrices, Dirac notation, Fourier

Maths toolkit: complex numbers, matrices, Dirac notation, Fourier Learning goalsHandle complex amplitudes and phases with Euler’s formula. Read and write states and operators in Dirac notation. Use eigenvalues, the matrix exponential and the Fourier relation between time and frequency. Convert comfortably between eV, Hz, nm, dBm and OD. Quantum optics uses a small set of mathematical ideas over and over. This primer collects them, with the lab numbers they will be applied to. If you studied linear algebra and complex numbers recently, skim; otherwise work the exercises at the end of each part.
P3
P3.1 Complex numbers and phases

P3.1 Complex numbers and phases Every oscillation in the notes is written with a complex exponential. A complex number z = a + ib has a magnitude |z| and a phase φ, and Euler’s formula links the two descriptions. Multiplying by eiφ rotates z by φ in the complex plane without changing its length: this is what a phase shift is. Quantum amplitudes are complex numbers; probabilities are their squared magnitudes, so a common phase never matters but a relative phase does (L2). P3.1\[ z=a+ib=|z|\,e^{i\varphi},\qquad e^{i\varphi}=\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi,\qquad |z|^2=zz^*=a^2+b^2,\qquad \cos\varphi=\tfrac12\big(e^{i\varphi}+e^{-i\varphi}\big). \] A clock hand Read it in wordsA complex number is an arrow in a plane. Its length is the magnitude; the angle from the horizontal is the phase. Multiplying by eiφ turns the arrow by φ. A real cosine is the horizontal shadow of a spinning arrow. AnalogyA clock hand: where it points is the phase, how long it is is the amplitude. Two clocks running at slightly different rates drift apart in phase, which is exactly what two light fields of different frequency do and what produces a beat note. Where it failsA classical wave’s real field is the shadow of the arrow, and only the shadow is measurable. For a quantum amplitude the arrow itself carries information (interference), but only through probabilities built from it.
P3
P3.2 Vectors, inner products and basis states

P3.2 Vectors, inner products and basis states A quantum state of an n-level system is a vector with n complex components. The inner product of two vectors measures their overlap; two states with zero overlap are orthogonal (perfectly distinguishable). A set of mutually orthogonal, normalised vectors is a basis; any state can be written as a weighted sum of basis vectors, and the weights are the amplitudes. For the two ground states |1⟩ and |2⟩ of the Λ system, or the lower and upper states |g⟩ and |e⟩, the basis is just “which level”. P3.2\[ \langle u|v\rangle=\sum_j u_j^*v_j,\qquad \langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1,\qquad |\psi\rangle=\sum_j c_j|j\rangle,\qquad c_j=\langle j|\psi\rangle,\qquad \sum_j|c_j|^2=1. \]
P3
P3.3 Matrices, eigenvalues and the matrix exponential

P3.3 Matrices, eigenvalues and the matrix exponential Physical quantities (energy, spin, polarization) are represented by matrices. The special vectors that a matrix only stretches, never rotates, are its eigenvectors, and the stretch factors are the eigenvalues. For the Hermitian matrices of quantum mechanics the eigenvalues are real (they are the possible measurement results) and the eigenvectors are orthogonal. Time evolution under a constant Hamiltonian is a matrix exponential: each energy eigenstate simply acquires a phase. P3.3\[ \hat H|n\rangle=E_n|n\rangle,\qquad \hat U(t)=e^{-i\hat Ht/\hbar},\qquad \hat U(t)|n\rangle=e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}|n\rangle,\qquad \hat H^\dagger=\hat H\ \Rightarrow\ E_n\ \text{real}. \] Natural modes of a guitar string Read it in wordsAn eigenstate of the Hamiltonian is a state whose shape never changes; only its phase turns, at a rate set by its energy. Any other state is a mixture of eigenstates, and the mixture changes in time because the phases turn at different rates. AnalogyA guitar string has natural modes. Pluck it in a mode and the shape stays; pluck it any other way and the shape changes in time because the modes oscillate at different rates. Eigenstates are the modes; the Hamiltonian is the string’s equation of motion. Where it failsA string’s mode amplitude is a real displacement. A quantum eigenstate’s phase is not directly observable, and measurements return one eigenvalue at random with a probability set by the amplitudes. Worked example · the simplest two-level problem Take two states coupled with strength ħΩ/2 and no detuning, Ĥ = (ħΩ/2)[[0, 1], [1, 0]]. The eigenvalues of [[0, 1], [1, 0]] are ±1 with eigenvectors (|g⟩ ± |e⟩)/√2, so the energies are ±ħΩ/2 and the two states are split by ħΩ. Starting in |g⟩ = (|+⟩ + |−⟩)/√2, the two components acquire phases e∓iΩt/2, and the amplitude to be in |e⟩ is −i sin(Ωt/2). That is a Rabi oscillation: P(e) = sin²(Ωt/2), reaching 1 at t = π/Ω. L3 derives it properly.
P3
P3.4 Dirac notation

P3.4 Dirac notation Dirac’s bra–ket notation is shorthand for vectors and their conjugate transposes: |ψ⟩ is a column vector (a “ket”), ⟨ψ| the corresponding conjugate row (a “bra”), ⟨φ|ψ⟩ an inner product (a number), and |ψ⟩⟨φ| an outer product (a matrix). The projector |e⟩⟨e| picks out the excited-state part of a state; the sum of projectors over a full basis is the identity (completeness). Operators like the lowering operator σ̂ = |g⟩⟨e| are written as outer products, which makes their action obvious: take the part in |e⟩ and put it in |g⟩. P3.4\[ \hat P_e=|e\rangle\langle e|,\qquad \hat\sigma=|g\rangle\langle e|,\qquad \sum_j|j\rangle\langle j|=\hat 1,\qquad \hat\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\ \ (\text{pure state}). \]
P3
P3.5 Fourier transform, pulses and line shapes

P3.5 Fourier transform, pulses and line shapes A signal in time and its spectrum in frequency are two views of the same thing, related by the Fourier transform. A short pulse has a broad spectrum; a long, steady wave has a narrow one. Two results are used constantly: a Gaussian pulse of FWHM duration Δt has FWHM bandwidth Δν = 0.441/Δt, and a field whose amplitude decays as e−Γt/2 has a Lorentzian power spectrum of FWHM Γ (in rad/s), that is Γ/2π in Hz. The second is the natural line shape of an atom (L4); the first limits how fast a pulse can be before it no longer fits inside the EIT window (L8). P3.5\[ \tilde E(\omega)=\int E(t)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt,\qquad \Delta\nu\,\Delta t=\frac{2\ln2}{\pi}\approx0.441\ \ (\text{Gaussian}),\qquad \mathcal L(\Delta)=\frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{\Delta^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}\ \ (\text{FWHM}=\Gamma). \] Pitch and note length Read it in wordsSqueeze a signal in time and it spreads in frequency, and vice versa: you cannot have both a very short pulse and a very pure colour. AnalogyA musician playing a very short click produces a smear of pitches; holding a note for a long time gives a clean pitch. The lab version: a 10 µs light pulse has a bandwidth of about 44 kHz, comparable to a narrow EIT window, which is why storing a pulse needs a long enough pulse for the window and a short enough one to fit in the cell. Where it failsThe musician’s “pitch” is a property of the sound wave we can measure at once. For a single photon, time and frequency are still conjugate, but you cannot assign both to one photon at the same time.
P3
P3.6 Differential equations you will meet

P3.6 Differential equations you will meet Two equations cover most of what follows. Exponential decay, dx/dt = −γx, gives x = x₀e−γt: populations and coherences decay this way. Harmonic oscillation, d²x/dt² = −ω²x, gives cos(ωt) and sin(ωt): a driven two-level atom oscillates between its states in just this way, as do the electromagnetic field and the polariton. A rotating frame is a change of variables that removes a fast oscillation (such as the 377 THz optical carrier) so that only slow changes remain: this is the idea behind the rotating-wave approximation (L3).
