Basic quantum mechanics for atoms and photons

Basic quantum mechanics for atoms and photons Learning goalsState the postulates of quantum mechanics in plain words. Use the Schrödinger equation, operators, commutators and the uncertainty relation. Describe spin-½, angular momentum and the quantum numbers of an atom. Understand the harmonic oscillator, which is the basis of light quantization. Quantum mechanics rests on a few rules (Griffiths & Schroeter; Sakurai & Napolitano; Feynman et al.). State: a system is described by a normalised vector |ψ⟩ in a complex vector space. Observables: each measurable quantity (energy, position, spin component) is a Hermitian operator; its eigenvalues are the possible results. Measurement: the probability of result a is |⟨a|ψ⟩|² (the Born rule, Born 1926), and afterwards the system is in the state |a⟩. Evolution: between measurements the state evolves smoothly under the Schrödinger equation (Schrödinger 1926). Combining systems: the state space of two systems is the tensor product of their spaces, which allows entanglement. P4.1\[ i\hbar\frac{d}{dt}|\psi\rangle=\hat H|\psi\rangle,\qquad \hat H|n\rangle=E_n|n\rangle\ \Rightarrow\ |\psi(t)\rangle=\sum_nc_n\,e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}|n\rangle,\qquad P(a)=|\langle a|\psi\rangle|^2. \] A film you can only watch by buying a ticket for one frame Read it in wordsBetween measurements the state moves smoothly and predictably (the Schrödinger equation). A measurement gives one definite answer with a probability set by the amplitudes, and resets the state. AnalogyImagine a film whose frames are smooth and fully determined, but you may look at only one frame, chosen by you, and looking changes the film. The smooth evolution is the equation; the single glimpse is the measurement. Where it failsIn a real film each frame exists whether or not you look. The quantum state has no definite value of the measured quantity before the measurement; and what “measurement” means physically is still a topic of debate, although the predictions are not.
P4
P4.1 Operators, commutators and uncertainty

P4.1 Operators, commutators and uncertainty Operators do not always commute: the order in which you apply them matters. The commutator [Â, B̂] = ÂB̂ − B̂Â measures how much. Position and momentum have the fundamental commutator [x̂, p̂] = iħ, which leads to the uncertainty relation: no state has both a sharply defined position and a sharply defined momentum (Griffiths & Schroeter). For atoms the more useful consequence is a Fourier relation between lifetime and linewidth: a level that lives for a time τ has a spectral width of order 1/(2πτ) (L4). P4.2\[ [\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar,\qquad \Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\frac{\hbar}{2},\qquad [\hat J_x,\hat J_y]=i\hbar\hat J_z\ \text{(and cyclic)},\qquad \Delta\nu=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau}\ \ (\text{natural linewidth}). \]
P4
P4.2 Spin-½, angular momentum and the Bloch sphere

P4.2 Spin-½, angular momentum and the Bloch sphere Angular momentum is quantized: the length of an angular momentum J has the value √(J(J+1))ħ and its projection on any axis takes only the 2J+1 values mħ, with m from −J to +J (Gerlach & Stern 1922). A spin-½ (an electron, a proton, or an effective two-level system) has just two projections, ±ħ/2, and is described by the Pauli matrices. Every pure state of a two-level system is a point on a sphere, the Bloch sphere (L2; Feynman et al. 1957). Rubidium’s valence electron has spin ½ and its nucleus has spin 3/2, and the sublevels of the experiment are the projections of the total angular momentum F (L5). P4.3\[ \hat\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \hat\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \hat\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \hat S_k=\frac{\hbar}{2}\hat\sigma_k,\qquad |\vec J|=\hbar\sqrt{J(J+1)},\ \ J_z=m\hbar. \] A spinning top that may only lean at certain angles Read it in wordsThe total angular momentum has a fixed length, but its component along a chosen axis can take only certain discrete values. The vector cannot point exactly along the axis: it must lean, and it precesses around it. AnalogyA top that is only allowed to lean at a few specific angles from the vertical and then precesses around the vertical at those angles. The magnetic field defines “vertical”. This is the vector model drawn in the Zeeman illustration of L5. Where it failsA top’s tilt and its precession angle can both be known. For a quantum spin, the components along different axes cannot all be sharp at once: if Jz is sharp, Jx and Jy are not.
P4
P4.3 The harmonic oscillator

P4.3 The harmonic oscillator The quantum harmonic oscillator is the most important model system in quantum optics because each mode of the electromagnetic field is one (Dirac 1927). Its energies are equally spaced, En = ħω(n + ½), with a zero-point energy ħω/2. Two operators, the lowering and raising (annihilation and creation) operators â and â†, move between levels. In the field picture they remove and add a photon of energy ħω, which is why the next primer can quantize light with the same algebra. P4.4\[ \hat H=\hbar\omega\Big(\hat a^\dagger\hat a+\tfrac12\Big),\qquad [\hat a,\hat a^\dagger]=1,\qquad \hat a|n\rangle=\sqrt n\,|n-1\rangle,\qquad \hat a^\dagger|n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle,\qquad E_n=\hbar\omega\big(n+\tfrac12\big). \]
P4
Q3. What is the zero-point energy of a mode of frequency 377 THz, and why can it not be removed?

P4.4 Atoms: quantum numbers, energy levels and selection rules In a hydrogen-like atom the energy depends mainly on the principal quantum number n (En ≈ −13.6 eV/n²). The electron’s orbital angular momentum l and spin ½ combine to J (fine structure), and J combines with the nuclear spin I to F (hyperfine structure). Alkali atoms such as rubidium have one valence electron outside closed shells, so they behave much like hydrogen with adjusted energies (Foot 2005). Light couples states through the electric-dipole interaction, which obeys selection rules: the orbital quantum number changes by one (Δl = ±1), and the magnetic quantum number changes by 0 or ±1 depending on the light’s polarization (L5). That is why the D lines of rubidium (5S → 5P) are strong and why σ⁺ and σ⁻ light connect different sublevels. P4.5\[ E_n\simeq-\frac{13.6\ \mathrm{eV}}{n^2},\qquad \Delta l=\pm1,\qquad \Delta m=0,\pm1,\qquad \Gamma_{i\to f}=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\,|\langle f|\hat V|i\rangle|^2\,\rho(E_f)\ \ (\text{Fermi's golden rule}). \] Worked example · scales in ⁸⁷Rb The 5S₁/₂ → 5P₁/₂ gap is 1.5596 eV (Steck). The hyperfine splitting of the ground state, 6.8347 GHz, is only 28 µeV: about 55 000 times smaller. The Zeeman splitting per gauss, 1.4 MHz × 0.5 for F = 2, is smaller again by ~10⁴. These three widely separated energy scales (optical, hyperfine, Zeeman) are why each part of the experiment can be treated separately: the laser addresses the first, the Λ system lives in the second and third, and the shield protects the third. Q1. A spin-1 object has how many projections, and which?2J + 1 = 3, namely m = −1, 0, +1 (in units of ħ). Q2. Why can a photon not take an atom from S to D in a single electric-dipole step?The dipole selection rule requires Δl = ±1, but S to D is Δl = 2. Such transitions are only possible through weaker (quadrupole) processes. Q3. What is the zero-point energy of a mode of frequency 377 THz, and why can it not be removed?ħω/2 = ½ × 1.5596 eV ≈ 0.78 eV (here ħω is the photon energy). It is a consequence of [â, â†] = 1: the lowest state still has non-zero energy, because position and momentum cannot both be zero. It sets the vacuum fluctuations that cause spontaneous emission (P5). Where it shows up: L2 states and measurementL5 atomic structureP5 quantized light P5

Basic quantum optics: photons, coherent states and emission

Basic quantum optics: photons, coherent states and emission Learning goalsDescribe a mode of light as a quantum harmonic oscillator and define number and coherent states. Explain absorption, stimulated emission and spontaneous emission with Einstein’s coefficients. Compute a decay rate from a dipole matrix element. Compare natural, Doppler and pressure line widths. The semiclassical picture, in which atoms are quantum but light is a classical wave, explains most of what follows (Rabi flopping, EIT, slow light). But three effects need the quantum light field: spontaneous emission, photon counting statistics, and the quantum state of a stored pulse (L8, L10, L11). The route is short: treat each mode of the electromagnetic field as a harmonic oscillator (P4.3) whose quanta are photons (Dirac 1927; Loudon; Gerry & Knight; Fox 2006). P5.1\[ \hat H_{\rm field}=\hbar\omega\Big(\hat a^\dagger\hat a+\tfrac12\Big),\qquad \hat E(t)=\mathcal E_0\big(\hat a\,e^{-i\omega t}+\hat a^\dagger e^{i\omega t}\big),\qquad \mathcal E_0=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar\omega}{2\epsilon_0V}},\qquad \hat n=\hat a^\dagger\hat a. \] A string whose loudness comes in whole units Read it in wordsOne mode of the field is like one oscillator. Its energy is ħω times (the number of photons + ½). The operator â removes one unit of energy, â† adds one. The field itself is the sum of â and â† terms. AnalogyA guitar string whose loudness can only change in whole steps. Each step is one photon. The “½” is the string’s residual hum even when silent: the vacuum. Where it failsA real string’s hum is a real motion we can in principle damp out. The vacuum fluctuation of the field is not removable, and shows up as spontaneous emission and as noise in an amplifier.
P5
P5.1 Number states and coherent states

P5.1 Number states and coherent states A number (Fock) state |n⟩ has exactly n photons and a completely undefined phase. A coherent state |α⟩ is the quantum version of an ideal classical wave: it is the eigenstate of the lowering operator, â|α⟩ = α|α⟩, with a mean photon number |α|² and a Poisson photon-number distribution (Glauber 1963). A well-stabilised laser emits light very close to a coherent state, which is why attenuating it never produces a single-photon source (L11). The price of a well-defined phase is an uncertain photon number: for a coherent state ΔN = √N̄ and the phase uncertainty is about 1/(2√N̄). P5.2\[ \hat a|\alpha\rangle=\alpha|\alpha\rangle,\qquad \bar n=|\alpha|^2,\qquad P(n)=e^{-|\alpha|^2}\frac{|\alpha|^{2n}}{n!},\qquad \Delta N=\sqrt{\bar n},\qquad \Delta\varphi\approx\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\bar n}}. \] Worked example · a µW beam is nowhere near a single photon 1 µW at 795 nm is 4.0 × 10¹² photons/s (L1). In a 10 µs pulse the mean number is n̄ = 4.0 × 10⁷, so the shot-noise uncertainty is √n̄ ≈ 6 300 photons (0.016 %). The phase uncertainty 1/(2√n̄) ≈ 8 × 10⁻⁵ rad. Such a pulse is classical for every practical purpose. To make it quantum, attenuate until n̄ ≈ 1; at that point the Poisson spread is as large as the mean (L11).

P5.2 Absorption, stimulated and spontaneous emission

P5.2 Absorption, stimulated and spontaneous emission Einstein (Einstein 1917) described the exchange of energy between atoms and radiation with three processes. An atom in the lower level can absorb a photon (rate ∝ B₁₂ times the radiation density). An atom in the upper level can be stimulated to emit a photon identical to the incoming one (rate ∝ B₂₁ times the same density), and can also decay on its own by spontaneous emission at rate A₂₁. Consistency with thermal radiation fixes the ratios between the coefficients. Left alone it will roll down on its own (spontaneous emission, rate A). A passer-by shoving it downhill is stimulated emission, and a shove uphill from below is absorption. The more light there is, the more shoves. AnalogyThe ball on the hill will always eventually roll even in an empty field, because the empty field is never perfectly still: the vacuum jiggles. The A coefficient is the rate of those unavoidable jiggles. Larger dipole moments make the atom couple to the vacuum more strongly and decay faster (the |d|² in P5.4). If a transition’s dipole moment doubles (same frequency), what happens to its lifetime?Γ ∝ |d|², so Γ rises by 4 and the lifetime falls by a factor of 4. Q3. Why does the Doppler width not simply wash out EIT?For a Λ system with nearly co-propagating beams, an atom moving with velocity v sees both frequencies shifted almost equally, so the difference (the two-photon detuning) hardly changes. EIT is a two-photon effect and so survives the one-photon Doppler broadening (L9). Quantum states, superposition and measurement Learning goalsWrite states in Dirac notation and normalise them. Distinguish probability amplitudes from probabilities. See why relative phase is physical and evolves in time. A quantum state is a vector |ψ⟩. For a two-state system with basis {|g⟩, |e⟩}, any state is a superposition with complex amplitudes. Measurement in that basis gives g or e with probabilities |cg|² and |ce|², and leaves the system in the outcome state. The relative phase between cg and ce does not change those probabilities, but it decides how the state interferes later. EIT is built entirely on such a phase (L7). L2.1\[ |\psi\rangle=c_g|g\rangle+c_e|e\rangle,\qquad |c_g|^2+|c_e|^2=1,\qquad P(e)=|\langle e|\psi\rangle|^2=|c_e|^2,\qquad c_j(t)=c_j(0)\,e^{-iE_jt/\hbar}. \] A compass needle and a yes/no question Read it in wordsThe state is a weighted, phased mixture of basis states. Probabilities are squared magnitudes. Each component’s phase rotates at its own energy, so the relative phase rotates at the energy difference divided by ħ. AnalogyA compass needle can point anywhere, but a measurement only asks “north or south?”. A needle at 45° answers north half the time. The relative phase is like the needle swinging east–west: invisible to a north/south question, but it changes what a later east/west question would give. Where it failsA real needle has a definite direction before you look. A quantum state does not have a definite outcome, and measuring it changes the state. Worked example · hyperfine superposition Prepare (|F=1⟩ + |F=2⟩)/√2 in ⁸⁷Rb. The relative phase advances at νhfs ≈ 6.834 683 GHz: a full turn every 1/νhfs ≈ 146.3 ps. A hyperfine (clock-type) Λ scheme would have to follow that rotation with a microwave field near 6.8 GHz; the Zeeman superposition rotates only at kHz (70 kHz at 50 mG, a 14 µs period). Q1. Is (|g⟩ + i|e⟩)/√2 different from (|g⟩ + |e⟩)/√2 if you only measure in the {g, e} basis?No. Both give 50/50. They differ in relative phase (90°), which shows up when the state interferes with something else, e.g. after another light pulse. Q2. Why does a global phase eiφ|ψ⟩ not matter, while a relative phase does?All probabilities involve |amplitude|², which is unchanged by a common factor eiφ. A relative phase changes how the amplitudes add when they are projected onto a different basis. Go deeper · the Bloch sphere, measurement in other bases, and Ramsey interference Two angles describe everything L2.2\[ |\psi\rangle=\cos\tfrac\theta2\,|e\rangle+e^{i\varphi}\sin\tfrac\theta2\,|g\rangle,\qquad (u,v,w)=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),\qquad P(\hat n)=\tfrac12\big(1+\vec r\cdot\hat n\big). \] The polar angle θ of the sphere is twice the angle that appears in the state, so orthogonal states (|e⟩ and |g⟩) sit at opposite poles. A measurement along any axis n̂ gives “+” with probability (1 + r⃗·n̂)/2. In the {g, e} basis only the height w = cos θ is visible; the azimuth φ becomes visible only if the state is first rotated, for instance by a laser pulse. Use the 3D illustration above to see this: sliding φ never changes P(e). Interference of amplitudes: Ramsey’s method Apply a π/2 pulse (|g⟩ goes to the equator), let the state precess freely for a time T at detuning Δ, then apply a second π/2 pulse. The final excited-state probability is P(e) = ½(1 + cos ΔT) for ideal pulses: it depends on the phase ΔT accumulated between the pulses, not on any population. This is the same relative-phase physics that makes EIT possible, and the origin of the narrowest spectroscopy and atomic clocks. Superposition, mixture and measurement A superposition has a definite phase between its parts and interferes; a mixture is a statistical ensemble of states and does not (L4). Whether the change on measurement is a physical collapse or a loss of coherence to the environment is an interpretation question on which textbooks differ (Griffiths & Schroeter; Sakurai & Napolitano); the predictions you will use are the same. Pitfalls. (1) A superposition (|g⟩ + |e⟩)/√2 is not “half excited atoms and half ground-state atoms”: that would be a mixture. (2) The unknown quantum state cannot be copied, so you cannot “measure it first and keep a copy” (no-cloning; see Nielsen & Chuang 2000). The two-level atom: dipole coupling, RWA, Rabi oscillations, Bloch sphere Learning goalsWrite the dipole Hamiltonian and apply the rotating-wave approximation. Predict Rabi oscillations, including the effect of detuning. Picture the state on the Bloch sphere. An atom with transition frequency ω₀ in a laser field E cos ωt feels the energy −d·E. Moving to a frame rotating at ω and dropping terms oscillating at 2ω (the RWA) leaves a simple 2×2 problem that depends only on the detuning Δ = ω − ω₀ and the Rabi frequency Ω. Here Ω = d·E₀/ħ is the full Rabi frequency, the rate of population cycling on resonance. The EIT paper defines Ω = µẼ/ħ with its own field convention; always check factors of 2 when comparing sources. L3.1\[ \hat H_{\rm RWA}=-\hbar\Delta\,|e\rangle\langle e|+\frac{\hbar\Omega}{2}\big(|e\rangle\langle g|+|g\rangle\langle e|\big),\qquad P_e(t)=\frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}\,\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}}{2}\,t\Big). \] Pushing a swing in rhythm, or slightly off-beat Read it in wordsOn resonance (Δ = 0) the population swings fully between g and e at rate Ω. Off resonance it swings faster (at √(Ω²+Δ²)) but never fully reaches e: the maximum is Ω²/(Ω²+Δ²). AnalogyPush a swing exactly at its natural rhythm and it goes higher and higher. Push slightly off-beat (detuning) and some pushes fight the motion: the swing goes up a little, comes back, and never reaches full height. Where it failsA swing’s amplitude can grow without limit. The atom’s population cannot exceed 1, so it swings back down even on resonance: g → e → g. That is coherent stimulated emission back into the laser. L3.2\[ \vec r=(u,v,w),\quad w=\rho_{ee}-\rho_{gg},\qquad \dot{\vec r}=\vec\Omega_{\rm eff}\times\vec r\ \ \text{(no decay)},\qquad \vec\Omega_{\rm eff}=(\Omega,0,-\Delta). \] A spinning top precessing Read it in wordsAny two-level state is a point on a sphere: north pole is |e⟩, south pole is |g⟩, and the equator holds equal superpositions with different phases. Detuning tilts that axis, so the vector traces a smaller circle that never reaches the north pole. Where it failsOpposite points on the Bloch sphere are orthogonal states, not opposite directions in space. With decay the vector also shrinks inside the sphere (L4). Go deeper · where the RWA comes from, dressed states and π-pulses Derivation sketch of the rotating-wave approximation With the field E₀ cos ωt, the coupling term is ħΩ cos(ωt)(|e⟩⟨g| + |g⟩⟨e|). Writing the cosine as ½(eiωt + e−iωt) and moving to a frame rotating at the laser frequency (|e⟩ acquires e−iωt), the coupling splits into two parts: a slowly varying one of size ħΩ/2, and a part that oscillates at 2ω. The fast part averages out. That leaves the time-independent HRWA of L3.1. The leading correction is the Bloch–Siegert shift of order Ω²/4ω₀: for Ω/2π = 2 MHz and ν₀ = 377 THz it is about 3 mHz, utterly negligible. Dressed states and the Autler–Townes splitting L3.3\[ E_\pm=\frac{\hbar}{2}\Big(-\Delta\pm\sqrt{\Delta^2+\Omega^2}\Big),\qquad \Omega_{\rm gen}=\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2},\qquad P_e^{\max}=\frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta^2},\qquad t_\pi=\frac{\pi}{\Omega}. \] The eigenstates of HRWA are the “dressed” states of atom plus field. On resonance they are split by exactly ħΩ, and a strong control field splits a level this way: the Autler–Townes doublet of L7. The population oscillates at the difference of the two dressed energies, √(Ω² + Δ²). Pulses A π pulse (area Ωt = π) transfers an atom from |g⟩ to |e⟩; a π/2 pulse puts it on the equator, in an equal superposition. With Ω/2π = 2 MHz, tπ = π/Ω = 250 ns. Pulse area, not just power, sets the result: that is the area theorem of coherent optics (Allen & Eberly 1975). Pitfalls The factor 2. Some books define Ω with the coupling ħΩ, so their Rabi oscillation runs at 2Ω; the EIT tutorial does this (Finkelstein et al. 2023). Always check the definition before using a formula. Rabi flopping in a warm vapour. It is hard to see: the Doppler spread gives every atom a different Δ, and spontaneous emission damps it (L4, L9). EIT works with steady-state dark states, not Rabi flopping. Open systems: density matrix, decay and dephasing Learning goalsUse the density matrix for mixed states. Distinguish populations from coherences. Read a Lindblad master equation and identify Γ, Γ/2 and pure dephasing. Real atoms leak energy (spontaneous emission) and lose phase (collisions, fields, motion). A state vector cannot describe a statistical mixture, but a density matrix can. Diagonal elements are populations (how many atoms are where); off-diagonal elements are coherences (how well-defined the relative phase is across the ensemble). EIT and memories live in coherences, so coherence lifetimes are the central figure of merit of the whole project. L4.1\[ \hat\rho=\begin{pmatrix}\rho_{ee}&\rho_{eg}\\ \rho_{ge}&\rho_{gg}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \dot{\hat\rho}=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[\hat H,\hat\rho]+\Gamma\Big(\hat\sigma\hat\rho\hat\sigma^\dagger-\tfrac12\{\hat\sigma^\dagger\hat\sigma,\hat\rho\}\Big),\qquad \hat\sigma=|g\rangle\langle e|. \] An audience clapping in time Read it in wordsPopulations decay at Γ. The coherence ρeg decays at Γ/2 from emission alone, plus any extra pure-dephasing rate. The commutator is the reversible part; the Lindblad term is irreversible. AnalogyAn audience clapping in unison is a coherence: everyone shares a phase. People leaving the hall is population decay. People staying but drifting off the beat is dephasing: the hall still holds the same number of clappers, but the rhythm (coherence) is gone. Where it failsEach atom is itself in a superposition, not just “clapping or not”. Dephasing can be partly reversible (inhomogeneous, e.g. Doppler) or truly irreversible (homogeneous). The audience picture blurs that distinction. Worked example · from lifetime to linewidth τ(5P₁/₂) = 27.679 ns Steck ⇒ Γ = 1/τ = 3.613 × 10⁷ s⁻¹ ⇒ Γ/2π = 5.750 MHz, matching Steck’s quoted natural linewidth. The optical coherence decays at Γ/2 (γ₁₃ ≈ 2π × 2.87 MHz without collisions). With 10 Torr of buffer gas, pressure broadening (~10 MHz/Torr, paper) dominates, at ~100 MHz. Q1. A state has ρee = ρgg = ½ and ρeg = 0. Is it a superposition?No. It is a 50/50 statistical mixture with no coherence. A superposition (|g⟩+|e⟩)/√2 would have |ρeg| = ½. Q2. Why is γ₁₂ (ground coherence) potentially millions of times smaller than γ₁₃?Ground states do not decay radiatively. γ₁₂ comes only from slow processes (transit, collisions, field gradients), typically kHz or less, while γ₁₃ includes the MHz radiative decay and collisional broadening. Go deeper · T₁, T₂, saturation and the scattering rate The optical Bloch equations L4.2\[ \dot u=\Delta v-\gamma_\perp u,\qquad \dot v=-\Delta u+\Omega w-\gamma_\perp v,\qquad \dot w=-\Omega v-\Gamma(w+1),\qquad \gamma_\perp=\frac\Gamma2+\gamma_{\rm deph}. \] These are L3.2 plus damping. Population decays at Γ (the time T₁ = 1/Γ) and the coherence at γ⊥ (T₂ = 1/γ⊥), with 1/T₂ = 1/(2T₁) + 1/T₂* where T₂* collects pure dephasing. So T₂ can never exceed 2T₁. In the steady state, set the derivatives to zero: L4.3\[ w_{\rm ss}=-\frac1{1+s},\qquad s=\frac{2\Omega^2}{\Gamma^2+4\Delta^2}\ \ (\gamma_{\rm deph}=0),\qquad R_{\rm sc}=\frac\Gamma2\,\frac{s}{1+s}. \] s is the saturation parameter, equal to I/Isat on resonance. At s = 1 the excited-state population reaches ¼ and the scattering rate is Γ/4; for s ≫ 1 the transition saturates at Γ/2 (Steck, Quantum and Atom Optics). Use the 3D decay illustration above: the violet dot is this steady state, and changing Ω moves it toward the centre of the sphere. Homogeneous and inhomogeneous dephasing Homogeneous dephasing (collisions, spontaneous emission) is irreversible for each atom. Inhomogeneous dephasing arises because atoms differ (different Doppler shifts or field strengths) and can be partly undone: the spin echo (Hahn 1950) rephases it by reversing the evolution. In a rubidium cell the ground-state coherence is limited by atom–atom and atom–buffer-gas collisions, by atoms leaving the beam, and by magnetic-field gradients (L9, L13). Pitfalls. (1) “Linewidth in MHz” is Γ/2π, not Γ. (2) Do not confuse coherence time (how long phase survives) with storage time (how long the retrieved efficiency stays useful): the second also depends on the first protocol’s losses. (3) The optical coherence decays at Γ/2 or faster: collisions only add to it. Atomic structure for alkalis Learning goalsBuild fine, hyperfine and Zeeman structure from angular-momentum addition. Apply dipole selection rules for σ⁺, σ⁻ and π light. Locate the Zeeman Λ system of Zeeman EIT in ⁸⁷Rb, and see how a hyperfine Λ system would differ. Rubidium’s single valence electron has orbital L and spin S = ½, which combine to J (fine structure: 5P₁/₂ vs 5P₃/₂, the D1 vs D2 lines). The nucleus has spin I = 3/2 for ⁸⁷Rb, and J and I combine to F (hyperfine). In a field B each F splits into 2F+1 sublevels mF. Light carries angular momentum: σ⁺ adds +1 to mF, σ⁻ subtracts 1, and π (polarized along B) adds 0. L5.1\[ |I-J|\le F\le I+J\ \Rightarrow\ F\in\{1,2\}\ (I=\tfrac32,\ J=\tfrac12),\qquad \Delta E_{\rm Z}=g_F\,\mu_B\,m_F\,B,\qquad \Delta F=0,\pm1,\quad \Delta m_F=0\ (\pi),\ \pm1\ (\sigma^\pm). \] A postal address Read it in wordsPossible F values run from |I−J| to I+J in integer steps. Each sublevel shifts in energy by gFµBmFB. Absorbing a photon can change F by at most one and mF by the photon’s angular momentum. AnalogyAn address narrows down step by step: building (n, L), floor (J), apartment (F), room (mF). The magnetic field is a lift that raises rooms on one side of the corridor and lowers those on the other. Selection rules are the doors: σ⁺ light only opens the door to the next room to the right. Where it failsRooms are places. These are angular-momentum states, and a superposition can be “in several rooms” at once, which is what Λ-EIT exploits. Worked example · counting and shifting ⁸⁷Rb 5S₁/₂ has 3 + 5 = 8 sublevels. With gF ≈ +½ (F=2), the shift is 0.70 MHz/G per mF Steck. Earth’s field (roughly half a gauss) would shift mF=+2 by about 0.7 MHz, enormous compared with a 10 kHz EIT line. That is why the cell sits inside µ-metal. Zeeman EIT uses the mF=+2/0 pair (1.40 kHz/mG); a hyperfine scheme would use F=1/F=2 clock pairs (m=0↔0, quadratic only). Q1. Why can σ⁺ light on F=2→F′=1 never excite mF=+2?It would need mF′=+3, which does not exist in F′=1 (maximum +1). mF=+1 is also dark, since F′=1 has no mF′=+2. Q2. Within a transition the sublevel strengths follow Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, which is why different mF couple with different Rabi frequencies. Optical pumping and the dark ends of the ladder Circularly polarized light moves population toward one end of the mF ladder because each absorption raises mF and spontaneous emission returns the atom on average to a slightly higher mF (HAPPER 1972). When the end states cannot absorb (as with σ⁺ light on F = 2 → F′ = 1, L5 Q1), the atoms collect there and the cell becomes transparent: optical pumping is itself a form of dark-state physics, and it competes with EIT in a multilevel atom (L7). When is the Zeeman shift linear? The linear formula ΔE = gFµBmFB holds while µBB is small compared with the hyperfine splitting: the Breit–Rabi formula gives the full dependence (Steck, Rb-87 data). Here B must be well below the ~5 kG at which 1.4 MHz/G × B reaches 6.8 GHz, so for any shielded cell the linear regime is excellent. The clock transition between mF = 0 states has no linear shift and only the small quadratic one: 575 Hz/G² means 575 Hz at 1 G but just 0.6 mHz at 1 mG. Pitfalls. (1) The F = 1 level has gF = −½, so its sublevels run the opposite way from F = 2. (2) Selection rules refer to the quantization axis, which is the magnetic-field direction, not the beam direction (they coincide in Zeeman EIT because the solenoid field is along the beams). (3) Hyperfine levels of the excited state are only 814 MHz apart, close to the Doppler width: neighbouring levels contribute at the edges of the line (L9). AnalogyOD counts sheets of tinted glass, each passing 1/e. For Kramers–Kronig, think of a road with a dip: wherever the surface dips (absorption line), the slope on either side (dispersion) must go down and come back up. A narrow dip means steep slopes. Where it failsGlass absorbs broadly. Atoms absorb in narrow lines, and the “dip” can be inverted (EIT carves a transparency hole) while the same causal link still produces steep dispersion. Lab connection: keeping the laser on the lineThe same absorption physics gives the laser its reference. In saturated absorption spectroscopy a strong pump burns narrow sub-Doppler dips into a reference cell’s absorption. A lock box turns the dip into a dispersive error signal (zero on the line, opposite signs either side, like a derivative of the dip) and feeds a correction back to the laser current. Why does a narrow absorption feature imply a strong dispersion feature?Kramers–Kronig: the refractive-index change scales with the absorption strength divided by its width, so narrower features give steeper index slopes. This is the root of slow light under EIT. Go deeper · susceptibility, absorption coefficient, group index and the EIT susceptibility From χ to what you measure L6.2\[ \alpha_{\rm abs}=\frac{\omega}{c}\,\chi''\ \ (n\approx1),\qquad n_g=n+\omega\frac{dn}{d\omega}\approx1+\frac{\omega}{2}\frac{d\chi'}{d\omega},\qquad \chi(\Delta)\propto\frac{i}{\gamma_{13}-i\Delta}\ \ (\text{two-level, weak probe}). \] Intensity decays as e−αabsz. The paper writes the optical depth as OD = 2α₀L, where α₀ is the field (amplitude) attenuation coefficient (Finkelstein et al. 2023); either way the intensity transmission is e−OD. The group index ng grows with the slope of the dispersion: a steep dχ′/dΔ means a slow pulse. For a plain Lorentzian absorber the dispersion slope at line centre is negative (anomalous dispersion: n falls as frequency rises, so ng < 1). In an EIT window the slope is steep and positive (normal dispersion), so ng is large. The 3D illustration above shows this reversal directly. The susceptibility with a control field L6.3\[ \chi(\Delta)\propto\frac{i\,(\gamma_{12}-i\Delta)}{(\gamma_{13}-i\Delta)(\gamma_{12}-i\Delta)+\Omega_c^2/4},\qquad \Omega_c\to0:\ \ \chi\to\frac{i}{\gamma_{13}-i\Delta}. \] This is the standard weak-probe, resonant-control result (with the Ω/2 convention of L3). At Δ = 0 and Ω_c ≫ γ₁₂ the numerator is small and the denominator large, so χ′ and χ″ both nearly vanish: the medium is transparent. The residual absorption is set by γ₁₂ (Fleischhauer et al. 2005; Finkelstein et al. 2023). Doppler broadening in practice In a warm vapour the one-photon resonance is smeared over ~530 MHz, so the peak absorption per atom is reduced by roughly the ratio of the natural to the Doppler width; optical depths of ~10 are reached by combining a long cell and high density (L9). The EIT calculation in a Doppler-broadened medium replaces γ₁₃ by an effective width (the lab above uses W) (Finkelstein et al. 2023). Kramers–Kronig, in one sentence Because the medium cannot respond before the field arrives (causality), the real and imaginary parts of χ are not independent: each is an integral transform of the other. A narrow absorption feature therefore must come with a narrow, steep dispersion feature; and when EIT cuts a narrow hole in absorption, the dispersion there becomes steep, so group velocities drop (Loudon; Boyd). Pitfalls. (1) OD defined with base 10 (filters) or base e (atoms). (2) The sign of χ′ below and above resonance depends on the convention for Δ; check the figure’s axis labels. (3) Group velocity can be slower than c or faster, even negative, for an absorbing medium: it is not the speed of information. Three-level interference: dark states, CPT, EIT, Autler–Townes Learning goalsCompare Λ, V and ladder schemes. Derive the dark state and the EIT window. Distinguish EIT (interference) from Autler–Townes splitting (level shifting). Add a second ground state and a second laser. Two excitation routes now lead to the same excited state, and their amplitudes can cancel. The cancelling superposition is the dark state. If the control is strong and the probe weak, the probe sees a narrow transparency window: EIT. With two comparable fields, atoms are trapped in the dark state: CPT. A strong control also splits the excited state into an Autler–Townes doublet (at ±Ωc in the paper’s convention, ±Ωc/2 in ours: see the note in “Go deeper”), which also reduces absorption at line centre, but without interference, so some residual absorption remains (paper refs [29], [30]). L7.1\[ |D\rangle=\frac{\Omega_p|2\rangle-\Omega_c|1\rangle}{\sqrt{|\Omega_p|^2+|\Omega_c|^2}},\qquad \gamma_{\rm EIT}=\gamma_{12}+\frac{|\Omega_c|^2}{\gamma_{13}},\qquad E_\pm=\pm\hbar\Omega_c\ \ (\text{Autler–Townes, paper Eq. 23, paper's Rabi convention}). \] Two pushes that cancel; noise-cancelling headphones Read it in wordsThe dark state mixes |1⟩ and |2⟩ with weights set by the opposite field and a minus sign. The transparency window has a width set by ground decoherence plus control power. Autler–Townes describes the control splitting the excited level into two. AnalogyTwo friends push a swing from opposite sides with matched rhythm: it stays still. The window is like noise-cancelling headphones: silence only in a band. Autler–Townes is different: it is like moving a single pothole into two smaller potholes on either side of your wheel. You miss them both, but not because anything cancelled. Where it failsNo light is added to cancel the probe; the cancellation is between quantum amplitudes inside each atom. Real experiments often sit between pure EIT and pure Autler–Townes, and distinguishing them takes careful fitting. Interactive · the EIT windowpaper Eq. 13 with γ₁₃ → W (effective optical width) Ωc/2π γ₁₂/2π OD W/2π transmissionphase (right axis)no control Worked example · width at the paper’s control power Ωc/2π = 1.9 MHz, effective optical width W/2π ≈ 300 MHz design estimate, γ₁₂/2π = 1 kHz. Then γEIT/2π ≈ 1 + 1900²/300 000 kHz ≈ 13 kHz (HWHM), i.e. FWHM ≈ 26 kHz. The paper measured 7.3 kHz FWHM at this control intensity, so the crude formula overestimates here by a factor of ~3. That is a reminder to measure, not assume. Q1. In the dark state with Ωp ≪ Ωc, where is almost all the population?In |1⟩, the state coupled by the weak probe. Weight of |1⟩ = |Ωc|²/(|Ωc|²+|Ωp|²) ≈ 1. That is exactly why the result is counter-intuitive. Q2. Halving the control intensity halves which term of γEIT?The power-broadening term |Ωc|²/γ₁₃ (Ω² ∝ intensity). γ₁₂ is unchanged. Go deeper · the Autler–Townes convention, telling EIT from AT, and what dark states are used for Convention check: the size of the Autler–Townes doubletThe EIT tutorial writes the strong-control dressed states as E± = ±ħΩc (its Eq. 23) because it defines the Rabi frequency with coupling ħΩ (Finkelstein et al. 2023). With the convention used in these notes (coupling ħΩ/2, so Ω is the on-resonance oscillation rate) the same doublet is at ±ħΩc/2, and the splitting between the two components is ħΩc (L3.3). The physics is identical; only the definition of Ωc differs by a factor 2. For example, the paper’s Ωc/2π = 1.9 MHz would be 3.8 MHz in the convention of L3. L7.1 above is stated in the paper’s convention; use the other whenever you compare with L3. How the dark state arises For probe and control resonant with |1⟩ → |3⟩ and |2⟩ → |3⟩, the interaction Hamiltonian is (ħ/2)(Ωp|3⟩⟨1| + Ωc|3⟩⟨2| + h.c.). Write a general ground-state superposition a|1⟩ + b|2⟩. It couples to |3⟩ with strength proportional to Ωpa + Ωcb. This vanishes for (a, b) ∝ (Ωc, −Ωp): the dark state of L7.1. The orthogonal combination, the bright state, couples with strength √(Ωp² + Ωc²) and decays as usual. Atoms optically pumped into the dark state stay there (coherent population trapping, Alzetta et al. 1976; Arimondo 1996), until the ground-state coherence decays at rate γ₁₂. EIT or Autler–Townes? A strong control opens a dip in the probe absorption in both cases, so the dip alone does not tell you which mechanism acts. In the Autler–Townes picture the dip is the gap between two displaced absorption lines; in EIT it is a quantum-interference hole whose width can be much narrower than any of the lines. Anisimov, Dowling and Sanders showed how to distinguish them objectively by comparing how well each model fits the measured spectrum (Anisimov et al. 2011); in a Doppler-broadened vapour the two often coexist (Finkelstein et al. 2023). What dark states are used for Slow and stored light (L8): the subject of this project (Fleischhauer & Lukin 2000; Phillips et al. 2001). CPT atomic clocks: the narrow dark resonance is used as a frequency reference (Vanier 2005). Magnetometry: the resonance shifts with magnetic field, and optical magnetometers use that sensitivity (Budker & Romalis 2007). EIT analogues in solids, superconducting circuits and optomechanics (Turukhin et al. 2001; Abdumalikov et al. 2010; Safavi-Naeini et al. 2011; Weis et al. 2010). Pitfalls. (1) The EIT window needs the two fields to be phase-coherent relative to each other (here guaranteed by deriving both from one laser through AOMs). (2) “Transparent” does not mean lossless: the residual absorption is ~γ₁₂/(γ₁₂ + Ω²/γ₁₃). (3) In real ⁸⁷Rb the dark state is one of many sublevels; leakage to other sublevels reduces the contrast below the three-level prediction (L5). Slow and stopped light: group velocity, polaritons, storage Learning goalsCompute group velocity and delay from an EIT spectrum. Describe the dark-state polariton and its mixing angle. Explain storage and retrieval as adiabatic transfer between light and spin wave. The steep dispersion inside the EIT window makes the group index huge, so a pulse crawls through the cell. In the Fleischhauer–Lukin picture (paper ref. [11]) the propagating excitation is a dark-state polariton, a superposition of the probe field and the collective spin coherence. Its mixing angle θ is set by the control. Lower the control adiabatically to zero and θ → 90°: the excitation becomes purely atomic and stops. Raise it again and the light returns. L8.1\[ v_g=\frac{c}{n_g}\approx c\cos^2\theta,\qquad \hat\Psi=\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathcal E}-\sin\theta\,\sqrt{N}\,\hat\rho_{12},\qquad \tan^2\theta=\frac{g^2N}{\Omega_c^2},\qquad \tau_{\rm delay}=\frac{\mathrm{OD}_{\rm EIT}}{\gamma_{\rm EIT}}. \] Traffic on a crowded road, and a relay baton Read it in wordsThe polariton Ψ is part light (cos θ) and part atomic spin wave (sin θ). g√N is the collective light–atom coupling, so more atoms means more atomic character. Group velocity falls as the excitation becomes more atomic. The delay follows from the measured ODEIT and γEIT. AnalogyA convoy entering a crowded road bunches up and slows: that is pulse compression. Storage is a relay race: the light runner hands the baton (the quantum state) to an atom runner who stands still holding it until the control says “go”. Where it failsThe convoy loses no cars, and the baton does not fade. In the atoms, energy is temporarily held by the atoms and control field, and the stored spin wave decays (γ₁₂) and diffuses while waiting. Worked example · slow light in numbers Take ODEIT ≈ 9.6 and γEIT/2π ≈ 21 kHz (the simulator’s Zeeman EIT reference, illustrative). τ = 9.6/(2π × 21 × 10³ s⁻¹) ≈ 73 µs. In an assumed 7.5 cm cell that is vg ≈ 0.075 m / 73 µs ≈ 1 km/s, about 3 × 10⁵ times slower than c. A 47 µs pulse is 14 km long in vacuum but ≈ 5 cm inside the cell: it fits, so it can be stored. Q1. What happens to vg if you halve the control intensity (power-broadening-dominated regime)?γEIT roughly halves, so the delay ODEIT/γEIT roughly doubles and vg roughly halves. Transparency (ODEIT) may also drop, which is the trade-off. Q2. Why must the control be turned off while the pulse is fully inside the cell?Only the part of the pulse inside the medium is converted to spin wave. Anything already out (or not yet in) is lost or unstored. That is why the delay must exceed the pulse length (time-bandwidth product ≈ √ODEIT > 1). Go deeper · group velocity, adiabatic storage and what limits retrieval Why slow The group velocity of a pulse is vg = c/ng with ng = n + ω dn/dω (L6.2). Inside the EIT window dn/dω is large and positive, so ng can reach 10⁵–10⁷ or more in a vapour. The 17 m/s of the famous ultracold-gas experiment (Hau et al. 1999), and the metre-per-second to hundreds-of-metres-per-second speeds reported soon after in warm vapours (Kash et al. 1999; Budker et al. 1999), show that the effect does not need ultracold atoms. The pulse is also compressed in space by vg/c as it enters, so a pulse that is kilometres long in vacuum fits inside a cell centimetres long. Why “stored light” is not “frozen photons” At θ → 90° the dark-state polariton is entirely atomic: the quantum state of the field has been transferred to the collective coherence ρ₁₂ of all atoms, a spin wave whose phase pattern copies the pulse’s envelope (Fleischhauer & Lukin 2000; Fleischhauer & Lukin 2002). Storing and retrieving light were first demonstrated in a vapour and in an atomic medium by Phillips et al. 2001 and Liu et al. 2001, and the same idea works for single photons (Chanelière et al. 2005; Eisaman et al. 2005). What makes it adiabatic The control must change slowly compared with the inverse of the EIT window (the pulse’s spectrum must fit inside the window) so that the state follows the dark state without exciting the bright one. If the control is switched off too fast, part of the pulse is converted to bright-state population and lost to spontaneous emission. Shaping the control to maximize efficiency for a given OD is an optimization problem solved in Gorshkov et al. 2007. What limits storage and retrieval Optical depth. Inefficiency scales as 1/ODEIT (L10): a bigger OD is the main resource. Bandwidth. A pulse longer than 1/(window width) fits inside the window; one that is too short leaks. Spin-wave decay. The coherence decays at γ₁₂ and the spin-wave pattern is washed out by atoms diffusing across its wavelength. In Zeeman EIT both fields have almost the same wavelength, so the spin wave has a very long period and is almost unaffected by motion along the beam. Control leakage. A mW control next to a nW signal: the Glan–Taylor, spectral and timing filters (L11, L13). Pitfalls. (1) The delay ODEIT/γEIT is an estimate; measure it. (2) A pulse that is not fully inside when the control turns off is only partly stored. (3) The light is a dark-state polariton, not a photon sitting still, and energy is not created: the control field supplies none of the stored excitation. Sources Fleischhauer & Lukin 2000, Fleischhauer & Lukin 2002, Lukin 2003 (the theory); Novikova et al. 2011 (warm-atom experiments, a review); Hau et al. 1999, Phillips et al. 2001, Liu et al. 2001 (the experiments); Milonni 2005; Finkelstein et al. 2023 (practical limits). Thermal vapour realities: Doppler, transit, collisions, buffer gas Learning goalsEstimate Doppler width and transit time for warm Rb. Explain why co-propagating Λ beams cancel Doppler broadening. Describe what a buffer gas buys and what it costs. Atoms in a warm cell move at hundreds of metres per second. Each motional effect is a time-of-flight T across a length l, giving broadening ≈ 1/T (paper Eq. 29). Over an optical wavelength this is Doppler broadening; across the beam it is transit broadening; across the two-photon wavelength it determines whether EIT survives motion. L9.1\[ v_{\rm th}=\sqrt{\frac{k_BT}{m}},\qquad \sigma_{\rm Dop}=v_{\rm th}k,\qquad \Gamma_{tt}\sim\frac{v_{\rm th}}{w_0}\ \text{(ballistic)},\ \ \frac{D}{w_0^2}\ \text{(diffusive)},\qquad \delta_{\rm Dop}^{(2)}=(\vec k_p-\vec k_c)\cdot\vec v. \] A siren, a spotlight and a crowded room Read it in wordsThermal speed sets the Doppler width. Beam size and speed (or diffusion) set the time in the beam. The two-photon Doppler shift depends only on the difference of the two wavevectors. AnalogyA passing ambulance siren changes pitch (Doppler), but two sirens on the same ambulance keep the same interval (co-propagating Λ). An atom crossing the beam is a runner crossing a spotlight: fast runners are lit only briefly. Buffer gas turns the stage into a crowded room, where the runner staggers about and stays in the light far longer. Where it failsBuffer-gas collisions also shift and broaden the optical line (pressure broadening), and very high pressure eventually destroys ground coherence too. Worked example · ⁸⁷Rb at 60 °C m = 86.909 u Steck, T = 333 K ⇒ vth ≈ 179 m/s. σDop/2π = vth/λ ≈ 225 MHz (the paper’s Fig. 6 uses 230 MHz). Ballistic crossing of a 0.75 mm beam radius takes ≈ 4.2 µs. With D ≈ 10 cm²/s (paper, 10 Torr), diffusion across it takes w₀²/D ≈ 0.56 ms, about 130 times longer derived. Q1. Why does a ladder (cascade) scheme prefer counter-propagating beams, while Λ prefers co-propagating?In Λ one photon is absorbed and one emitted, so the effective wavevector is kp − kc, which is small when the beams travel together. In a ladder both photons are absorbed, so it is kp + kc, which is minimised by opposite directions (paper Fig. 9 inset). Q2. A beam angle of 0.1 mrad between probe and control: roughly how much residual broadening without buffer gas?σDopθ ≈ 225 MHz × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 20 kHz: “tens of kHz”, as the paper says. With buffer gas, Dicke narrowing makes it quadratic in θ and much smaller. Go deeper · numbers for a warm cell, buffer gas, Dicke narrowing and its costs The numbers L9.2\[ f(v)\propto e^{-mv^2/2k_BT},\qquad \Delta\omega=-\vec k\cdot\vec v,\qquad n_{\rm at}=\frac{P_{\rm vap}}{k_BT}. \] Rubidium’s vapour pressure at 25 °C is 3.92 × 10⁻⁷ Torr Steck, which is 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ Pa: the ideal-gas law gives n = 5.2 × 10⁻⁵/(1.381 × 10⁻²³ × 298) = 1.3 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³ = 1.3 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. The density rises roughly exponentially with temperature, so raising the cell from 25 °C to 60 °C raises it by about 20 to 25 times design estimate: the heater is an optical-depth knob. At the higher density atom–atom collisions (spin exchange) start to limit the coherence, which is the trade-off the paper describes (Finkelstein et al. 2023). What a buffer gas does and costs A few Torr of an inert gas (here neon) make the active atoms diffuse instead of flying straight, which keeps them in the beam far longer (diffusion D ≈ 10 cm²/s at 10 Torr, paper) and, when the mean free path is shorter than the relevant wavelength, narrows the Doppler contribution (Dicke narrowing, Dicke 1953). For the two-photon coherence the relevant length is the microwave or Zeeman wavelength, which is centimetres or longer, so narrowing is complete; for the one-photon optical transition it is not (Finkelstein et al. 2023). The costs: pressure broadening of the optical line (~10 MHz/Torr, so ~100 MHz at 10 Torr, about 17 times the natural width), a lower peak absorption per atom (so a higher temperature may be needed for the same OD), and collisional dephasing of the ground states that grows with pressure. Alternatives to a buffer gas Anti-relaxation wall coatings (paraffin-type coatings) preserve ground-state coherence through wall collisions and allow very long lifetimes in small cells, at the price of a limited temperature range. Slow light in a vapour with slow ground-state relaxation was reported by Budker et al. 1999. Which is better depends on the target: coatings favour long storage in small cells, buffer gas favours simplicity and tolerance of beam size. Pitfalls. (1) A small angle between probe and control gives residual two-photon Doppler broadening of ~σDopθ without buffer gas: 0.1 mrad is already ~20 kHz. (2) Thermal gradients in the cell make the coldest spot (the stem) set the density. (3) Temperature stability matters as much as accuracy: OD drifts with T. Quantum memories: metrics, repeaters, networks Learning goalsDefine efficiency, fidelity, storage time, bandwidth and multimode capacity. Explain why repeaters need memories. Place the project’s Rb platform among memory goals. A quantum memory stores a quantum state of light and releases it on demand. Photon loss in fibre grows exponentially with distance and a quantum state cannot be copied, so long-distance links need repeaters. Repeaters create entanglement over short segments and connect them, and they need memories to hold one segment’s success while the others try. The DLCZ proposal (paper ref. [47]) used atomic ensembles for exactly this. Published Rb and Cs ensemble memories report high efficiencies and fidelities (e.g. Hsiao et al. 2018, paper ref. [114]); read the originals for the numbers. L10.1\[ \eta=\frac{E_{\rm out}}{E_{\rm in}},\qquad \mathcal F=|\langle\psi_{\rm in}|\psi_{\rm out}\rangle|^2\ \ (\text{pure states}),\qquad \eta(\tau)\approx\eta_0\,e^{-\tau/T_{\rm mem}},\qquad 1-\eta_0\propto\frac{1}{\mathrm{OD}_{\rm EIT}},\qquad B\tau_{\rm delay}\approx\sqrt{\mathrm{OD}_{\rm EIT}}. \] A left-luggage office Read it in wordsEfficiency is how much of the stored energy (or how many photons) comes back. Fidelity is how faithfully the state comes back. Memory time is how long before efficiency decays. Inefficiency shrinks with OD (paper). The time–bandwidth product says how many pulses fit in the medium. AnalogyA left-luggage office. Efficiency: the fraction of bags you get back. Fidelity: whether they come back undamaged and unopened. Storage time: how long before bags start going missing. Bandwidth: how big a bag fits through the door. Multimode capacity: how many lockers there are. Where it failsA luggage office can photocopy your documents; a quantum memory cannot copy an unknown state (no-cloning). A “lost bag” in a memory can also become noise added to other bags. Worked example · how many pulses fit? With ODEIT ≈ 9.6 the time–bandwidth product is √9.6 ≈ 3. Only about three distinguishable pulses fit in the medium at once. Raising it to 30 gives ≈ 5.5. This is why OD is the resource (paper Sec. IV). The exponential storage-decay form above is a simple model; real decay curves can be non-exponential (e.g. diffusion). Q1. Can a memory have 99 % fidelity and 10 % efficiency?Yes. Fidelity (conditional on retrieval) and efficiency are separate figures of merit. Many demonstrations report both. Q2. Why does the project first benchmark with classical (attenuated) light?Efficiency, delay, bandwidth and storage time can be measured with weak classical pulses on standard photodiodes. Atomic frequency comb and related rare-earth schemes: multimode storage in an inhomogeneously broadened solid (Afzelius et al. 2009). Always check what was measured, with what input (classical pulses or single photons), and in what basis. Quantum states of light: coherent, Fock, single photons, g⁽²⁾(0) Learning goalsContrast coherent states (lasers) with Fock states (single photons). Use Poisson statistics to analyse attenuated laser pulses. Interpret the second-order correlation g⁽²⁾(0). A laser, however strongly attenuated, emits a coherent state: the photon number in a pulse is Poisson-distributed. Attenuation lowers the mean but never removes the chance of two photons. A true single-photon source (e.g. the α-MoO₃ emitters planned for Objective 3 in the project plan; see the source note in L12) ideally emits a Fock state |1⟩ with zero chance of two. The Hanbury Brown–Twiss measurement of g⁽²⁾(0) tells them apart. L11.1\[ P(n)=e^{-\bar n}\frac{\bar n^{\,n}}{n!},\qquad g^{(2)}(0)=\frac{\langle\hat a^\dagger\hat a^\dagger\hat a\hat a\rangle}{\langle\hat a^\dagger\hat a\rangle^2}=\begin{cases}1&\text{coherent}\\ 2&\text{thermal}\\ 0&\text{single-photon Fock state}\end{cases} \] Rain on a tile versus a vending machine Read it in wordsFor a coherent state, the probability of n photons follows a Poisson law with mean n̄. g⁽²⁾(0) compares the chance of detecting two photons at the same time with what independent arrivals would give: 1 for a laser, 2 for thermal (bunched) light, 0 for an ideal single-photon source. AnalogyRaindrops hitting one floor tile arrive randomly: sometimes none, occasionally two at once (Poisson, g⁽²⁾ = 1). A vending machine drops exactly one can per button press, never two (Fock state, g⁽²⁾ = 0). Where it failsRaindrops are classical particles. Light’s statistics come from the quantum state of a field mode, and a single photon can still be split between two paths without being divided. Worked example · attenuated probe pulses A 10 µs, 1 µW pulse at 795 nm holds ≈ 4.0 × 10⁷ photons (L1). For n̄ = 1, attenuate by 4 × 10⁷ (ND ≈ 7.6). At n̄ = 0.1: P(0) = 0.905, P(1) = 0.090, P(≥2) = 0.0047. About 5 % of non-empty pulses still contain two or more photons, which is why “single-photon-level” classical probes are not single photons. Q1. What g⁽²⁾(0) would you measure for the Zeeman EIT probe laser?≈ 1 (coherent light), regardless of attenuation. Q2. Why does storing true single photons demand much better control filtering than storing a µW probe?The signal is ~1 photon per pulse, while a mW control leaks, scatters and fluoresces. Even a 10⁻⁵ extinction (Glan–Taylor) leaves many control photons per pulse. Spectral filtering and timing gates are then needed too. Go deeper · measuring photon statistics, sources of single photons, and the numbers for attenuated pulses The Hanbury Brown–Twiss measurement Send the light to a 50:50 beamsplitter with a detector on each output and count coincidences. Independent (Poissonian) arrivals give coincidences at the rate expected from chance; bunched (thermal) light gives more; a single photon cannot go to both detectors and gives none. The ratio is g(2)(0). The method originates with BROWN & TWISS 1956 (correlations between photons in two beams); the quantum theory is Glauber’s (Glauber 1963; Glauber 1963, Nobel Prize 2005, Nobel 2005); antibunching was first observed in resonance fluorescence by Kimble et al. 1977. State ⟨n⟩ g(2)(0) Photon-number distribution Coherent |α⟩ |α|² 1 Poisson Thermal n̄ 2 geometric (Bose–Einstein) Fock |n⟩, n ≥ 1 n 1 − 1/n (0 for n = 1) exactly n Squeezed vacuum sinh²r 3 + 1/⟨n⟩ even photon numbers only The 3D Wigner-function illustration above shows what each of these looks like in phase space; the numbers it reports are exactly this table. Why attenuation never makes a single-photon source L11.2\[ P(\ge2)=1-e^{-\bar n}(1+\bar n)\simeq\frac{\bar n^2}{2}\ \ (\bar n\ll1),\qquad \frac{P(\ge2)}{P(\ge1)}\simeq\frac{\bar n}{2}. \] At n̄ = 0.1, P(≥2) = 0.0047 and the fraction of non-empty pulses with two or more photons is ≈ n̄/2 = 5 %: reducing n̄ lowers the multi-photon probability only in proportion, while the empty pulses (90 %) increasingly dominate. A real single-photon source suppresses multi-photon events without making most pulses empty. Real single-photon sources Heralded sources detect one photon of a pair to announce the other, including atomic-ensemble sources (Kuzmich et al. 2003). Single quantum emitters (quantum dots, defects, molecules) emit one photon per excitation cycle (Michler et al. 2000); solid-state emitters are reviewed in Aharonovich et al. 2016. For each, the figures of merit are g(2)(0) (purity), brightness, indistinguishability and bandwidth. Matching the emitter’s photons in colour, bandwidth and timing to a memory is a major challenge (L10 and L12). Pitfalls. (1) Background light and detector dark counts raise g(2)(0) above its true value, so “g(2) < 0.5” alone is not proof of a single emitter without care. (2) “Single-photon level” attenuated pulses are still coherent states. (3) A detector’s dead time and timing jitter limit the shortest delays you can resolve. Sources Loudon, Gerry & Knight, Fox 2006, Garrison & Chiao 2008, Kok & Lovett 2010; originals: BROWN & TWISS 1956, Glauber 1963, Kimble et al. 1977; sources: Michler et al. 2000, Aharonovich et al. 2016, Kuzmich et al. 2003. Strong coupling, cavity QED and polaritons in solids: the bridge to Objective 3 Learning goalsDefine the strong-coupling condition and cooperativity. See how an ensemble gives collective enhancement g√N. Understand, without overclaiming, how microcavity polaritons relate to this project. Put an emitter in an optical cavity. If the emitter–photon coupling g beats both the cavity loss κ and the emitter decay γ, energy oscillates back and forth and the spectrum splits into two polariton peaks separated by the vacuum Rabi splitting. N emitters coupled to the same mode act collectively with g√N. The EIT paper makes the same point for vapours: strong light–matter coupling arises from collective enhancement of a large ensemble, and “no high-quality cavity is required”. Objective 3 concerns solid-state systems. The solid-state literature includes studies of P3HT under ultrastrong coupling (Nagarajan et al. 2020) and of low-loss phonon polaritons in α-MoO₃ (Ma et al. 2018). Whether such systems can support EIT-like storage at room temperature is precisely the open question the calibrated Rb platform is meant to help test. Nothing here should be read as a claim that they do (see the source note in “Go deeper”). L12.1\[ g\gg\kappa,\gamma\ \ (\text{strong coupling}),\qquad C=\frac{4g^2}{\kappa\gamma},\qquad \hbar\Omega_R=2\hbar g\sqrt{N}\ \ (\text{collective vacuum Rabi splitting}),\qquad \frac{g}{\omega}\gtrsim0.1\ \ (\text{a common ultrastrong criterion}). \] Two pendulums joined by a spring Read it in wordsStrong coupling means the exchange rate g outruns both loss channels. Cooperativity C summarises how good the coupling is. N emitters together couple √N times more strongly. “Ultrastrong” is a regime where g becomes a sizeable fraction of the bare frequency itself; ~0.1 is a commonly used threshold. AnalogyTwo pendulums joined by a spring trade their swing back and forth. Strongly joined, they no longer swing at their own frequencies but in two new shared modes, one faster and one slower. That frequency split is the Rabi splitting, and the shared modes are the polaritons. Where it failsPendulums are classical. Vacuum Rabi splitting exists even with zero photons in the cavity, and polariton storage needs long-lived matter coherence. A large splitting alone does not guarantee that. Worked example · same idea, different scales In the Rb cell, the “coupling” that matters is collective: OD ≈ 10 means the ensemble absorbs strongly without any cavity. In ultrastrong-coupling studies of solids the Rabi splitting is a sizeable fraction of the transition energy itself (the criterion g/ω ≳ 0.1 in L12.1), whereas in the Rb cell the collective coupling is tiny compared with the 1.56 eV (377 THz) photon energy of L1 and it is the optical depth, not a large splitting, that matters. These are very different physical regimes, which is why Objective 3 begins with careful calibration on the Rb platform. Q1. Why does an atomic ensemble not need a cavity to reach strong collective coupling?The relevant figure, OD, grows with atom number. Many atoms each weakly coupled add up (g√N, or OD ∝ N L), so a single pass through a dense cell gives strong light–matter interaction. Q2. Does a large Rabi splitting imply a good quantum memory?No. A memory also needs a long-lived, controllable coherence (like γ₁₂ in Rb) and a way to switch the coupling on and off. Splitting measures coupling strength, not storage time. Go deeper · the Jaynes–Cummings ladder, polaritons in solids, and what the project plan does and does not establish The Jaynes–Cummings model L12.2\[ \hat H_{\rm JC}=\hbar\omega_c\hat a^\dagger\hat a+\hbar\omega_a\hat\sigma^\dagger\hat\sigma+\hbar g\big(\hat a\hat\sigma^\dagger+\hat a^\dagger\hat\sigma\big),\qquad E_{n,\pm}=\hbar\omega\Big(n+\tfrac12\Big)\pm\hbar g\sqrt{n+1}\ \ (\text{on resonance; }n=\text{photons in the }g\text{ component}). \] One two-level emitter and one mode (Jaynes & Cummings 1963; the cavity-QED experiments are reviewed in Haroche & Raimond 2006 and the Nobel lecture Haroche 2013). On resonance the states split into doublets with a gap 2g√(n + 1): for the first excitation, the vacuum Rabi splitting 2g. The ladder’s square-root spacing is a purely quantum signature. N identical emitters sharing the mode give √N-enhanced coupling, which is the collective strong coupling of an atomic ensemble and of molecular or excitonic layers in cavities (Törmä & Barnes 2014; Ebbesen 2016). The 3D avoided-crossing illustration shows the semiclassical two-mode limit of the same physics. Polaritons in solids A polariton is a mixed light–matter excitation. In a crystal, the coupling of light to excitons gives exciton polaritons (Hopfield 1958); in a semiconductor microcavity the exciton–photon mode splitting was reported by Weisbuch et al. 1992 and polariton condensation by Kasprzak et al. 2006. In polar crystals the matter part can be a lattice vibration (phonon polaritons): for example the low-loss, in-plane anisotropic phonon polaritons in α-MoO₃ (Ma et al. 2018). The wider literature on strong and ultrastrong coupling between light and matter, including the criteria g/ω ≳ 0.1 for ultrastrong coupling, is reviewed in Frisk Kockum et al. 2019 and Forn-Díaz et al. 2019; a broad overview of polaritons across materials is Basov et al. 2020. Organic semiconductors such as P3HT have been studied under ultrastrong coupling in the context of conductivity and photoconductivity (Nagarajan et al. 2020). What this does and does not tell you about Objective 3 Be careful with claimsA large splitting shows that light and matter are strongly coupled, not that the system can store a quantum state: a memory also needs a long-lived coherence that can be switched on and off (L7, L8, L10). In a room-temperature solid the relevant coherences are generally much shorter-lived than the ground-state coherence of an atomic vapour, so whether EIT-like storage can work in a given material is an open experimental question. Light-matter coupling has been demonstrated, and EIT-type transparency has been seen in several solid-state systems (Turukhin et al. 2001; Longdell et al. 2005), but not at room temperature in the specific materials of the project’s next stage; this page makes no claim that it will. Source check: an earlier version of this lecture quoted a Rabi splitting of ~0.6 eV for P3HT from the project plan. That value could not be matched to the literature consulted for this revision, so it has been removed; the cited publications should be checked directly. Likewise the use of α-MoO₃ as a single-photon emitter is the project plan’s own statement: the α-MoO₃ literature cited here concerns phonon polaritons, so check the plan’s source for the emitter claim. Pitfalls. (1) Strong coupling needs g > κ and γ: a large g with a lossy cavity or emitter shows no resolved splitting. (2) A Rabi splitting seen in a transmission spectrum can also come from effects that do not involve strong coupling (for example overlapping absorption and cavity lines); compare with the criteria in the reviews. (3) Do not carry numbers between platforms: a collective vapour coupling and a single quantum emitter in a cavity are in different regimes. Sources Jaynes & Cummings 1963, Haroche & Raimond 2006, Haroche 2013; polaritons: Hopfield 1958, Weisbuch et al. 1992, Kasprzak et al. 2006, Basov et al. 2020; strong and ultrastrong coupling: Törmä & Barnes 2014, Frisk Kockum et al. 2019, Forn-Díaz et al. 2019, Ebbesen 2016; materials: Ma et al. 2018, Nagarajan et al. 2020; EIT in solids: Turukhin et al. 2001, Longdell et al. 2005, Abdumalikov et al. 2010.
