Lab fundamentals for the project: polarization, Gaussian beams, AOMs, locking, cells, detectors, safety

Lab fundamentals for the project: polarization, Gaussian beams, AOMs, locking, cells, detectors, safety Learning goalsPredict how waveplates, PBSs and Glan–Taylor polarizers turn H and V light into σ⁺ and σ⁻, and why the order matters. Calculate beam size, Rayleigh range, intensity and Rabi frequency from a power and a waist. Explain how an acousto-optic modulator and a double pass set the two-photon detuning. Understand saturated-absorption locking, the field requirement for the cell, and the noise of a photodiode. Work safely with an invisible 795 nm beam. Lectures L1–L12 explain the atomic physics. This lecture explains the bench: the optical and electronic tools that turn the physics into a measurement, in the same order that the 3D bench simulator lays them out. Each part ends with what to check on the real bench, because every number in the model has to be measured, not assumed.
Q2. In Zeeman EIT the control power fraction is set by an HWP before a PBS. If the plate angle is θ and the input is H, what fraction goes to the transmitted (H) port?

L13.1 Polarization: Jones vectors, waveplates and the Poincaré sphere Light that is fully polarized is described by a two-component Jones vector (the amplitudes along horizontal and vertical, with their relative phase; Jones 1941). Optical elements are 2×2 matrices acting on it. A half-wave plate at angle θ to horizontal reflects the polarization about its fast axis: linear light at angle φ leaves at 2θ − φ. A quarter-wave plate turns linear light at 45° to its axis into circular light and vice versa. A polarizing beamsplitter transmits H and reflects V. Zeeman EIT uses all three: an HWP and PBS to set the probe/control split, a QWP to make σ⁺ and σ⁻, and a Glan–Taylor polarizer, whose extinction is of order 10⁵ (the paper), to remove the control after the cell (a PBS manages only about 10³). L13.1\[ \mathbf J_{\rm H}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\ \ \mathbf J_{\rm V}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix},\ \ \mathbf J_{\sigma^\pm}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \pm i\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf M_{\rm HWP}(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\theta&\sin2\theta\\ \sin2\theta&-\cos2\theta\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf M_{\rm QWP}(\theta)=\mathbf R(-\theta)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix}\mathbf R(\theta). \] L13.2\[ S_0=|E_H|^2+|E_V|^2,\quad S_1=|E_H|^2-|E_V|^2,\quad S_2=2\,\mathrm{Re}(E_H^*E_V),\quad S_3=2\,\mathrm{Im}(E_H^*E_V),\qquad S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2=S_0^2\ \ (\text{fully polarized}). \] A globe where the poles are circular light Read it in wordsEvery fully polarized state is a point on the Poincaré sphere, with horizontal and vertical on opposite ends of one axis, ±45° linear on another, and σ⁺ and σ⁻ at the poles. Orthogonal polarizations are always antipodal. A waveplate rotates the whole sphere about an axis in the equatorial plane: a half-wave plate by 180°, a quarter-wave plate by 90°. AnalogyA globe that you spin about a horizontal axis (the waveplate axis). A point on the equator (linear light) is carried up toward a pole (circular light) by a quarter-turn. Two points that start opposite each other, such as H and V, stay opposite after any rotation: this is why a single QWP turns the control and probe into opposite circular states. Where it failsThe sphere describes fully polarized light only. Partially polarized light lies inside the sphere, and real waveplates have retardance errors and a wavelength dependence that move the end points slightly. Worked example · why the plate angles are what they are With the convention of L13.1 (field E = Re[J e−iωt], so σ⁺ rotates counter-clockwise about the beam), a QWP at +45° gives M = ½[[1+i, 1−i], [1−i, 1+i]]. Then H = (1, 0) → ½(1+i, 1−i) ∝ (1, −i)/√2 = σ⁻, and V = (0, 1) → ½(1−i, 1+i) ∝ (1, i)/√2 = σ⁺. The probe (H) and the control (V) therefore enter the cell with opposite circular polarizations, as the Λ system needs (L5, L7). After the cell, a second QWP at −45° maps σ⁺/σ⁻ back to V/H, and a Glan–Taylor set to pass the probe’s polarization removes the control. The same QWP at +45° would turn a σ⁺ beam into H. Which circular state is which depends on the sign convention of the quantization axis and on whether a mirror has reflected the beam, so always check the sense with the experiment (or the simulator’s Stokes readout) rather than relying on a label. Pitfalls. (1) Reflection from a mirror reverses the helicity relative to the propagation direction. (2) A waveplate’s “zero order, 780 nm” design is close to, but not exactly, a quarter-wave at 795 nm: check the retardance and tune the angle for best circular purity. (3) Polarization-maintaining fibre carries only the axes it is aligned to: a few degrees of misalignment leaks power into the wrong polarization and into the SAS reference. Q1. What does an HWP at 22.5° do to horizontal light?It rotates the polarization by 2 × 22.5° = 45°: H → D (+45° linear), a point on the S₂ axis of the Poincaré sphere. Q2. In Zeeman EIT the control power fraction is set by an HWP before a PBS. If the plate angle is θ and the input is H, what fraction goes to the transmitted (H) port?cos²(2θ), and the reflected (V) port gets sin²(2θ), with θ measured from horizontal. In the reference bench the light reaching this plate is pure H (the pick-off PBS has already cleaned it), and a plate at 10° sends sin²(20°) ≈ 12 % to the probe port.
Q2. Why is a beam that is 1.5 mm in diameter at the AOM aperture often focused in the crystal?

L13.2 Gaussian beams: size, focus, intensity A laser beam in free space is a Gaussian beam: its intensity across the beam is a Gaussian, and its radius w(z) (where the intensity has fallen to 1/e² of the peak) is smallest at the waist w₀ and grows on either side (Kogelnik & Li 1966; Siegman 1986; Saleh & Teich). The distance over which the beam stays roughly collimated is the Rayleigh range zR. These few formulas decide four things on the bench: the intensity that sets the Rabi frequency (L3), the time atoms spend in the beam (L9), whether the beam fits through an AOM crystal, and how to focus into the cat’s-eye of a double pass. L13.3\[ w(z)=w_0\sqrt{1+(z/z_R)^2},\qquad z_R=\frac{\pi w_0^2}{\lambda},\qquad I_0=\frac{2P}{\pi w_0^2},\qquad w_0'=\frac{\lambda f}{\pi w}\ \ (\text{beam of radius }w\text{ focused by a lens of focal length }f). \] Worked example · from power to Rabi frequency For a collimated beam of waist w₀ = 0.75 mm at 794.979 nm: zR = π(0.75 mm)²/λ = 2.2 m, so the beam stays nearly parallel over the whole table; the half-angle divergence is λ/(πw₀) = 0.34 mrad. Its peak intensity for P = 1 mW is 2P/(πw₀²) = 113 mW/cm². The paper’s control intensities were 1.3 and 5.5 mW/cm² (Finkelstein et al. 2023); for a beam of radius 2.55 mm (the value used in the simulator) these correspond to only P = I₀πw²/2 ≈ 0.13 mW and 0.56 mW. With Γ/2π = 5.750 MHz and the far-detuned π-light Isat = 4.488 mW/cm² Steck, the two-level estimate of L3 gives Ω/2π = (Γ/2π)√(I/2Isat) ≈ 2.2 MHz at 1.3 mW/cm² (the paper quotes 1.9 MHz). A lens of f = 100 mm focuses a beam of w = 0.75 mm to w₀′ = λf/(πw) ≈ 34 µm, with zR ≈ 4.5 mm: tight focusing is only forgiving over millimetres, which is why the position of the AOM crystal and of the cat’s-eye mirror matters. Q1. Doubling the waist radius at constant power changes the peak intensity by what factor?I₀ ∝ 1/w₀², so it falls by 4. The Rabi frequency ∝ √I falls by 2. Q2. Why is a beam that is 1.5 mm in diameter at the AOM aperture often focused in the crystal?The crystal’s useful aperture is about as large as the beam, so an unfocused beam clips at the edges and loses efficiency. Focusing inside the crystal shrinks the beam so it fits easily (and a smaller beam also gives a faster rise time, see L13.3). The price is a larger divergence, which the following lens must re-collimate.
Q2. Why is a high-power RF amplifier needed at all?

L13.3 Acousto-optic modulators and the double pass In an AOM a radio-frequency signal drives a transducer that launches a sound wave through a crystal. The sound is a moving diffraction grating: light entering at the Bragg angle is diffracted into a first order that is shifted in frequency by the sound frequency (Siegman 1986; Saleh & Teich). The deflection angle depends on the RF frequency, which is a nuisance when the beam must stay aligned. The double pass (Donley et al. 2005) fixes it: the first order is focused by a lens onto a mirror at the lens focus (a cat’s-eye), which sends it back through the AOM along its own path. The returning beam is diffracted a second time onto the original axis, so the output direction no longer depends on the RF frequency, and the total shift is doubled. A quarter-wave plate crossed twice turns the polarization by 90°, so a polarizing beamsplitter can lift the returning beam out of the input path. Zeeman EIT uses one such double pass per arm. L13.4\[ \theta_{\rm defl}\simeq\frac{\lambda f_{\rm RF}}{v_s},\qquad \Delta\nu_{\rm out}=\pm2f_{\rm RF}\ \ (\text{double pass}),\qquad \delta=2\big(f_{\rm RF,c}-f_{\rm RF,p}\big)=\mu_Bg\,\Delta m\,B/h,\qquad t_{\rm rise}\approx0.64\,\frac{D}{v_s}. \] A moving corrugated mirror Read it in wordsThe sound wave is a travelling pattern of compressed and stretched crystal that acts as a grating. Light bouncing off a grating that moves picks up a Doppler shift equal to the grating’s frequency, and is steered by an angle that grows with the sound frequency. Passing twice doubles the shift, and sending it back along its path undoes the steering. AnalogyA tennis ball hits a moving racket twice in a row: each hit changes its speed by the same amount, so two hits change it twice as much; and if you arrange to hit it back exactly the way it came, the direction you chose for the first hit no longer matters. Where it failsA racket gives the ball a definite speed change every time. The AOM diffracts only a fraction of the light into the first order (efficiency η per pass, so η² for a double pass), and the rest goes to the zero order, which must be dumped. Worked example · numbers for the 80 MHz TeO₂ AOMs The slow shear acoustic mode of TeO₂ has a sound velocity of about 0.62 km/s (617 m/s along ⟨110⟩ in the literature on TeO₂ acousto-optic devices); this low velocity is what gives the large deflection angles. For λ = 795 nm and fRF = 80 MHz the deflection is θ ≈ λf/vs = (795 nm × 80 MHz)/617 m/s ≈ 0.10 rad ≈ 6° estimate: check the device data sheet. That is why the simulator draws the first order at an exaggerated 8°. A beam of diameter D = 1.5 mm has a rise time of about 0.64 × D/vs ≈ 1.6 µs rule of thumb, which limits how fast the control can be switched in the storage sequence (L8). In the reference bench the control RF is 80.000 MHz and the probe RF 79.965 MHz, so after the double pass they differ by 2 × 35 kHz = 70 kHz, equal to the Zeeman splitting 1.40 kHz/mG × 50 mG of the mF = +2 and 0 pair (L5). Both beams are also shifted by about +160 MHz from the laser, so the laser lock must be planned with that offset in mind (see the Zeeman EIT architecture). Pitfalls. (1) Align the cat’s-eye by watching the returning beam while sweeping the RF frequency: when it is right, the returning beam does not walk. (2) Never run the RF amplifier without the AOM (or a 50 Ω load) attached. (3) The 0th-order and the unwanted returning-pass light must go to beam dumps; otherwise they scatter onto the detector. (4) Leave the RF on during alignment: thermal changes in the crystal shift the optimum angle. Q1. The control AOM runs at 80.000 MHz and the probe AOM at 79.950 MHz, both double-passed. What is the probe–control frequency difference?2 × (79.950 − 80.000) MHz = −100 kHz. The sign depends on which order each AOM uses; in the reference bench both use the +1 order. Q2. Why is a high-power RF amplifier needed at all?The first-order efficiency depends on the acoustic power, and an AOM typically needs hundreds of milliwatts to a watt or two of RF for good efficiency (check the data sheet). The synthesizer outputs far less, so each arm has an attenuator/switch (to set the level and gate the arm) followed by an amplifier.
L13.4 Saturated-absorption spectroscopy and locking the laser

L13.4 Saturated-absorption spectroscopy and locking the laser A free-running diode laser drifts by tens of MHz; Zeeman EIT needs the one-photon detuning stable to the MHz scale (L9, L7). The reference is the atom itself, read out by saturated-absorption spectroscopy (Preston 1996; MacAdam et al. 1992; Demtröder). A strong pump and a weak probe cross the same vapour from opposite directions. Atoms moving along the beam see the pump and probe at opposite Doppler shifts, so only atoms with nearly zero velocity along the beam are resonant with both. The pump saturates them, and the probe sees a narrow dip (as narrow as the natural width, here a few MHz) in the 500 MHz-wide Doppler absorption. Where two lines share a velocity class, a crossover resonance appears exactly midway between them. To lock on such a dip you need an error signal that is zero on the line and changes sign across it: the derivative of the dip. A small current dither on the diode, with lock-in detection at the dither frequency, gives it. The lock box feeds the error back to the laser current, and slow drifts are removed by retuning the temperature, since a DFB has no piezo (Wieman & Hollberg 1991; the dither/lock-in and the Pound–Drever–Hall method are compared in Black 2001 and Drever et al. 1983). L13.5\[ e(\Delta)\propto-\frac{d}{d\Delta}\,\mathcal L(\Delta)=\frac{2\Delta/(\Gamma/2)^2}{\big[1+(2\Delta/\Gamma)^2\big]^2},\qquad \Delta\nu_{\rm Dop}^{\rm FWHM}\approx530\ \mathrm{MHz}\ \gg\ \Gamma/2\pi=5.75\ \mathrm{MHz}. \] A thermostat that reads the slope, not the height Read it in wordsThe error signal is the slope of the absorption dip. It is zero at the bottom and has opposite signs on each side, so it tells the servo which way the laser has drifted and by roughly how much. AnalogyA marble at the bottom of a bowl. You cannot tell from its height that it has moved, but you can feel the slope pushing it back. The lock box applies the opposite push to the laser. Where it failsA real servo can only correct within the width of the slope: if the laser jumps far outside the dip, the error signal is zero or points the wrong way, and the loop can lock to a neighbouring line. A wrong slope sign or too much gain makes the loop run away or oscillate (the simulator reproduces both). Worked example · why the SAS shows resolved features on D1 For ⁸⁷Rb D1, the ground hyperfine splitting is 6 834.683 MHz and the excited-state splitting F′ = 1 to F′ = 2 is 814.5(13) MHz Steck. The Doppler FWHM is about 530 MHz, so the F = 2 and F = 1 absorption lines are completely separate, and each shows two Doppler dips (to F′ = 1 and F′ = 2), partly resolved, 814 MHz apart. Zeeman EIT locks near F = 2 → F′ = 1 (see the Zeeman EIT architecture). The AOM shifts (about +160 MHz in total) must be taken into account so that the beam reaching the cell, not just the SAS beam, ends up on the intended atomic resonance.
Q2. Why is the heater wound bifilar (current flowing out and back in adjacent wires)?

L13.5 The vapour cell, the field and the shield The optical depth of the cell rises steeply with temperature, because the density of rubidium vapour follows the vapour pressure, which grows roughly exponentially with T (Steck, Rb-87 data, vapour-pressure model). At 25 °C the vapour pressure is 3.92 × 10⁻⁷ Torr, which with the ideal-gas law gives n = P/kBT ≈ 1.3 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ Steck; at 60 °C the density is roughly 20 to 25 times higher design estimate, in the range 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³ that the paper treats as typical (Finkelstein et al. 2023). Heating the cell is therefore the main OD knob. Magnetic fields are the other. The two-photon resonance of Zeeman EIT moves by 1.40 kHz per milligauss (L5), while the EIT line is only about 7 to 26 kHz wide: a stray field of just 5 mG shifts the resonance by 7 kHz, which is as large as the linewidth. Earth’s field is roughly 0.5 G, a hundred times bigger. That is why the cell sits in a µ-metal shield (three nested layers in the paper) with a solenoid inside to provide a small, known, stable bias field along the beams, and why the shield must be degaussed after assembly: leftover magnetization otherwise sets the residual field. L13.6\[ B=\mu_0\,\frac{N}{L_{\rm sol}}\,I,\qquad \delta_{\rm Zeeman}=\frac{2\,g_F\,\mu_B}{h}\,B=1.40\ \mathrm{kHz/mG}\times B\ \ (m_F=+2\leftrightarrow0,\ g_F=\tfrac12),\qquad n_{\rm at}=\frac{P_{\rm vap}}{k_BT}. \] Worked example · the solenoid and its current source A long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre produces B = μ₀(N/L)I = 12.6 mG for every milliampere. To make 50 mG you need I = 50/12.57 ≈ 4.0 mA. A current error of 1 µA changes B by 12.6 µG, which moves the two-photon resonance by 1.40 kHz/mG × 0.0126 mG ≈ 18 Hz: negligible against a 7 kHz line. But a 1 % drift (40 µA) shifts B by 0.5 mG, i.e. 0.7 kHz: a visible fraction of the linewidth. So the coil supply needs ~0.1 % stability, and the bias should be well above the residual field the shield leaves behind (otherwise the residual, not the coil, sets the resonance). A fluxgate magnetometer measures the residual and calibrates the coil. Q1. Earth’s field is 0.5 G and the EIT line is 10 kHz wide. By what factor must the shield reduce the field to keep the shift below the line width?0.5 G = 500 mG shifts the pair by 500 × 1.40 kHz = 700 kHz. To get below 10 kHz you need B ≲ 7 mG, a reduction by at least 70. In practice you want a much smaller shift (a small fraction of the line), so a shielding factor of several hundred or more. Q2. Why is the heater wound bifilar (current flowing out and back in adjacent wires)?The two opposite currents produce opposite magnetic fields that cancel at a distance. A single-wire winding of the same current would add a field of its own at the atoms and shift or broaden the resonance.
Q1. A probe of 10 nW at 795 nm on a silicon photodiode with R = 0.5 A/W gives what photocurrent, and what voltage through 1 MΩ?

L13.6 Detectors and noise A photodiode converts power P into a current I = RP with responsivity R = ηeλ/hc, about 0.64 A/W per unit quantum efficiency at 795 nm; silicon photodiodes are around 0.5 A/W near 800 nm (check the data sheet). The current is converted to a voltage by a transimpedance amplifier. Three noise sources compete: shot noise of the photocurrent itself, thermal (Johnson) noise of the feedback resistor, and amplifier noise (Saleh & Teich). At the microwatt power levels of the probe the resistor and shot noise are comparable, and below that the resistor noise wins, so the signal-to-noise ratio improves by averaging (the scope) or by using a lower bandwidth. L13.7\[ I=RP,\quad R=\frac{\eta e\lambda}{hc}\approx0.64\,\eta\ \mathrm{A/W},\qquad i_{\rm shot}=\sqrt{2eI\,\Delta f},\qquad i_{\rm Johnson}=\sqrt{\frac{4k_BT\,\Delta f}{R_f}}. \] Worked example · is the probe signal shot-noise limited? Take R = 0.5 A/W, P = 1 µW and a measurement bandwidth Δf = 1 MHz. The photocurrent is 0.5 µA and the shot noise is √(2 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁶) ≈ 0.40 nA (signal-to-noise 1250). A feedback resistor Rf = 100 kΩ at 300 K adds √(4 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 × 10⁶/10⁵) ≈ 0.41 nA, the same size: at 1 µW the two are equal (the crossover is at I = 2kBT/(eRf) ≈ 0.52 µA). For the weaker probe powers typical of EIT the resistor noise wins, so a larger Rf (at the cost of bandwidth) or averaging is the way to gain, and single-photon work needs a different detector altogether (L1 Q2, L11). Also check the scope’s input: a 1 MΩ input with a long cable forms a low-pass filter that narrows the real bandwidth. Q1. A probe of 10 nW at 795 nm on a silicon photodiode with R = 0.5 A/W gives what photocurrent, and what voltage through 1 MΩ?I = 0.5 × 10⁻⁸ = 5 nA, so V = 5 nA × 1 MΩ = 5 mV. Small, but well above the shot noise; the amplifier and scope noise will decide visibility.
L13.7 Laser safety

L13.7 Laser safety The 795 nm beam is in the near infrared: invisible, but focused by the eye onto the retina like visible light. Because you cannot see it, the blink reflex does not protect you, and the damage is permanent. Beam powers of a few to tens of milliwatts in the experiment generally fall in laser classes 3R or 3B under the international standard (IEC 60825-1) and the corresponding American one (ANSI Z136.1); the exact class depends on power and wavelength-dependent limits, so confirm the classification with your institution’s laser safety officer and follow the local rules. Habits that keep the bench safe Wear eyewear whose optical density at 795 nm is marked on the glasses (OD 6 or more at the working power is typical): the marking must cover the exact wavelength, and the glasses are specific to the laser. Keep all beams in the plane of the table and below eye level when seated or standing. Remove watches and reflective jewellery. Align at low power. Use an IR viewing card or an IR camera, never your eye. Block every unused order and every leakage port with a beam dump; reflections from optics are beams too. Enclose the beam path where possible. Put up warning signs and tell everyone entering when the laser is on. Before changing anything in a beam path, block the beam. After changing it, re-check where every reflection goes.

L13.8 Alignment and measurement routines The reference bench in the simulator is not just a diagram: it is a checklist. Three habits prevent most problems. First, fix the master axis with two mirrors and two irises before adding anything else: centre the beam on both irises by adjusting the mirrors alternately; every optic between them is then on axis. Second, measure each stage: the power after the isolator, the pick-off ratio, the control/probe split, the AOM efficiency (first-order power over input) and the double-pass efficiency, the polarization purity after each PBS, and the power at the cell. Compare each with what the simulator predicted for the same settings; a discrepancy is information. Third, change one thing at a time and write it down: plate angle, RF frequency, temperature, bias current. A logbook is the cheapest instrument in the lab. Reading of the bench

Reading of the bench Left breadboard: laser input and SAS lock. Fibre-coupled laser light (blue PM patch cables with green FC/APC connectors), isolator, steering mirrors, a pick-off, and the saturated-absorption arm with the white 3D-printed reference-cell module (banana jacks and a small board on top). Right breadboard (Thorlabs MB4545/M): the EIT board. Two red-housed AOMs with gold SMA inputs, many waveplates, cubes and lenses, the white EIT-cell module with red heater and coil leads, and a black detector or camera housing at the right edge. Shelf behind the boards: two Thorlabs benchtop controllers, two Rigol generators, two TENMA DC supplies labelled HEATER and COILS, and a Rigol DS1102 oscilloscope at each end of the boards. Assumption about the lock. The two double-pass AOMs shift the beams by +160 MHz, and the SAS arm has no AOM. The simulator treats the lock point as the atomic resonance, which hides that offset. A real bench needs the lock moved by about 160 MHz (for example with an AOM in the SAS arm), and the photograph does not show how this is done.

The EIT cell label: TRT-Rb/Ne-10T-20x75 (Triad Technology Inc.)

The EIT cell label: TRT-Rb/Ne-10T-20x75 (Triad Technology Inc.) The videos of this bench show the label TRT-Rb/Ne-10T-20x75 on the EIT cell, and the maker is Triad Technology Inc. (given by the owner of this guide). The name “TRT-…” is not in Triad’s standard catalogue, which lists cells as TT-RB-75-V-x (natural Rb), TT-RB85-… and TT-RB87-…, in two sizes only: Ø25 × 75 mm Pyrex and Ø19 × 75 mm quartz. Triad says neon and other buffer gases and custom cells are available on request. So the reading below is an interpretation from that naming, not a specification. Part of the label Reading Status TRT a Triad series or order code for a custom cell; not defined in the public catalogue or in the Sacher brochure of Triad cells unknown Rb rubidium. In Triad’s naming plain “RB” is natural rubidium (72 % 85Rb, 28 % 87Rb); isotope cells are written RB85 or RB87 likely natural Ne neon buffer gas clear 10T 10 Torr of neon (the same fill as the cell of the published Zeeman-EIT set-up that our guide follows) likely 20x75 20 mm diameter × 75 mm length (assumed order). Ø20 is not a Triad standard size (their standard cells are Ø25 or Ø19), so probably a custom size likely What it would mean (calculated for this guide, see the Q&A on this label): Long cell. A 75 mm path has three times the optical depth of our 25 mm path at the same temperature. For an optical depth of about 10 on the 87Rb line a natural-Rb cell needs about 62 °C (about 47 °C if it were enriched). The 1.2 W DC heater seen on the shelf (about 2.4 V and 0.5 A) would hold such a cell near 45 to 50 °C, where a natural cell has an optical depth of only about 2 to 4: enough for clear EIT, with less contrast. This is a guess. Natural rubidium works for this line. The nearest 85Rb line is about 1.7 GHz from the 87Rb F = 2 → F′ = 1 line, so 85Rb takes only about 5 to 20 % of the probe (optical depth 0.05 to 0.2) at 45 to 62 °C. The price is the lower 87Rb density (28 %), which the long path makes up for. Neon at 10 Torr broadens the D1 line by about 100 MHz, shifts it by about −11 MHz, and slows the diffusion of the atoms so that their coherence lasts much longer than the time they take to cross the beam. A 75 mm cell needs a long, uniform magnetic field. The coil of our guide (42 turns, 140 mm) would give a field spread of 2.4 % over 75 mm instead of 0.2 % over 25 mm. How well the Spain-style coil does is not known; a broader line is likely.

Cost estimate of this bench (units are public, prices need the group password)

What this bench can do Laser lock to the Rb D1 line. The SAS arm and the reference cell on board 1, with the Thorlabs current and TEC controllers (about 147 mA is a normal 795 nm DFB drive current) and a Rigol generator for the dither, read on a scope. Continuous-wave Zeeman EIT. Control and probe from two AOM arms, opposite circular polarizations, an EIT cell with a heater (about 1.2 W DC) and a solenoid (about 80 mA); linewidth versus control intensity, magnetic field and temperature. Slow light and light storage. The two-channel Rigol generator can drive the probe pulse and switch the control AOM off and on, with the second scope on the probe and the trigger. Field sensing. The Zeeman EIT line moves 1.4 kHz per milligauss, so the bench can double as a magnetometer. Parts the guide’s list does not have: the cat’s-eye lenses in the two AOM arms need a focal length of about 75 mm (80 mm after the AOM, 70 mm to the retro mirror); the control beam expander is f = 30 mm plus f = 100 mm, 130 mm apart. Not possible with what is visible: hyperfine (6.8 GHz) EIT (no microwave source or EOM), single-photon-level detection (no photon counters), and absolute efficiency measurements (no calibrated detection). Laser: 795 nm, invisible

Laser: 795 nm, invisible The DFB label says Class 4. Wear goggles rated for 795 nm, keep every beam in a dump or a tube (D10), and never look along a beam or at a reflection. Build and test the electronics (D3 to D8) with the laser off.

Mains (only D4) The degaussing drive uses a variac on the mains. Build it in a closed, earthed metal box with fuses and cable clamps, and only if you are competent to do mains wiring. The alternative with a function generator needs no mains work.

Magnetism No steel, nickel-plated or magnetic part inside or near the shield: screws, tweezers, connector shells, clips, soldering-iron stands. Test suspect parts with a small compass. Keep magnets, magnetic screwdrivers and phones away from the shield.

Solenoid former and winding

Solenoid former and winding The 50 mG bias field along the beams, inside the shield BOM C07about 8 h + machiningneeds the shield bore The solenoid makes the uniform magnetic field along the beams that splits the Zeeman levels: 50 mG gives a two-photon splitting of 70 kHz (1.4 kHz per mG). The EIT line is only about 7 kHz wide, so the field must be the same everywhere in the cell to a fraction of 0.2 % (0.1 mG, a 140 Hz shift). The design below was computed ring by ring with the exact Biot–Savart formula (checked against a brute-force sum to 10⁻¹²) and gives 0.20 % over the cell. Turns 42 36 at 3.6 mm pitch, plus 3 at 1.8 mm at each end Wire Ø0.50 mm enamelled copper (Ø0.55 mm over the enamel) Field at the centre 3.39 mG/mA free space; calibrate in the shield Current for 50 mG 14.7 mA free-space value Field error over the cell 0.20 % 0.42 % without the end turns Resistance, inductance 0.58 Ω, 16 µH with 0.8 m leads Solenoid (3D model)µ-metal shieldVapour cellFluxgate (D7) Build it in 3D firstOpen the 3D build simulator: 30 steps from the shield check and the compass test, through turning the former, cutting the groove and winding the 42 turns, to the cell stack, the three shield layers, degaussing and calibration. Every part is drawn to scale; each step has its check, and some have a question to answer before you go on.
d1
What the design does

What the design does One helical groove in a plastic tube holds the wire exactly: 36 turns at 3.6 mm pitch in the middle and 3 turns at 1.8 mm pitch at each end. The closer end turns make up for the field that falls off at the ends of a finite coil: the error over the cell drops from 0.42 % to 0.20 %. Four end turns would give more margin. The design just meets the 0.2 % target at the very ends of the 25 mm path (about half of it on average). Four turns at 1.8 mm at each end (a groove 144 mm long, 44 turns) give 0.15 %: use them if you cannot centre the cell to better than 1 mm. Two return wires 180° apart run back along the axis, each carrying half the current. A helix carries a net axial current; a single return wire would add a transverse field of 0.10 mG per mA at the axis, and two wires at 180° cancel it. Plastic only (PEEK, Delrin or printed PETG): any steel or nickel near the shield magnetises it and shifts the field by amounts far larger than 0.1 mG.

Tools

Tools Lathe with a thread-cutting tool, or a CNC lathe or mill, or a 3D printer (the groove is a non-standard 3.6 mm pitch with a 1.8 mm pitch at both ends, so ask the workshop first). Digital calliper (0.01 mm), steel rule kept away from the shield, a winding rig: the former on a rod in two supports, turned by hand, with the wire spool on a friction brake (50 to 100 g pull). Soldering iron 25 to 40 W, multimeter with a 4-wire resistance range if you have one, brass or plastic tweezers, a small compass to test for magnetic parts.

3D-printed former (PETG, Bambu Lab A1, 0.2 mm nozzle)

3D-printed former (PETG, Bambu Lab A1, 0.2 mm nozzle) The former can be printed instead of machined. Print it upright, cable end on the plate: the helix then comes from the Z axis of the printer, which is its most accurate axis, and the upper flank of the groove is made at 45° so it needs no support. At the surface the groove is 1.00 mm wide; the wire seat at the bottom is 0.60 wide and 0.40 deep, as in the drawing. A small slot at the cable end marks 0°, where the helix starts and the leads leave; the notch of the cable-end spacer ring goes over it, and both point up, towards the cable holes of the shield caps. A shallow ring marks the mid-plane. Inside, a channel 10 mm wide and 0.6 mm deep runs along the top of the bore (on the 0° line, over the lead mark) from the cable end to 86 mm, just past the mid-plane: the stem of the cell (D2) slides along it, so the stem has 1.1 mm to spare instead of 0.5 mm, and the bore may print a little undersize. Under the wire seats the wall is still 1.0 mm thick. Both ends of the bore have a 1 mm chamfer. Build steps

Build steps Get the shield data. Ask the maker, or read the drawing, for the innermost bore, the inner length and the end-cap holes: a Ø14 mm beam hole on the axis and a Ø12 mm cable hole 16 mm off the axis, lined up in all three caps at both ends. The beam goes through the beam hole; the coil leads, the cell cables, the fluxgate cable and the degaussing bundle go through the cable holes, so nothing crosses the beam. The former needs a bore of at least Ø46 mm (the former plus 3.45 mm of radial clearance), an inner length of at least 250 mm, and the winding then stays about 55 mm from each end cap. A smaller bore needs a thinner former and a new field calculation, because the winding radius enters directly.Check You have the bore, the length and the hole positions in writing. Make the former. Follow the former drawing. Cut the groove as one right-hand helix, 0.60 wide and 0.40 deep, rounded at the edges (a sharp edge cuts the enamel). Scribe a light ring at the mid-plane and mark the cable end (the end where the leads leave).Check wall 2.0 ± 0.1 mm; ten pitches measure 36.0 ± 0.2 mm; the groove starts and ends 70.2 mm from the mid-plane (140.4 mm long); no burrs. Prepare the wire and the rig. Cut off 5.9 m for the helix with its start lead (0.8 m of lead + 4.98 m of helix + a little spare) and keep the rest of the reel for the two return wires (0.2 m each) and the finish lead (0.8 m). Put the spool on a friction brake so that the wire runs under 50 to 100 g of pull. Handle it only with plastic or brass tools.Check the wire runs without kinks and the enamel is not scraped. Wind the helix. Start at the cable end (z = −70.2 mm). Lay 3 turns at 1.8 mm pitch, then 36 turns at 3.6 mm, then 3 turns at 1.8 mm; the finish is at z = +70.2 mm. Count aloud and mark every tenth turn with a dot of marker on the former.Check exactly 42 turns. The resistance of the helix alone is about 0.44 Ω (4.98 m at 0.0876 Ω/m). Fix the end turns. Put a drop of cyanoacrylate or epoxy on the first and last 3 turns and on every tenth turn. Do not glue the other turns: glue stress on the wire shifts it in the groove.Check no turn can move when you push it with a plastic tool. Lay the two return wires. At the far end, scrape the enamel from the helix end and from one end of each return wire, twist the three together and solder (one joint). Lay the returns along the axis at 90° and 270° (see the winding plan), tape them every 40 mm with polyimide tape, and at the cable end solder them together into the finish lead.Check resistance from start lead to finish lead: 0.58 Ω ± 0.03 (the two returns in parallel add only 0.007 Ω). Twist the leads. Twist the start and finish leads together, about one twist per 20 mm, and solder the plug of D3 (LD OUT). Mark the start lead red.Check no loop of area in the leads: they run as one twisted pair. Check the field outside the shield. Put the former on a plastic stand a metre away from steel, with the fluxgate (D7) at the centre. Apply +10.00 mA, record the reading, apply −10.00 mA and record again. The difference removes the Earth field (about 0.4 G) and the sensor offset.Check B(+10 mA) − B(−10 mA) = 67.8 mG ± 5 % (3.39 mG/mA × 20 mA). Mark the field direction. With the same measurement, note which current polarity gives a field along the beam direction (z, away from the laser) and engrave or label “B+” on the former.Check the label agrees with the fluxgate sign. Install and calibrate in the shield. Push the former into the innermost layer with the cell stack (D2) inside, centre it with the two spacer rings (former slot and ring notch up, towards the cable holes; the ring recesses then face sideways, where the flat degaussing bundle lies) and close the end caps with all cables through the cable hole. The shield rests on the printed cradle with its axis at the 100 mm beam height. After the degauss (D4), put the fluxgate plate (D7) in place of the cell and measure B against I at ±5, ±10 and ±15 mA.Check a straight line B = k·I; use the measured k (a few per cent above 3.39 mG/mA, because the shield pulls the flux in) in every later experiment, not the formula. The fluxgate scale is good to ± 2 %: confirm k with the atoms (the EIT line moves 1.4 kHz per mG).

Mistakes to avoid

Mistakes to avoid Steel tools, steel screws or nickel-plated connector shells near the former or the shield: they magnetise and the field no longer follows the formula. A helix without the two return wires, or with only one: the transverse field is 0.10 mG per mA, 1.5 mG at 14.7 mA. Winding under too much pull: the groove edge cuts the enamel and two turns short together. Different pitch at the ends: the error over the cell rises from 0.20 % to 0.42 %. Loose, untwisted leads that move: the loop area changes and the field at the cell follows. Confirm before you startInnermost shield bore ≥ Ø46 mm, inner length ≥ 250 mm, and end caps with a Ø14 mm beam hole on the axis and a Ø12 mm cable hole 16 mm off the axis, lined up in all three caps at both ends. The BOM line “Ø~70 × 250 mm, 3 layers” gives only the overall size: three layers and two gaps would share the 12 mm of radius between Ø46 and Ø70 (gaps of about 4 mm). Cell dimensions and the stem from the vendor drawing (D2). Who cuts the groove and with which pitch tolerance: the drawing needs ± 0.05 mm per pitch. D2

What the design does

What the design does NTC and not Pt100. The ITC502 resolves 1 Ω on its thermistor range: a Pt100 gives 2.6 K per ohm, a 10 kΩ NTC gives 14 mK per ohm at 65 °C. Foam sleeve and two Delrin tubes hold the temperature with 0.9 to 2.1 W and keep the whole stack on the axis: tube 63 + sleeve 34 + tube 63 = 160 mm, the length of the former. Diode in series with the heater. A resistor cannot cool: when the controller asks for cooling it would reverse the current, which heats again and runs away. The diode lets only one polarity through; its orientation is found with the dummy-load test of D3. Unpaired heater wire is a coil. One unpaired turn of 0.54 A at the end of the heater gives 97 mG at the cell centre, 2000 times what we can accept. That is why the pattern is paired. Is a heater wrapped round the cell safe?Yes, with the current limit set. The heater lies on the barrel only, never on a window, and spreads 1 to 2 W over 68 × 24 mm (about 0.1 W per cm²), so the wire runs only a little warmer than the glass and quartz takes the slow warm-up easily. It works at a few volts (12 Ω, under 0.42 A). The real risk is a runaway, for example if the NTC comes off the glass: the controller then drives the full limit. Set I TEC LIM so that even that stays safe: 0.50 A on the open bench (3.0 W, at most about 84 °C) and 0.33 A inside the closed shield (1.3 W, at most about 84 °C), below the 100 °C rating of the foam and the epoxy. Keep the windows a little warmer than the stem, so rubidium does not condense on them.

If the stem is taller

If the stem is taller The cell must slide into the former after the winding, so the bore sets the tallest stem: bore radius = 12.5 + stem + 0.5 mm. A larger bore means a larger winding radius (the field gets less uniform, a few more end turns fix it) and a larger shield, because the winding must keep its clearance to the innermost layer. Ring model of D1, same 3.6 mm main pitch and 36 main turns: Stem height Former bore / outside Winding radius Field spread over the cell mG per mA (with the extra end turns) Innermost shield bore ≤ 4 mm Ø34 / Ø38 18.9 mm 0.20 % with 3 end turns; 0.15 % with 4 3.40 Ø46 mm ≤ 6 mm Ø38 / Ø42 20.9 mm 0.24 % with 3 end turns; 0.18 % with 4 3.38 Ø50 mm ≤ 10 mm Ø46 / Ø50 24.9 mm 0.33 % with 3 end turns; 0.17 % with 5 3.36 Ø58 mm The first row is the design on this page. A stem pushed through a hole in the winding was also calculated (Biot–Savart on the true helix, wire bent round the hole): in the beam (within 3 mm of the axis) the field spread stays about 0.2 %, but near the glass under the stem it reaches 1 to 4 %; the real problems are that the cell can no longer slide in and the stem tip leaves the heater. So the stem is limited by the bore, not passed through the winding. Estimates on this page: the loss at 65 °C (2.1 W in free air, 0.9 W inside the former and the shield) and the time constants (166 and 379 s) come from a simple model (foam k = 0.05 W/m/K, h = 8 W/m²K, heat capacity 8 J/K). Design for the larger loss; measure your own stack and replace them.

Mistakes to avoid

Mistakes to avoid A heater wound as one coil, or a foil with a return bus along one edge: that is an unpaired turn (97 mG at the cell from 0.54 A). Always run the on-and-off test. A Pt100 on the ITC502: 1 Ω is 2.6 K, so the temperature would step by 2.6 K. No diode: a resistor heater runs away when the controller tries to cool. A cold window: Rb condenses on the coldest glass, and the Rb vapour density follows the temperature of that coldest point. It should be the stem (in its heater gap, a little colder than the barrel), never a window: keep the windows inside the foam sleeve ends, and if Rb droplets appear on a window after a day at temperature, add foam over the window rims. Cutting a slot in the former or the winding for a stem: the wrapped cell could then never slide into the wound former, and a stem that sticks out of the heater becomes the coldest point and lowers the Rb density. Order a short stem instead. Thermistor leads running through the heater field region as a loop: twist them and keep them flat. Confirm before you startThe real cell: diameter, length, window diameter and thickness, and the stem: position and height. The drawings assume Ø25 × 28 mm with a stem at mid-length at most 4 mm high. Real cells have a torch-sealed stem on the side: Thorlabs’ drawing of its Ø19 × 75 mm cell gives a Ø6 mm stem up to 10 mm high and windows Ø21 mm on the Ø19 mm tube; the Precision Glassblowing stock cell shows a short nub. Ask the vendor for a short tip-off. Foam and epoxy: the temperature rating and the absence of iron or nickel in the data sheets. A bought foil heater: ask for the trace layout and accept only a paired or symmetric pattern, then run the on-and-off test. D3

What the design does

What the design does Heater: TEC pins 5, 6, 7 are tied together as “+”, pins 13, 14, 15 as “−” (the manual says always use all three pins), the thermistor on pins 4 and 3. The diode is in the heater + wire. Solenoid: anode pin 8 (polarity CG) and ground pin 3 carry the current. Pins 9 and 6 can sense the voltage at the coil (optional). A link between pins 1 and 5 is the interlock: without it the output does not switch on. Never plug a laser diode into the coil cable. It has no monitor-diode wiring. Label the plug.

Degaussing coil and drive

Degaussing coil and drive Removes the magnetisation that assembly, shocks and the Earth’s field leave in the shield BOM C06about 6 hmains wiring: closed earthed box Opening the shield lets the Earth’s field (about 50 µT) magnetise the inner layers a little; after reassembly a remanent field of 10 to 100 nT remains (Twinleaf). Our line needs less than 20 nT (0.2 mG). Degaussing removes it: drive the layers into saturation with an oscillating field, then bring the amplitude down to zero slowly and smoothly. The coil has to pass through the shield so that the flux circulates round the wall of every layer, and it should be spread round the circumference: a toroidal winding through the bore and back outside in at least three groups. Coil 30 turns 0.5 mm² wire, 24 m, 0.83 Ω Drive ≤ 2 A rms 50 Hz from a variac; variac at about 106 V of 230 V for 2 A Field in the wall 193 A/m peak, outer layer, at 1 A rms (270 A/m at the inner layer) Series resistor 4.7 Ω, 25 W dissipates 18.8 W at 2 A rms Ramp 100 to 300 s longer is better (Twinleaf); about 737 J turned into heat Degaussing coil + variacµ-metal shieldPower supplyMultimeterFluxgate (D7) Mains: read before you buildThe variac is an autotransformer: its output is not isolated from the mains. The 24 V isolating transformer after it is what makes the coil side safe. Build the mains part in a closed, earthed metal box with fuses and cable clamps, and only if you are competent to do mains wiring. If not, use the alternative drive at the end of this part, which needs no mains work.
d4
What the design does

What the design does Toroidal winding. The field in the wall of a layer at radius r is H = N·√2·I / (2π r): 193 A/m peak at 1 A rms in the outer layer. Mu-metal saturates at a few tens of A/m, so 1 A rms is already well above saturation in every layer, and the procedure uses up to 2 A rms. Find the knee, then ramp. Twinleaf: start low and raise the amplitude step by step; saturation shows as the coil current rising sharply above an applied voltage. Then use an amplitude above the knee and ramp down linearly in 100 to 300 s. 50 Hz has a limit. The skin depth in mu-metal at 50 Hz is only about 0.4 mm (relative permeability near 2 × 10⁴), less than the wall of a 1 mm layer. The mains drive works best on thin layers; for thick layers use the low-frequency alternative (1 to 10 Hz).

Build steps

Build steps Measure the shield. Length of the layers, the outer radius, and the cable holes of the end caps (Ø12 mm, 16 mm off the axis, lined up in all three caps). The inner bundle (30 wires of Ø1.3 mm, flat: 39 mm wide, 1.3 mm thick) has to lie in the 3.45 mm gap between the former and the bore, and the round bundle (about Ø8 mm) has to pass the cable holes at both ends; it must never cross the beam hole on the axis. If the holes are smaller, use a thinner wire or fewer turns and raise the current (the ampere-turns matter: 30 turns × 2.8 A peak = 85 A).Check the cable holes are at least Ø12 mm and line up through all three caps. Wind the coil. Cut 24 m of wire and leave 0.8 m for each lead. Pass the wire through the bore, back along the outside in group 1, through the bore again, back in group 2, then group 3, and repeat until there are 30 passes through the bore (10 turns per group).Check 30 wires in the bore, 10 on the outside in each group. Lay and tie the bundles. Lay the 30 inner wires flat against the inner wall, tie them every 50 mm with polyimide tape, and tie the three outside groups to the outer layer at 120° with Velcro, cross-wires 10 mm apart.Check resistance of the coil 0.83 Ω ± 0.05; no wire touches a steel part. Build the drive box. With the cord unplugged: mains live through the 2 A fuse and the switch to the variac IN L; the neutral to IN N; the transformer primary across the variac OUT and COM; the secondary through the 3.15 A fuse, the 4.7 Ω resistor and the ammeter to the two output sockets. Join mains earth to the box, the variac frame and the transformer core.Check earth to box, variac frame and core: below 0.5 Ω; mains to box: above 10 MΩ. Dry test on the bench. Connect the coil in the air, away from the shield, switch on with the variac at zero and raise it slowly.Check the current rises linearly with the setting; 2 A rms at a setting of about 106 V; the resistor is only warm after a minute. Find the knee. With the shield closed and everything inside non-magnetic, raise the variac slowly from zero while you read the ammeter. The knee is where the current starts to rise much faster than the voltage.Check you can write down the variac setting of the knee. Degauss. Go to about 1.5 times the knee (our rule of thumb; Twinleaf only says “high enough to ensure saturation”), at most 2 A rms. Hold 5 seconds, then turn the knob down steadily to zero in 100 to 300 seconds. Do not stop and do not jerk.Check the ammeter falls smoothly to zero. Disconnect. Variac at zero, mains switch off, then unplug the coil from the drive. Twinleaf’s commercial unit disconnects the coil with relays when it is finished, so that no noise couples into the shield.Check the coil is open-circuit. Repeat once and measure. Repeat the degauss, then read the field with the fluxgate plate (D7) or by looking at the atoms (the EIT line against the coil current, reversed once).Check two runs in a row give the same field to ± 0.1 mG.

Mistakes to avoid

Mistakes to avoid Stopping or jerking the knob during the ramp: the last small oscillation leaves the magnetisation behind. Turn it down smoothly to zero. A coil that does not go through the shield: the flux then does not circulate in the wall and the layers are not degaussed. Steel clips, steel screws or a steel table leg close to the shield: they re-magnetise it. Leaving the coil connected to the transformer: it picks up noise. Unplug it after each run. Opening the shield after the degauss: every opening magnetises the layers again. Degauss last, with the shield closed.

Alternative drive without mains wiring

Alternative drive without mains wiring An arbitrary waveform generator makes a sine of 1 to 10 Hz with a slowly decreasing amplitude (for example by amplitude modulation with a ramp), and a DC-coupled power amplifier drives the coil with up to 3 A. The series resistor and the same ammeter are used. An audio amplifier is AC-coupled and can leave a small direct current in the coil, which would magnetise the shield: do not use one. This route also suits thick layers better than 50 Hz. Confirm before you startEnd-cap holes: a Ø14 mm beam hole on the axis, and a Ø12 mm cable hole 16 mm off it, lined up in all three caps at both ends, for the degaussing bundle and the cell cables. Twinleaf’s guide gives no hole size; ask your shield maker, and whether they supply a degaussing coil or port. Layer thickness and number: the skin depth at 50 Hz (about 0.4 mm) against the wall thickness decides whether 50 Hz is enough or the low-frequency drive is needed. Whether the fluxgate sensor tolerates the field of the coil: the data sheet of the FLC 100 does not say. Keep it unpowered during the degauss and check its offset afterwards. D5

What the design does

What the design does Levels. With the synthesizer at +1 dBm the switch (insertion loss 1.3 dB typ at 80 MHz) and the attenuator (1.5 dB typ at 0 dB) leave -1.8 dBm, and the amplifier (gain 29 dB minimum, 32 dB typical; the data sheet gives no maximum) brings it to about +30 dBm, 1.05 W. The amplifier takes at most +10 dBm at its input, and the attenuator sets the working level from 0 to 31.5 dB in 0.5 dB steps. Safe state first. The DIP switches start with all six bits on (31.5 dB). The attenuator is wired in direct mode (latch enable tied high), so its state follows the switches and, at power-up, is whatever they say. Gate polarity. With the TTL input of the switch high, OUT 1 is off and OUT 2 is on (datasheet). The AOM sits on OUT 2, so gate high means RF on, and OUT 1 gets a 50 Ω load. Rails from ±12 V. The ±5 V come from an LM7805 and an LM7905; the +3.0 V and −3.1 V from an LM317 and an LM337 fed from the raw ±12 V, because 5 V − 3 V leaves only 2 V of head-room, which the adjustable regulators do not have.

Mistakes to avoid

Mistakes to avoid An open or shorted amplifier output: the data sheet says an open load can damage it and derates the maximum input by 20 dB. Always have the AOM or a 50 Ω load connected. Powering the amplifier before the bias box, or the synthesizer before the amplifier: use the order bias box, +24 V, synthesizer; and the reverse to switch off. The synthesizer above 0 dBm: 0 dBm already gives about +30 dBm out, and the amplifier takes at most +10 dBm in. DC on an RF line: the switch and the attenuator both require the RF ports to be held at 0 V or DC-blocked. Overheating the DC pins of the attenuator when soldering; or soldering the wrong rail to the wrong pin (P2 Vdd +3 V, P4 Vss −3 V). Mixing the two arms: label them, and keep the 35 kHz difference between 80.000 and 79.965 MHz in the synthesizer, not in the amplifiers. Confirm before you startPart numbers for SMA. The BOM lines R02 and R06 named the BNC models ZHL-1-2W+ and ZFDC-20-4+; they now name the SMA models ZHL-1-2W-S+ and ZFDC-20-4-S+, which the drawings use. Check the connector letters on your order. DC on the RF lines. Check that the SynthHD output and the AOM input are DC-blocked or at 0 V, because the switch and the attenuator require it. The AOM’s RF power: the FAOM-780-80-2-L-T-A-K data sheet says 2 W (+33 dBm) as the maximum; the vendor wrote that the best efficiency is at the highest RF power and that it works in CW. With the attenuator at 0 dB and the synthesizer at +1 dBm the chain gives about +30 dBm (1 W, the typical gain), half the rating: expect about half of the 85 % efficiency curve (an estimate, to measure). Never raise the synthesizer above +2 dBm and read the coupler: stop at +32 dBm. At 2 W for long, put the AOM on a heat sink. The lock offset (decided 14 Oct 2026). Both AOMs work in the −1 order, so the EIT beams sit 160 MHz below the F = 2 → F′ = 1 line the laser is locked to; EIT depends only on the kHz difference of the two arms. No third AOM. Details in the questions and answers (AOM specification). D9

AOM yaw platform and the Bragg set-up

AOM yaw platform and the Bragg set-up A micrometer on an 80 mm lever sets the Bragg angle to 0.1 mrad; then the double pass is aligned BOM M04, O17, O08about 8 hneeds the AOM drawing An AOM diffracts well only when the beam meets the sound fronts at the Bragg angle θB = λf / 2v: 7.57 mrad (0.43°) at 795 nm and 80 MHz, with v = 4.2 mm/µs (the data sheet of the FAOM-780-80-2-L-T-A-K). The acceptance of a 0.9 mm beam is only about 0.9 mrad, so the AOM needs an angular adjustment of about 0.1 mrad about the vertical axis. A micrometer pushing a tail 80 mm from the pivot gives 0.125 mrad per 10 µm division and ±81 mrad of range. After the platform, the double pass is aligned: a quarter-wave plate, the f = 100 mm lens as a cat’s eye, a retro mirror, a razor blade that stops the 0th order, and the polarizing beamsplitter that picks the returned beam. What the design does

What the design does Lever and micrometer. A carrier plate turns on a brass pivot; the micrometer spindle pushes its tail and a spring plunger pushes back, so there is no play. One division (10 µm) at 80 mm is 0.125 mrad, about a fifth of the Bragg angle, so the maximum can be found by hand. Cat’s eye. The lens puts the retro mirror at its focus, so a change of the RF frequency (which changes the deflection angle) does not walk the returning beam. With f = 100 mm the two orders are 1.5 mm apart at the mirror; a razor-blade edge placed between them on a small stage stops the zeroth order. Polarization. The quarter-wave plate is crossed twice, so the returned beam is turned by 90° and the polarizing beamsplitter sends it out of the arm. The two passes through the AOM therefore have crossed polarizations. The vendor of the FAOM did not say which polarization the 85 % is for, so one pass may be the weak one: on arrival measure the single-pass efficiency with the input polarization turned by 90° (a half-wave plate before the AOM). If the second pass is much weaker, the double pass cannot work as drawn: the fallback is a single pass (80 MHz offset in place of 160 MHz, the arms still differ by 35 kHz). Which order. Use the −1 order in both passes (−160 MHz), as decided for the lock offset. Whether a given side of the zeroth order is +1 or −1 depends on the direction of the sound (from the transducer, marked on the AOM drawing) relative to the beam: ask the supplier, or check the sign once on the bench.

Build steps

Build steps Read the AOM drawing. The vendor’s one-page drawing (the same outline on the 1 mm and the 2 mm data sheets) gives the housing as about 41.8 × 25 × 13.5 mm with two Ø4 through holes (12.9 mm from the end), two M2 × 0.4 tapped holes (4 mm deep, 13 mm apart) and an SMA jack at one end; the optical axis is 8.2 mm above the base (vendor end view, 22 Oct 2026). From the unit, check the hole pattern and the height, and find which face is the +1 order side (the drawing does not show it).Check you have the real numbers on paper. Make the plates. Cut the base and the carrier from aluminium, drill the pivot hole (Ø4.1) in the middle of the carrier, the M4 holes for the AOM, and the M6 holes of the base on the 25 mm grid. Deburr.Check the carrier turns without play on the pivot. Fit the micrometer. Clamp the micrometer in its bracket on the base at the top edge so that its spindle touches the tail 80 mm from the pivot; fit the spring plunger on the other side of the tail.Check the spindle and the plunger hold the tail with light force. Mount the AOM. Screw the AOM to the carrier with nylon or brass screws and a thin shim set so that its aperture is at the beam height (100 mm). Plug in the SMA cable with some slack.Check the aperture centre is at 100 mm ± 0.5 mm above the breadboard. Find the first order. Beam about Ø0.9 mm (the FiberPort output; up to about 1.5 mm is fine), collimated, through the middle of the 2 mm aperture. RF at 80 MHz with the attenuator at 16 dB. Turn the micrometer slowly: the first order appears 1.5 mm per 100 mm off the zeroth.Check a bright first-order spot on the IR card. Maximise, then raise the RF. Maximise the first-order power with the micrometer, then lower the attenuator in steps and stop at the plateau.Check single-pass efficiency of about 50 % at 1 W of RF and up to 85 % at 2 W (measure with the power meter). Build the cat’s eye. Put the lens one focal length (100 mm) from the retro mirror, the quarter-wave plate between the AOM and the lens, and the razor blade at the mirror plane between the two foci; set the plate at 45°.Check the first order hits the mirror centre; the blade stops the zeroth order only. Close the double pass. Walk the retro mirror until the returned beam retraces the incoming one through the irises; set the polarizing beamsplitter so that the returned beam leaves through the side port.Check the returned beam is on the output axis; its polarization is turned by 90°. Measure and tune. Measure the double-pass efficiency and trim the plate angle and the RF level. Change the RF by ± 5 MHz.Check the output spot moves by less than 0.1 mm at 1 m (the cat’s-eye property); about 30 % overall at 1 W of RF is expected (more at 2 W). Lock and log. Clamp the micrometer and write the setting on the platform.Check the setting is on the label.

Tests before use Test How Pass Angle resolution micrometer one division a visible change of the first-order power; ≈ 0.125 mrad Single-pass efficiency first-order power / input power at the plateau ≈ 50 % at 1 W of RF, up to 85 % at 2 W Zeroth order blocked IR card behind the blade no light past the blade in the first-order path Return irises on the input path the returned beam passes both irises Frequency tracking change the RF by ± 5 MHz output spot moves < 0.1 mm at 1 m The data sheet of the FAOM-780-80-2-L-T-A-K gives TeO₂ in longitudinal mode, 750 to 860 nm (795 nm typical), 80 MHz with ±20 MHz bandwidth, 4.2 mm/µs, a clear aperture of 3 × 2 mm, RF power 2 W, diffraction efficiency 85 % (the vendor: at the highest RF power), rise time at most 350 ns (about 139 ns for our 0.9 mm beam), 50 Ω, VSWR 1.2:1, deflection 15 mrad (rounded; 15.14 mrad at 795 nm). Mistakes to avoid

Mistakes to avoid Adjusting the tilt (pitch) instead of the yaw: the first order walks up and down and the efficiency stays low. The micrometer must turn the AOM about the vertical axis. A beam bigger than the aperture: the clear aperture is 3 × 2 mm and the 2 mm is the sound width. The FiberPort output (about Ø0.9 mm) fits without loss; keep the beam under about 1.5 mm. The old Ø2 mm collimator beam does not fit: keep the AOM behind the fibre output, or add a reducing telescope. Tightening the clamp of the micrometer with a steel set screw near the cell: use the clamp of the head. Hurrying the warm-up: 1 W of RF warms the crystal, and the efficiency drifts for the first 10 to 15 minutes. The retro mirror not exactly at the focus: the returned beam then depends on the frequency. Confirm before you startThe unit you receive: FAOM-780-80-2-L-T-A-K (chosen on 21 Oct 2026 from the vendor’s two data sheets; test report with the delivery, 12 months of warranty from shipping). Check on arrival: the axis height and hole pattern against the drawing, the efficiency in both polarizations, and the efficiency at 1 W and at the highest RF power. The RF power for full efficiency: 2 W on the data sheet, so our 1 W is half; the vendor was asked for the efficiency at 1 W and did not say at which beam size or polarization the 85 % was measured. The PR01/M dimensions if you use it. D10

Beam dumps and light-tight covers

Beam dumps and light-tight covers Black blocks that absorb every unused beam, and hardboard covers over the AOM arms BOM O12, M05about 6 hlaser safety The bench has 12 beam dumps: 4 for AOM zeroth orders, 1 for the Glan–Taylor reject, 1 for the SAS pump and 6 for PBS leakage ports. The strongest is the zeroth order of the control arm when its AOM is switched off: about 10 mW once the 100 mW of the Yanban is turned down at the source; the dump right after the isolation takes the rest, about 90 mW, and needs a bore that spreads it (a Thorlabs-type beam trap or a deep anodised block, never a thin card). Stray 795 nm light is invisible and it scatters onto the detector. A dump is a black block with a deep bore and a tilted entry, so the beam bounces many times in the matte black wall and dies. Over each AOM arm a hardboard cover keeps room light and draughts out and stray beams in. Build steps Read the cell drawing. Tube and window diameters, length over the windows, window tilt, and the position and height of the fill stem. On a ½-inch post with the M4 screw (head in the counterbore), or with two M6 screws on the breadboard. Post height = beam height − 20 mm = 80 mm.Check the base is level and the cell axis is at 100 mm. Lay in the cell. With gloves, stem up, centred between the saddles; touch only the barrel.Check the cell rests on both pads and does not rock. Fit the straps. One over each saddle; tighten the nylon screws evenly until the strap just meets the saddle top. The 2° wedged windows deviate the beam slightly: steer with the mirrors, not by tilting the holder.Check both beams pass the full cell without clipping the windows. Fit the cover. Mistakes to avoid

Mistakes to avoid Clamping the glass hard: tighten only until the strap meets the saddle. A stem pointing into a saddle or the base: turn the cell so it points straight up. Glossy filament or no cover: room light and reflections reach the SAS photodiode. Using this holder for the EIT cell: that cell is heated to 65 °C inside the shield (D2), where PETG would be too close to its softening point and the cradle does not fit. Build steps

Build steps Measure the cubes. All three edges of two cubes with a calliper. The holder is drawn for 12.7 mm with 0.2 mm clearance per side.Check the cubes are 12.7 ± 0.1 mm; if not, ask for a file with another pocket. Print and test the insert coupon. Press an insert into each of the three holes with a soldering iron at about the PETG printing temperature (230 to 250 °C), straight down, light pressure, until it is flush.Check one hole gives a straight, flush insert that does not turn when an M4 screw is tightened by hand; use that size (the holder file has Ø5.5). Print one holder and one clamp. Remove any strings from the pocket and the ribs.Check the cube drops into the pocket without force and does not rattle; the ribs are straight. Fit the insert. From below, flush with the bottom face of the base.Check the insert is not proud: a proud insert lifts the holder off the post and lets it rock. Screw the holder onto the post. Hand-tight on the M4 stud of a ½-inch post, then set the post in its post holder with the post top 84.65 mm above the breadboard.Check the beam height mark (15.35 mm above the post top) is at 100 mm. Put the cube in. With gloves; touch only the top and bottom faces. Turn it so the coating diagonal reflects towards the side you need (if the cube has a mark for the input face, follow it). Push it lightly into one corner.Check all four faces you use are free and clean. Fit the clamp. Nut into the trap on the underside, nylon screw through it. Clamp on the pillars, two M3 × 12 screws into diagonal pillars, then the nylon screw down until it just touches the cube and a quarter turn more.Check the cube does not move when you push it with a finger; nothing is forced. Align. Rotate the post for the direction of the reflected beam; steer with the mirrors before the cube, not by tilting the holder.Check the transmitted and reflected beams leave through the middle of the open faces. Drift test (before printing the rest). Mark the reflected spot on a wall about 2 m away. Check it again after a day and after gently tapping the post.Check the spot moves less than 0.5 mm (0.25 mrad); then print the other holders.
Mistakes to avoid

Mistakes to avoid Tightening the nylon screw hard: stress in the glass makes it birefringent and lowers the extinction. Finger-tight is enough. A tilted or proud insert: the holder rocks on the post. Glue, tape or fingerprints on an optical face. Using the screw version without removing the stud from the post, or the insert version with the stud removed. Clear or glossy filament next to the beams. Confirm before you startThe cube size and tolerance from the supplier (the pocket is 13.1 mm for a 12.7 mm cube). The insert: length and the hole size its maker recommends (the coupon tests Ø5.3 to Ø5.7). The post stud: it must reach at least 4 mm into the insert; check how far it stands out of your posts. 12

Calculations

Calculations Solenoid field and uniformity: exact ring-by-ring Biot–Savart sum (elliptic integrals), checked against a brute-force sum to 10⁻¹²; the volume is the cell, ρ ≤ 12.5 mm and |z| ≤ 12.5 mm; the shield is not modelled (it raises the field by a few per cent): calibrate in place. Heater and thermal numbers: a lumped estimate with foam k = 0.05 W/m/K, h = 8 W/m²K and a heat capacity of 8 J/K, once for the stack in free air (upper bound of the loss) and once as a series chain through the former, the shield gaps and the outside. They are estimates: measure your own stack. RF levels: the arithmetic of the data-sheet values (typical gain 32 dB, insertion loss 1.3 dB and 1.5 dB); the coupler read-out is Vpp = √(8 · 50 Ω · 10(P − 19.5)/10 / 1000). AOM numbers: θB = λf / 2v with v = 4.2 mm/µs; the saturation power at 795 nm scales with λ² from the 633 nm value (an estimate). All numbers in the text and in the drawings come from the same set of parameters, so they agree with each other. No prices are on this page: costs are kept in the group’s private records. Rubidium-87 EIT & light storage: study guide and bench simulator. Prepared October 2026 for the IMEN quantum photonics programme (Objectives 1–2). Laser safety: 795 nm is invisible near-infrared radiation. Wear appropriate eyewear and follow institutional laser-safety rules. The 3D pictures are schematic and not to scale. Mains and RF work must be done by a competent person.

3Double-pass AOM (cat's eye): the distances that matter RF centre frequency (MHz) Acoustic velocity (mm/µs)TeO₂ longitudinal, G&H 3080-125 drawing Cat's-eye lens f (mm)AC254-100-B (BOM O08) Beam diameter in the AOM (mm) AOM → lens distance d: Mirror offset from the focus δ: RF scan of the probe (± kHz)spec: ±200 kHz around 79.965 MHz Distance from the AOM to the cell (mm) PBS → AOM (mm) Result Value Formula Why d = f and the mirror at f. The ABCD matrix of the unfolded arm (AOM → d → lens → f + δ → mirror → back) has B = 2(f − d) and C = 2δ/f² for small offsets. B = 0 (d = f) means the returning beam comes back through the same point of the AOM whatever the RF frequency; C = 0 (δ = 0) means it comes back collimated. For our ±200 kHz scan B hardly matters (sub-micrometre walk), so the lens-to-mirror distance is the one to get right: put the mirror where the returning beam has the same size far away as the incoming one (or where the 0th and 1st orders are sharpest on a card). A delay τ leaves a relative phase variance 2πΔντ (a Lorentzian, white-frequency-noise laser, as in delayed self-heterodyne theory); the noisy part is spread over about a megahertz, far wider than the kilohertz EIT line, so it only lowers the contrast.
